c.x: what well-rounded means here the base: character and thinking. honesty, curiosity, care for people, and clear reasoning grounded in mathematics, the scientific method and philosophy. ai can generate code; it cannot supply judgement or integrity. see behaviours and the thinking & character tabs. the foundation: shared fundamentals. every engineer needs these: sql, one language well (java or python), linux, docker, networking and the web, git and ci/cd, testing, security basics, and reading logs. breadth across the system. enough of data, services, design, cloud and operations to read the code, follow a design discussion, and find the right person or doc. depth where you choose. real expertise in one or two areas. many engineers on this kind of system go deep in data (bigquery, dbt, pipelines) or platform (cloud, kubernetes, delivery), or both; the shape is sometimes drawn as a t or a y. ai across all of it. you build features on models and use assistants to work faster, with the same discipline as everything else. "know enough" below is the bar for breadth: what any engineer should manage without help. "go deep" is what a specialist in that area owns.

not only for engineers we get one life, and whatever job we do, we can make the journey beautiful. the tabs under thinking & character ( mathematics , science & method , philosophy , being a good human and body, mind & nature ) and the behaviours page are written for engineers, but they hold for anyone: a nurse, a teacher, an accountant, a builder. read them that way. the engineering tabs show what "fundamentals first" looks like in one craft; every craft has its own.

from data to wisdom there is more information within reach today than ever, but information is not understanding. a useful way to think about learning is a ladder of four steps, often called dikw: data: raw facts. a stack trace, a column of numbers, a snippet of code. information: data with meaning. this error happens when that field is empty. knowledge: understanding how and why. the field is empty because the upstream system sends dates in another format. wisdom: knowing what to do, and what not to do. validate at the boundary, and design so this whole kind of error cannot happen again. a search result or an ai answer can hand you information, sometimes even text shaped like knowledge. wisdom only comes from understanding the fundamentals and applying them yourself, again and again. nobody can learn everything; the aim is enough foundations to climb from data to wisdom in whatever you take on. this guide is here to help you climb.

c.h: Fundamentals first: be the site manager, not a vibe coder
c.x: fundamentals first: be the site manager, not a vibe coder ai hands every engineer a bulldozer. a bulldozer on a building site is only safe with a site manager who knows how buildings stand up: the foundations, the materials, the regulations, and what to inspect before anyone moves in. "vibe coding", accepting whatever the model produces because it looks right, is a bulldozer with nobody in charge of the site. it feels fast until the first thing breaks and nobody can say why. on a learn this way: do it by hand once. write the loop, the sql query, the dockerfile, the deploy, the test yourself before asking ai to do it for you. then you can judge its version. use ai as a tutor keep going back to basics: when something surprises you, the gap is almost always in a fundamental, not in the tool. ai raises the floor of what anyone can produce. fundamentals raise the ceiling of what you can be trusted with.

c.h: An engineer who uses AI, not a prompt engineer
c.x: an engineer who uses ai, not a prompt engineer writing a good prompt is one skill among many, and the smallest one. what makes ai work in production is engineering: data: the model is only as good as what you retrieve and feed it. that is sql, pipelines, chunking and freshness, the data tabs of this guide. evaluation: a test set and a score, so a change to the prompt or model is measured, not judged by eye. systems: timeouts, retries, caching, cost limits, logging, and a fallback when the model is down or refuses. security: untrusted text can carry instructions (prompt injection). least-privilege tools, no secrets in prompts, output treated as untrusted input. judgement with assistants: ai-written code gets the same review, tests and doc checks as yours. you stay responsible for what ships. the ai tab covers each of these. a prompt engineer stops at the prompt; a well-rounded engineer ships, measures and operates the whole feature.

c.h: The four levels used on every tab
c.x: the four levels used on every tab 1 foundation can use it with examples and guidance. reads it, runs it, makes small changes safely, and knows when to ask. 2 practitioner works independently. builds and ships features with it, tests them, debugs ordinary problems, follows the team's standards. 3 senior designs with it. makes trade-offs, reviews others' work, handles the hard incidents, and mentors. 4 expert sets direction across teams. knows the internals, writes the standards and blueprints, and leads migrations and decisions. where a well-rounded engineer aims: senior in the one or two areas they go deep in; practitioner in the foundations, testing, security, and the thinking and character tabs; at least foundation everywhere else. expert in one or two areas comes with time and is not expected of everyone. each tab ends with its own level expectations and an "explore further" card of official docs, books and topics to study next.

self-check: the foundations you should be able to do all of these without asking: explain what a query will cost before you run it. read a stack trace or a job log and name the line that failed. say why a service cannot reach another: dns, firewall, or auth. read a terraform plan and spot a destroy or a replace. write a test that fails before your fix and passes after it. roll back a bad deploy. get a shell in a running container and find why it exited. say what a prompt-based feature returns when the model is down, and how you would know.

self-check: ai return validated json from a model instead of parsing free text. build a small eval set and show a change improved the score. explain how retrieved documents could smuggle instructions into a prompt, and how you limit the damage. estimate the monthly cost of a feature from tokens per call and calls per day. reject an ai-suggested change because a test or the docs show it is wrong.

self-check: depth in data design a partitioned, clustered table for a given query pattern. choose between merge, insert_overwrite and microbatch for a dbt model, and explain why. make a dag rerun for one date without duplicating data. find rows a parse silently turned into null, and stop it happening again. explain a bigquery bill from information_schema.jobs.

self-check: depth in platform write the terraform for a cloud run job, its service account, its iam and its schedule. give a service a fixed egress ip and private access to cloud sql. ship a canary revision and move traffic in steps. size memory and cpu for a jvm container and justify the numbers. debug a crashloopbackoff or a "failed to listen on port" from logs alone.

where i started i started as an electronics engineer, moved into computer hardware, and then into software. when i began, it was windows 98, and we booted machines from floppy disks. memory was scarce: we worked with 128 mb of ram, and 256 mb was a luxury. in my first software job, at one of the smallest startups you can imagine, our internet came over a dial-up line. java, as i remember it, was at version 1.1. we could not download the documentation, so we used javap to read a class's methods and worked out the rest. we wrote code in notepad. then we found editplus, wired it to javac and java so we could compile and run from the editor, and the coloured code alone made us feel we had arrived.

learning from the platform up we learned core java, then servlets and applets, and within two years we were building web applications. struts arrived around then: an apache project, founded in may 2000 by craig mcclanahan (started, as i remember it, as a holiday project). hans bergsten's writing on jsp was how many of us learned, and i remember puzzling over the difference between the servlet context and the page context. browsers were not standard. what we now call ajax worked through microsoft's xmlhttp object in internet explorer, so we wrote separate code for internet explorer and netscape. there was no chrome.

the ejb years at one of the biggest retail software companies of the time, we built with enterprise javabeans: stateless session beans to read data, entity beans for the database, and, in booking systems of that era, stateful session beans holding a conversation while the database held the lock on a ticket. xslt generated our screens from data, and uml and model-driven architecture promised that drawing the model would write the code.

c.h: We generated code long before AI
c.x: we generated code long before ai code generation is not new. i used database metadata to generate reusable boilerplate code, much as people use ai today, and xslt templates to turn data into dynamic screens. we generated the javascript for tree structures, pagination and web-based tutorials. the lesson has stayed with me: generating code is easy; understanding what you generate is the job.

the framework years enterprise java was hard. we wrestled with corba and its interface definitions, with two-phase commits for transactions that spanned systems, and later with enterprise service buses. then came spring, which its own documentation says came into being in 2003 as a response to the complexity of the early j2ee specifications. rod johnson had argued for simpler designs in his book expert one-on-one j2ee design and development (wrox), which is still on my shelf; as i remember it, his ideas about plain java objects were at spring's heart, and after vmware took the company over, spring became the standard choice. for many of us, it started with a single core jar. something changed in those years. many engineers learned the frameworks without ever looking at a servlet. the frameworks were good, but the foundations underneath them became invisible.

my bookshelf the first technical book i read cover to cover was hunter and crawford's java servlet programming (o'reilly). my first uml tool was magicdraw. at my first startup, from 2000 to 2002, i could not afford enterprise java with uml (arrington and rayhan, wiley). when i could, in 2003, i bought it for myself, out of love for it: it explained every layer, why dtos exist, and when a plain hash map is enough. seeing why each layer is there is what today's polished frameworks and generated answers rarely show. beside them still: java message service (monson-haefel and chappell), java enterprise best practices , javaserver pages and rod johnson's expert one-on-one j2ee design and development , packed away for a house move and going back on a shelf soon.

what worries me now i do not want to generalise, but i see a newer version of the same pattern. some new engineers go straight to ai without learning the fundamentals, or even the frameworks. they can get an answer, but they cannot always tell whether it is right, or fix it when it breaks. at the same time, much of the simple knowledge people once found on a website, and followed through themselves, is now asked of an ai, one question at a time. every one of those questions costs tokens, energy and data-centre capacity, often for something a page could answer with a click.

why this guide is free i would rather spend my own tokens once, building something useful, than have thousands of people spend theirs asking for the same basics. so this guide is free, and so are the frameworks we build: culvert , penstock , cistern and the others on the home page , all open source. a click is cheaper than a prompt. for what is already known, read the tab. use ai where it earns its keep: complex business logic, building frameworks, investigating a hard problem, or when you genuinely need to move fast. ai is here to stay; use it in the right context. and keep the foundations. they are what let you tell a good answer from one that only looks good. joseph aruja · start with start here

the thread through it all every era wrestled with the same four questions: how do two programs agree on a contract, where does state live, what happens when something fails, and how do we see what went wrong? the answers moved from heavy and agreed in advance, to light and flexible, and back again whenever the light way hurt. the questions never went away.

c.h: Distributed objects: everything agreed in advance
c.x: distributed objects: everything agreed in advance corba , from the object management group, let programs in different languages call each other's objects across a network. you wrote the contract in an interface definition language and generated client stubs and server skeletons before anything could talk. java rmi did the same between java programs, more simply, and java could load the classes it needed over the network. application servers such as weblogic wrapped this with transactions, security and pooling. powerful, and heavy. what it taught us: a remote call is not a local call. it can be slow, fail halfway, or never answer.

c.h: Enterprise JavaBeans: the beans we lived with
c.x: enterprise javabeans: the beans we lived with session beans held business logic. stateless ones served any caller and were pooled, so they suited reads and simple operations. stateful ones kept a conversation with one client across calls. stateful session beans and database locks were how some booking and ticketing systems held a seat while a customer finished: the bean kept the conversation, the database kept the lock. entity beans represented rows in the database, with the container managing how they were loaded and saved. they were heavy and slow to work with, and plain java objects mapped by tools such as hibernate, and later jpa, replaced them. message-driven beans consumed messages from a jms queue or topic, bringing event-driven work inside the application server. what it taught us: the ideas (stateless services, conversations, transactions, messaging) were right; the weight was not. spring, and later ejb itself, kept the ideas and dropped the ceremony.

models, uml and generated screens uml , which appeared in 1997, gave teams one language for drawing systems: class diagrams, sequence diagrams, use cases. grady booch, james rumbaugh and ivar jacobson brought their methods together into it. model-driven architecture , from the object management group, went further: draw the model, then generate the code from it. it worked well for some layers and poorly for the rest. xslt transformed xml into html, so screens could be generated from data and templates rather than written by hand. what it taught us: generating code from a model is powerful when the model is the truth, and painful when people edit the generated code. the same lesson applies to ai-generated code today.

c.h: The early web: stateless by design
c.x: the early web: stateless by design http forgets you between requests. to remember who you were, pages carried state in hidden form fields , in the url (url rewriting) and, increasingly, in cookies. html was standardised in the mid-1990s, but browsers still differed: code checked whether it ran in internet explorer or netscape, and what we now call ajax worked first through microsoft's xmlhttp object. caching mattered because bandwidth was precious on dial-up: browsers and proxies kept copies, and pages said how long a copy stayed fresh. what it taught us: statelessness scales, and every bit of state has to live somewhere on purpose.

pages made on the server cgi scripts started a new process for every request. php began in 1994 as rasmus lerdorf's "personal home page" tools and grew into a language for building web pages on the server. java servlets and jsp ran inside a long-lived server, handling many requests without starting a process each time. struts , an apache project founded in may 2000, brought the model-view-controller pattern to java web applications.

c.h: Runtimes get fast, and get company
c.x: runtimes get fast, and get company java began by interpreting bytecode, which was slow. just-in-time (jit) compilers, which compile the busiest code to machine code while the program runs, made it fast, and the jvm's hotspot became the standard approach. microsoft's c# and .net arrived in the early 2000s with many of the same ideas: a managed runtime, garbage collection and code compiled just in time. what it taught us: a good runtime lets you write simpler code and still go fast, and ideas spread quickly once they work.

c.h: Integration: buses, services and lighter ways
c.x: integration: buses, services and lighter ways soap web services brought back contracts agreed in advance, written in wsdl, with generated clients, much as corba had done. enterprise service buses put routing, transformation and orchestration into one large central product. lighter tools followed. apache camel implemented the patterns from hohpe and woolf's enterprise integration patterns as a library. spring came into being in 2003, by its own account, as a response to the complexity of the early j2ee specifications. what it taught us: one big central hub becomes the bottleneck and the single point of failure.

rest, long journeys, and sagas rest , which roy fielding described in his doctoral dissertation, used the web's own design (resources, urls, standard methods, caching) instead of a custom remote-call layer. without distributed transactions, a long piece of work becomes a journey of steps. if it fails halfway, you undo the completed steps in reverse order, which only works if you recorded every step you took. this idea is old. it was described as the "saga" in a 1987 database paper by hector garcia-molina and kenneth salem, long before microservices made the word popular again. see architecture .

c.h: Microservices, cloud, and seeing what happens
c.x: microservices, cloud, and seeing what happens microservices split systems into small services that each own their data. they brought back every distributed-systems problem at once, now spread across many teams. for years, failures were hard to follow from one service to the next. observability caught up: logs, metrics and traces, and a shared trace context passed with every call (the w3c traceparent header). see observability . the cloud turned servers into something you rent by the minute and declare in code.

the people behind the ideas we remember the famous product launches and forget many of the people whose ideas we use every day. a few worth knowing, and reading: the "gang of four" , erich gamma, richard helm, ralph johnson and john vlissides, wrote design patterns: elements of reusable object-oriented software , which gave us a shared vocabulary: factory, observer, strategy, adapter. martin fowler wrote refactoring (its second edition with kent beck) and patterns of enterprise application architecture , and has explained ideas such as continuous integration and microservices to a generation of engineers. he calls the gang of four's book "the best book ever written on object-oriented design". kent beck developed extreme programming, and test-driven development within it, in the late 1990s. grady booch, james rumbaugh and ivar jacobson created uml. gregor hohpe and bobby woolf wrote enterprise integration patterns . roy fielding described rest. hector garcia-molina and kenneth salem described sagas. and thousands of open-source maintainers whose names most of us never learn, whose work runs in almost everything we build. before you ask an ai to explain a pattern, read the person who named it. the original is usually clearer, and it tells you why. start with fowler on the gang of four , extreme programming and test-driven development .

and now, ai ai can generate the code that each of these eras made us write by hand: the stubs, the boilerplate, the glue. but the four questions have not changed: contracts, state, failure, and seeing what went wrong. people who know this history recognise an old problem in a new form, and do not mistake generated code for understanding. see ai for engineers . dates here are given where we could check them against the project's own record; elsewhere the page speaks in eras rather than years.

c.h: The headline: engaged, not prompting and resting
c.x: the headline: engaged, not prompting and resting ai gives every engineer a bulldozer instead of a shovel . that raises the bar, not lowers it. a well-rounded engineer does not write a prompt, accept whatever comes back, and take the rest of the day off. they decide where the bulldozer goes, prepare the ground, watch it work, check the result against evidence, and fix the road for the next person. the time ai saves is spent on what it cannot do: understanding the problem, testing assumptions, reviewing, and learning. prompting and resting engaged engineering accepts the first answer that looks plausible runs it, tests it, reads it, and checks it against the docs says "the ai wrote it" when it breaks owns every line that ships, whoever typed it uses saved time to do less uses saved time to understand more and improve the system re-explains the same context every day writes it into the repo once so every session and colleague benefits generates a new copy of the same boilerplate builds or extends the shared framework stops learning because the tool "knows" learns faster, because the tool removes the typing, not the thinking

c.h: Learn by doing, not by opinion
c.x: learn by doing, not by opinion be slow to opinion, quick to experiment. before arguing for a tool, pattern or fix, build the smallest thing that tests it: a spike, a benchmark, a query, a prototype. let the result decide. "i ran it on 10,000 real rows and p95 went from 900 ms to 120 ms" ends a debate that opinions cannot. say what you have and have not tried. "i have read about it" and "i have run it in production" are different levels of confidence; name which one you have. change your mind when the evidence does, and say so plainly. hands on the keyboard: read the code, run the command, open the log. second-hand summaries, including an ai's, are a starting point, not a conclusion. write down what you learned so the next person starts from your result, not from zero.

evidence and honesty claims match evidence. "tests pass" means you saw them pass, with the output. a check that could not run is reported as not run. say what you checked in the sentence: "no schedule in the file (searched the whole file)", not "there is no schedule". "cannot see" is not "nothing there". when a source is down, report unknown, never a confident zero. verify state, not proxies: config saying something is enabled is not proof that it is. surface bad news early: a risk raised on day one is a plan; on launch day it is an incident.

ownership you build it, you run it: care what happens after merge: deploys, alerts, users, cost. finish things: small, complete changes over large half-done ones. done means tested, reviewed, deployed and observed. leave the system better: fix the stale doc, the flaky test, the missing alert you tripped over. turn every mistake into a guard: a test, a hook, a rule, so it cannot happen twice. know when to stop: after a few failed attempts at the same problem, step back, write down what you know, and ask, rather than thrashing.

quality habits a failing test before the fix; a passing one after. read the official docs for the version you use before relying on an api. never weaken a check to get to green. review your own diff before asking anyone else to. prefer the simplest design that meets today's need, and write down the trade-off. treat security, privacy and cost as part of "working", not extras.

communication write clearly: pr descriptions that say what changed, why, and how it was verified; design docs others can build from. lead with the answer, then the evidence, then the detail. plain words and real numbers beat adjectives: "40% fewer bytes scanned", not "much faster". ask early and specifically: what you tried, what you saw, what you need. claim before you build: say what you are about to change so others do not duplicate it.

collaboration review generously and honestly: catch real problems, explain why, suggest a fix; skip personal taste. assume good intent; discuss the system, not the person, especially after incidents. teach what you know: pair, document, record the trap you hit. respect decisions once made; reopen them with new evidence, not repeated opinion. make others faster: the best contribution is often a tool, template or fix that removes work for the whole team.

breadth and curiosity learn the layer below and the layer above your own work: the database under your service, the user above your api. follow a request or a row end to end at least once: client, network, service, database, pipeline, warehouse. spend time outside your area of depth: data people learn deploys and on-call; platform people learn sql and modelling. read incidents and postmortems from your own systems and others'. keep a list of things you do not understand yet, and work through it.

attitude, knowledge, adaptability, persistence quality looks like does not look like attitude curious, humble about what you do not know, positive about hard problems, generous with credit defensive about mistakes; "not my job"; cynicism about every change knowledge fundamentals understood deeply enough to reason from them; breadth across the stack; knows where to look and checks the source collecting tool names; answers from memory without checking; depth in one tool only adaptability picks up a new language, cloud or tool when the problem needs it; drops a favourite approach when evidence says so; adjusts to new team practices, including ai "we have always done it this way"; refusing new tools, or chasing every new one persistence (never give up) stays with a hard problem until it is solved or clearly handed over; changes approach after each failed attempt; asks for help with evidence; finishes the last 10% repeating the same failing attempt; quietly abandoning work; declaring victory before the check is green never giving up is not the same as never stopping. after a few failed attempts at the same thing, step back: write down what you tried and what you saw, change the approach, or bring someone in. the goal is never abandoned; the method is changed.

c.h: "I'll learn it", not just "I don't know"
c.x: "i'll learn it", not just "i don't know" when you meet something new, answer with what you will do, honestly. instead of say "i don't know kafka." "i haven't used kafka in production yet. i learn quickly: i'll run it locally this week and come back with what i find." "not my area." "i don't know that part of the system yet. who owns it? i'll read the code and pair with them." bluffing an answer "i'm not sure. i'll check the docs and confirm by end of day." be exact about your current level: honesty about what you have not done is what makes "i learn quickly" believable. follow through: a promise to learn that is kept builds more trust than pretending to know. show the evidence of learning: a lab, a spike, a written summary.

behaviours with ai behaviour looks like does not look like direct the work a clear brief: goal, context, rules, definition of done, what to report "make this better" prepare the ground context files, exact test commands, guardrails, pinned docs in the repo re-explaining the project every session verify runs the tests, reads the diff, checks claims against docs and data trusting confident output own answers for every line that ships "the ai did it" protect no secrets or personal data in prompts; least-privilege tools pasting production credentials into a chat build roads extends frameworks and blueprints; writes codemods generating the same boilerplate again keep learning asks the tool to explain, then confirms by doing shipping code you could not explain stay engaged watches the run, steps in when it drifts, reviews the result prompt, walk away, merge whatever comes back

behaviours by level 1 foundation asks for help with specifics: what was tried and seen tests own changes; reports results honestly reviews ai output line by line before committing writes down what they learn 2 practitioner owns features from design to production and after proves ideas with spikes and measurements before arguing turns repeated mistakes into tests and rules gives useful, kind reviews 3 senior makes the evidence standard for the team ("what did you check?") builds the blueprints and guardrails others use, including for ai agents raises risks early and stops work that is going wrong mentors through pairing and written examples 4 expert shapes culture: blameless learning, honest status, small safe changes changes direction when the evidence says so, publicly multiplies the organisation through platforms, standards and teaching holds the line on quality when deadlines push against it

weekly self-check did every claim i made this week have evidence behind it? did i try something myself before forming an opinion on it? did i review and understand all the ai-written code i shipped? did i leave one thing better than i found it? did i turn a mistake into a guard? did i learn something outside my usual area? did i help someone else get faster?

c.h: Questions to ask in reviews and interviews
c.x: questions to ask in reviews and interviews "how do you know it works?" (looking for evidence, not confidence) "what did you try before deciding?" (looking for experiments) "what would make you change your mind?" "walk me through what the ai produced and why you kept or changed it." "tell me about something you broke and what you changed afterwards." "what happens if this dependency is down?"

set up once machine: a laptop with 16 gb ram is enough for most labs; an old pc or mini pc running linux makes a good always-on lab server. tools: git, docker (or podman), kubectl , kind or k3d , helm, python 3.12+ (3.13+ for lab 5), a jdk 21 or newer, and the gcloud cli. cloud, carefully: new google cloud accounts get free-trial credit, and bigquery has a free sandbox. set a budget alert on day one and delete what you are not using. your lab journal: one git repository with a folder per lab and a readme in each: goal, steps, numbers you measured, what broke and why. this becomes your portfolio. mkdir -p ~/lab && cd ~/lab && git init kind create cluster --name lab # a kubernetes cluster in docker kubectl get nodes

lab 1: microservices on kubernetes repo: googlecloudplatform/microservices-demo (online boutique: about ten services in several languages). kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/googlecloudplatform/microservices-demo/main/release/kubernetes-manifests.yaml kubectl get pods -w kubectl port-forward deploy/frontend 8080:8080 # open http://localhost:8080 then: delete a pod and watch it come back; scale a deployment; set a memory limit too low and read the oomkilled event; break a readiness probe. done when: you can explain, from kubectl describe and events alone, why each thing you broke failed. tabs: kubernetes , microservices .

lab 2: observability stack repo: prometheus-community/helm-charts (kube-prometheus-stack) on the lab 1 cluster; or open-telemetry/opentelemetry-demo with docker compose. helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts helm install monitoring prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack -n monitoring --create-namespace kubectl port-forward -n monitoring svc/monitoring-grafana 3000:80 # or the opentelemetry demo (traces, metrics, logs across many services) git clone https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-demo cd opentelemetry-demo && docker compose up -d then: write one promql alert for an error ratio, make it fire on purpose, and find the failing span in a trace. done when: an alert you wrote fires for a failure you caused, and you traced it to the line of code. tabs: observability , ops tooling .

lab 3: service mesh repo: istio/istio (its samples/bookinfo application) on a kind cluster. # after downloading an istio release and adding istioctl to path istioctl install --set profile=default -y kubectl label namespace default istio-injection=enabled kubectl apply -f samples/bookinfo/platform/kube/bookinfo.yaml istioctl analyze then: turn on strict mtls, split traffic 90/10 between review versions, inject a delay, and write an authorizationpolicy that denies one service. done when: you can produce, then explain, a 403 and a 503 from proxy logs. tab: service mesh .

lab 4: gitops and helm repo: argoproj/argocd-example-apps , with argo cd installed on your cluster. kubectl create namespace argocd kubectl apply -n argocd -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/stable/manifests/install.yaml kubectl port-forward -n argocd svc/argocd-server 8443:443 then: fork the example repo, point an argo cd application at its helm example, change a value in git and watch it roll out; change something by hand in the cluster and watch argo cd report the drift. done when: every change reaches the cluster only through a git commit. tabs: helm charts , devops .

c.h: Lab 5: a data pipeline on your laptop
c.x: lab 5: a data pipeline on your laptop repo: dbt-labs/jaffle_shop_duckdb (dbt's demo project, running on duckdb, no cloud account). git clone https://github.com/dbt-labs/jaffle_shop_duckdb cd jaffle_shop_duckdb python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate # this repo asks for python 3.13+ pip install -r requirements.txt # or: uv sync dbt build # seeds, models and tests dbt docs generate && dbt docs serve then: add an incremental model, a unit test and a test that fails on purpose; load a public dataset of your own (bigquery public datasets or the registry of open data on aws) into duckdb and model it in layers. done when: running the pipeline twice gives identical results, and a bad row is rejected and counted, not silently nulled. tabs: data engineering , dbt , data libraries .

lab 6: orchestrate it repo: apache/airflow , using the official docker compose quick start from the airflow documentation. then: write a dag that runs lab 5's dbt build daily, uses data intervals, retries, and records a run summary; backfill a week; make one day fail and rerun just that day. done when: a rerun of any single day changes nothing else, and a missing run raises an alert. tab: airflow dags .

lab 7: culvert against emulators repo: enrichmeai/culvert . its stack runs against local emulators, so no cloud account is needed. git clone https://github.com/enrichmeai/culvert pip install 'culvert[gcp]' # then follow the repository's docs to start the emulators and run a pipeline then: write a small pipeline against the blobstore and warehouse contracts, run it on the emulators, then read the conformance suite to see what every adapter must guarantee. done when: your pipeline code imports no cloud sdk. tabs: culvert , frameworks vs ai .

lab 8: events with kafka repo: the official apache/kafka docker image, plus a producer and consumer you write. docker run -d --name kafka -p 9092:9092 apache/kafka:latest # pin a version once it works docker exec -it kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh \ --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic order.placed --partitions 3 then: write a consumer that is idempotent, kill it mid-batch, restart it and prove no event was applied twice; add a dead-letter topic for a poison message. done when: you can show consumer lag rising and recovering, and duplicates handled. tab: kafka .

c.h: Lab 9: RAG and an MCP server
c.x: lab 9: rag and an mcp server repos: anthropics/anthropic-quickstarts for starting points, modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk for the server, and the pgvector/pgvector docker image for search. docker run -d --name pg -e postgres_password=pw -p 5432:5432 pgvector/pgvector:pg17 pip install "mcp[cli]" anthropic psycopg then: chunk and embed a small document set, build hybrid search, answer questions with citations, write 30 golden questions and measure recall; wrap lab 5's run records in a read-only mcp server and use it from claude code. done when: your eval score is written down, and the mcp tool says "could not read" when the database is stopped. tabs: rag , mcp .

lab 10: infrastructure as code start: hashicorp's "get started with docker" terraform tutorial (local, free), then a small google cloud project behind a budget alert. then: declare a bucket, a dataset and a cloud run job in terraform; rename a resource with a moved block; import something created by hand; destroy everything at the end. done when: terraform plan shows no changes after apply, and nothing you made is left running. tabs: terraform , cloud run .

lab 11: payments in test mode start: a stripe or razorpay test account. stripe's cli forwards test webhooks to your laptop. stripe login stripe listen --forward-to localhost:8080/webhooks/stripe stripe trigger payment_intent.succeeded then: build order → checkout → signature check → webhook; replay the same webhook twice; simulate a timeout and reconcile. done when: no replay or retry can mark an order paid twice. tab: payment gateways .

lab 12: game day repo: chaos-mesh/chaos-mesh on your kind cluster, or just kubectl delete and tc by hand. then: with a friend, one person breaks something on the lab 1–3 stack without saying what; the other detects, mitigates and writes a blameless postmortem using the template on the sre tab. done when: the postmortem has at least one action that adds a guard (an alert, a test, a limit). tab: sre .

rules for lab work predict, then run: write down what you expect before each experiment; the gap is the lesson. break it on purpose: every lab includes a failure you cause and explain. measure: record latency, cost, row counts or recovery time, not impressions. use ai as the bulldozer, not the driver: let it scaffold and explain, then verify everything it claims by running it. pin versions once something works, and note them in the readme so the lab is repeatable. clean up: kind delete cluster , docker compose down -v , terraform destroy , and check the cloud billing page. write it up: a short post or readme per lab. teaching what you learned is the final test that you learned it.

everyday mathematics, for everyone you do not need advanced maths to live well, but a handful of ideas protect your money, your health and your judgement every day. none of this is about being "good at maths"; it is about not being fooled, including by yourself.

percentages and money up and down are not equal. a price that rises 50% and then falls 50% ends at 75% of where it started (1.5 × 0.5 = 0.75). down 20% then up 20% leaves you at 96%. percent is not percentage points. an interest rate going from 2% to 3% is up one percentage point, but up 50% in percent terms. watch which one you are being told. quick mental maths: 10% is the number with the decimal point moved one place; 5% is half of that; 15% is the two added; 1% is the point moved two places. compare unit prices, per kilo or per litre, not pack prices. the bigger pack is not always cheaper. small amounts add up: £4 a day is £1,460 a year, and £14,600 over ten years, before any interest.

c.h: Compound growth, for you and against you
c.x: compound growth, for you and against you compounding means growth on growth. £1,000 at 5% a year becomes about £1,629 after ten years if the interest is reinvested, against £1,500 if it is not. the rule of 72: divide 72 by the yearly rate to estimate how many years it takes to double. at 6% about 12 years (exactly 11.9); at 3% about 24 (exactly 23.4). debt compounds too. a balance at 24% a year, left unpaid, doubles in about 3 years (72 ÷ 24). pay off the most expensive debt first. inflation is compounding in reverse: at 3% a year, money left in a drawer loses half its buying power in about 24 years. start early. time does more of the work than the amount: small, regular savings started young often end up ahead of larger ones started late.

risk and chance relative risk can mislead. "doubles your risk" may mean going from 1 in 10,000 to 2 in 10,000. always ask: out of how many? base rates matter. suppose a test is 99% accurate both ways and the condition affects 1 person in 1,000. of everyone who tests positive, only about 9% actually have it, because the false positives from the 999 healthy people outnumber the true ones. expected value: multiply each outcome by its chance and add them up. lotteries and most casino games pay back less than you put in, on average, by design. streaks happen by chance. a coin that lands heads five times is not "due" tails; each toss is independent.

reading numbers in the news average or median? a few very high incomes pull the average up; the median (the middle value) is often a fairer picture of a typical person. correlation is not causation. two things rising together may share a third cause, or be coincidence. check the chart's axis. a bar chart whose axis does not start at zero can make a small difference look huge. ask for the size of the sample and who was asked. a survey of 20 people, or only of fans, says little. feel the size of big numbers: a million seconds is about 11.6 days; a billion seconds is about 31.7 years. the engineering cards below build on the same ideas: medians and percentiles, probability and estimation.

c.h: Complexity you should feel, not just know
c.x: complexity you should feel, not just know growth example n = 1 million o(1) hash table lookup 1 step o(log n) binary search, b-tree index lookup about 20 steps o(n) scanning a list or a table 1 million steps o(n log n) good sorting about 20 million steps o(n²) nested loops, a self-join without an index 1 trillion steps o(2ⁿ) trying every subset never finishes at a million items, the jump from o(n log n) to o(n²) is a factor of about 50,000: a fraction of a second becomes many minutes, and at larger sizes, days. an n+1 query pattern and a nested loop over two big lists are the usual ways it sneaks in.

numbers computers get "wrong" >>> 0.1 + 0.2 0.30000000000000004 # binary floating point cannot store 0.1 exactly >>> 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 false >>> from decimal import decimal >>> decimal("0.1") + decimal("0.2") == decimal("0.3") true # decimal arithmetic for money // java: int overflow wraps around silently int max = integer.max_value; // 2,147,483,647 max + 1 // -2,147,483,648 math.addexact(max, 1) // throws arithmeticexception instead use decimal types or integer minor units (paise, cents) for money. never compare floats with == ; compare within a tolerance. know your integer sizes: a signed 32-bit counter of milliseconds overflows in under 25 days (unsigned, about 50).

statistics that keep you honest median and percentiles beat the mean for skewed data such as latency: one slow request moves the mean, not the median. variance matters: two systems with the same average can have very different worst cases. sample size: a difference seen in 20 requests may be noise; in 20,000 it is more likely real. base rates (bayes): a 99% accurate alert for a problem that happens 1 time in 10,000 fires falsely about 100 times for each real case. correlation is not causation: two metrics rising together may share a cause. survivorship: you only see the systems, users or rows that made it through. multiple comparisons: test twenty things at 95% confidence and you should expect about one "significant" result by chance.

probability in operations # availability of dependencies in series multiplies 0.999 * 0.999 * 0.999 # ≈ 0.997 (three 99.9% services) # chance at least one of n calls is slow, if each is slow with p = 0.01 1 - (1 - 0.01) ** 100 # ≈ 0.63 # birthday paradox: random 32-bit ids collide sooner than you think import math math.sqrt(2 ** 32) * 1.1774 # ≈ 77,000 ids for a 50% chance of a collision the birthday bound is why ids are 128-bit uuids or longer, and why hash collisions are planned for, not assumed away.

linear algebra behind embeddings an embedding is a vector: a list of numbers that places a text in a space where similar meanings are close. dot product: multiply matching entries and add them up. cosine similarity = dot product ÷ (length of a × length of b): 1 means same direction, 0 unrelated. for vectors already normalised to length 1, cosine similarity and dot product are the same, which is why many vector databases normalise first. import numpy as np a, b = np.array([0.2, 0.8, 0.1]), np.array([0.25, 0.7, 0.0]) cosine = a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b)) # ≈ 0.99: very similar

c.h: Estimation: powers of two and orders of magnitude
c.x: estimation: powers of two and orders of magnitude power approx. name 2¹⁰ 1 thousand kib 2²⁰ 1 million mib 2³⁰ 1 billion gib 2⁴⁰ 1 trillion tib round to one significant figure and multiply orders of magnitude: being within 2× is good enough to choose a design. check units at every step; most estimation errors are unit errors. sanity-check against something known: a day is about 10⁵ seconds; a year about 3 × 10⁷.

c.h: How to learn it as an adult engineer
c.x: how to learn it as an adult engineer learn each topic through a problem you have: statistics through your latency data, graphs through your dag, linear algebra through your embeddings. work examples by hand on paper , then check them in python. use ai as a patient tutor: ask for an explanation, then for exercises, then check your answers yourself. fifteen minutes a day beats a weekend once a year.

the method, applied to engineering step in science in engineering observe notice something unexplained p95 latency doubled after tuesday's deploy hypothesise a testable explanation the new query skips the index on store_id predict what must be true if the hypothesis holds explain will show a sequential scan; reverting the query will restore latency test an experiment that could prove it wrong run explain analyze ; try the fix on a copy with production-sized data conclude accept, reject or refine sequential scan confirmed; index added; p95 back to normal, measured share publish so others can check pr description with before/after numbers; a regression test the key word is falsifiable : a good hypothesis says what result would prove it wrong. "something in the network is flaky" cannot be tested; "the timeouts happen only on calls through the nat gateway" can.

c.h: What science can answer, and what it cannot settle alone
c.x: what science can answer, and what it cannot settle alone science is the best method we have for questions about what is true of the world and how it works: questions an observation or an experiment could answer. keep it for those, and keep a balance. trying to find every answer in science is the same mistake as trying to find every answer in a religion, or in any single tradition: one tool treated as the whole toolbox. what is, and how it works. does this index make the query faster? does this drug lower blood pressure? observation, measurement and experiment answer these: this is science's home ground. what we ought to do. should we collect this data at all? is this model fair to the people it scores? ethics, law and judgement answer these, informed by evidence about what the consequences will be. what matters, and why. what makes work worth doing? what gives a life meaning? people find these answers in philosophy, faith, tradition, art, relationships and their own experience. an "is" does not give an "ought" on its own. david hume noticed that arguments slide from what is the case to what should be done without saying how. data tells you what users do, not what you should build for them. metrics guide; values decide. science rests on assumptions it does not prove by its own method: that nature behaves regularly, that instruments and senses are roughly reliable, that results are reported honestly. they are good assumptions, and they are still assumptions. treating science as the answer to every question has a name, scientism . it is a philosophical position, not a scientific finding. people disagree about how far the domains overlap. stephen jay gould argued that science and religion answer different questions ("non-overlapping magisteria"); others argue they do overlap. you do not need to settle it to work well with people of every view. respect people whose answers differ from yours. many careful scientists hold a religious faith and many hold none. a team works best when what is measurable is measured, and what is not is discussed with humility. use each kind of knowledge for the questions it can answer, and be honest about where every one of them runs out, including your own favourite.

debugging as an experiment reproduce first. a bug you cannot reproduce is a bug you cannot prove you fixed. change one variable at a time, or you will not know which change mattered. bisect: halve the search space each step ( git bisect , removing half the input, disabling half the config). write down each hypothesis and its result, including the ones that failed. they narrow the search. prefer evidence that could surprise you: look at the raw log, the packet, the row, not a summary that agrees with your guess. stop when the evidence explains everything, not when you have a plausible story.

measurement accuracy vs precision: a clock that is consistently 5 minutes fast is precise but not accurate. know your instrument: what it measures, its resolution, what it misses, and what it reports when it cannot measure. units on every number. "latency 200" means nothing. error bars: run a benchmark several times and report the spread, not one lucky run. baseline first: measure before the change, in the same conditions, or the comparison is meaningless. the observer effect: profilers, debug logging and tracing change what they measure. account for it.

experiments with data and users control group: compare against something that did not get the change, at the same time. randomise who gets which variant, so other differences average out. decide the metric and sample size before you look, or you will find what you hoped for (p-hacking). confounders: a feature launched in the same week as a holiday cannot be judged on that week alone. reproducibility: pin data versions, code versions and random seeds so someone else gets the same answer.

biases that fool engineers bias looks like confirmation bias only looking for logs that support your theory anchoring sticking to the first estimate or cause you heard availability blaming the cause of the last incident because it is fresh survivorship studying only the services that did not fail sunk cost continuing a failing approach because of time already spent automation bias trusting a tool's output, including an ai's, over contrary evidence overconfidence "it works on my machine" as proof

how computers physically work cpu: executes instructions in cycles; modern cores run billions per second and work on several instructions at once. memory hierarchy: registers, then cpu caches (l1, l2, l3), then ram, then ssd, then network. each step is roughly 10–1,000 times slower than the one before. code that reads memory in order is far faster than code that jumps around. storage: ssds read randomly far faster than spinning disks, but sequential reads are still fastest. networks: limited by the speed of light; a round trip across a continent cannot be faster than tens of milliseconds. energy and heat: compute has a physical cost, which is also a cost in money and carbon. these physical limits explain most performance rules on the performance and system design tabs.

reading research and technical papers first pass (minutes): title, abstract, introduction, headings, conclusions. decide if it is worth more time. second pass (an hour): figures, tables, the main argument; note what you do not understand. third pass (hours): recreate the work in your head or in code; challenge every assumption. ask of any claim: what was measured, on what data, compared with what, and could the result be explained another way?

levels: what to expect 1 foundation reproduce a bug before fixing it change one thing at a time and measure before and after write down hypotheses and results while debugging 2 practitioner debug systematically with falsifiable hypotheses and bisection run fair benchmarks with baselines and error bars spot common biases in your own reasoning 3 senior design controlled experiments and a/b tests correctly read papers critically and apply their results with care teach the method through how you run investigations 4 expert build a culture of evidence and experiment across the organisation lead research-style work with rigour and reproducibility judge competing claims across fields each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

epistemology: how do you know? knowledge needs justification: a belief that turns out true by luck is not knowledge. "the tests passed" is justified only if you saw them run. sources differ in reliability: the running system beats the config, the config beats the docs, the docs beat memory, memory beats rumour. absence of evidence is evidence of absence only if you looked properly. say how thoroughly you looked. calibration: match your confidence to your evidence, and say how sure you are. testimony, including an ai's answer or a colleague's summary, is a reason to check, not a replacement for checking. different questions need different methods: experiments settle what is true of the world; ethics, judgement and tradition speak to what we should do and what matters. see what science can answer, and what it cannot settle alone .

reasoning well kind shape engineering example deduction if the premises are true, the conclusion must be "every write goes through this function; it validates input; so every write is validated." induction generalising from observations "it failed on every run with a null date; nulls probably cause it." abduction the best explanation for what you see "latency rose right after the deploy; the deploy is the most likely cause." only deduction is certain, and only if the premises are. induction and abduction give hypotheses to test, which is where the scientific method takes over.

fallacies in technical debates appeal to authority: "big company uses it, so it is right for us." bandwagon: "everyone is moving to x." false dilemma: "either we rewrite everything or we live with it." straw man: arguing against a weaker version of a colleague's proposal. ad hominem: judging the idea by who proposed it. post hoc: "it broke after my change, so my change broke it." maybe, but test it. appeal to novelty or tradition: new is not better, old is not proven.

useful razors and principles occam's razor: prefer the explanation or design with the fewest assumptions. hanlon's razor: do not assume malice where a mistake explains it. most broken things are accidents. chesterton's fence: do not remove something until you know why it was put there. first principles: reason from what is known to be true rather than from analogy and habit. inversion: ask how this could fail, then prevent that. goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. tests written to raise coverage, not to catch bugs, are an example.

systems thinking feedback loops: reinforcing loops amplify (retries cause load, load causes timeouts, timeouts cause retries); balancing loops stabilise (autoscaling). second-order effects: ask "and then what?" a cache speeds reads, and then serves stale data, and then someone acts on it. delays in a system cause overshoot: scaling decisions based on old metrics oscillate. the structure produces the behaviour: repeated incidents point to a system to change, not a person to blame. leverage points: small changes in rules, incentives and information flows often matter more than large changes in parameters.

why big organisations move slowly their processes are scar tissue. most approvals, reviews and controls exist because something went wrong once. each one made sense; together they slow everything down. more people, many more conversations. ten people have 45 possible pairs to keep in step; a hundred have 4,950. agreement gets expensive. blame is lopsided. a change that fails is noticed and blamed; a chance that was missed is rarely noticed at all. so people learn that "no" is safer than "yes". today's customers pull hard. clayton christensen's the innovator's dilemma (1997) showed how successful companies, by doing what their best customers ask, can miss the new thing that replaces them. the system mirrors the organisation. conway's law (melvin conway, 1968): a system's design copies the communication structure of the organisation that built it, so changing one often means changing the other. some slowness is care. a bank or a hospital that changes something wrongly hurts millions of people. slow is sometimes the right speed. what helps: small teams that own their area, decisions made close to the work, and telling reversible decisions (move fast) from one-way doors (take care). amazon's 2015 shareholder letter calls these "two-way" and "one-way" doors.

c.h: Why people find it hard to change
c.x: why people find it hard to change habits save effort. the brain turns what we repeat into habit, so it needs little thought. changing means thinking hard again about things that used to be easy. skill becomes identity. after years in one technology or one way of working, "i am the person who knows x" is part of who you are. change can feel like losing that, and becoming a beginner again. losses feel bigger than gains. kahneman and tversky's research showed people weigh a loss more heavily than an equal gain, so what we might lose looms larger than what we might win. we prefer what we have: status quo bias. and the more we have invested in a path, the harder it is to leave it, even when we should (the sunk-cost trap). old scars: people who lived through a change that went badly remember it, and they are not wrong to. what helps: explain why, start with a small experiment, make it safe to be a beginner, let people shape the change, and value the experience they bring to it. the brain keeps learning at any age (see body, mind & nature ); change is hard, not impossible. be patient with others, and honest with yourself about your own habits.

c.h: Why every decision has people for it and against it
c.x: why every decision has people for it and against it for every option we choose, some people will find it right and some will find it wrong. usually that is not because one side is foolish. it is because they stand in different places. they see different things: the person on call sees the risk, the product owner sees the customer waiting, finance sees the cost, the new joiner sees what nobody questions any more. they pay different prices. every option has a cost, and it falls on someone. a choice that is cheap for one team is extra work, or risk, for another. they value different things: speed or safety, simplicity or flexibility, today or next year. these are trade-offs, not right and wrong answers. so two honest, sensible people can disagree. assume good faith first. what to do about it: say the trade-offs out loud, name who pays the cost, and listen hardest to the people who disagree, because they often see the risk you missed. then decide, write down why (an architecture decision record is one way), and agree when you will look again. once a decision is made, commit to making it work, even if you argued against it: amazon calls this "disagree and commit". aim for decisions people understand, not decisions everyone likes.

c.h: Ethics: what we owe users and society
c.x: ethics: what we owe users and society lens asks in an engineering decision consequences what outcomes does this cause, for whom? who is harmed if this model is wrong, and how badly? duties and rights what rules and rights apply, regardless of outcome? do we have consent to use this data? can users delete it? virtue what would a person of good character do? would i be comfortable explaining this design to the people it affects? fairness are burdens and benefits shared justly? does this work as well for users with disabilities, in other languages, on cheaper phones? professional codes (acm, ieee) put the public good, honesty, and avoiding harm first. ai raises the stakes: automated decisions at scale, opaque reasoning, and content that can mislead. build in human review where harm is possible. you may be asked to build something wrong. raise it, explain the harm, propose an alternative, and know where your line is.

stoic habits for hard days separate what you control from what you do not: you control your response to an incident, not that it happened. expect setbacks: plan for failure, so it is a known path, not a shock. judge actions, not outcomes alone: a good decision can turn out badly; learn from it without self-blame. daily review: what went well, what to do differently, what you learned.

c.h: Socratic questions for reviews and design
c.x: socratic questions for reviews and design what exactly do you mean by…? how do we know that is true? what are we assuming? what would change your mind? what is the strongest argument against this? what follows if we are wrong? asked with curiosity, these improve the work. asked to win, they damage trust.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation ask "how do we know?" before accepting a claim recognise common fallacies in debates know the professional codes of ethics exist and what they ask 2 practitioner reason clearly with deduction, induction and abduction use razors and principles (occam, chesterton, goodhart) in decisions raise ethical concerns about a feature constructively 3 senior apply systems thinking to recurring problems and incentives weigh ethical trade-offs in designs with several lenses lead discussions with socratic questions that improve the work 4 expert shape organisational values, incentives and ethical standards advise on ai ethics and societal impact model wise judgement under uncertainty each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

core qualities, in practice quality looks like at work honesty saying "i broke it", "i don't know yet", "this estimate was wrong" early and plainly integrity doing the right thing when nobody would notice: the test you could skip, the shortcut with user data kindness reviewing code without contempt; helping a struggling colleague; patience with beginners humility assuming you might be wrong; learning from juniors and from mistakes; sharing credit respect listening fully, valuing different backgrounds and roles, respecting people's time gratitude thanking people specifically for what they did responsibility owning outcomes, keeping promises, finishing what you start generosity teaching, mentoring, documenting, contributing back to open source and the community

psychological safety teams do their best work when people can ask questions, admit mistakes and disagree without fear. google's study of its own teams (project aristotle) found it was the most important factor in team effectiveness. admit your own mistakes first; it makes it safe for others. thank people for raising problems, even when the timing is bad. ask quieter people for their view. criticise the work and the system, never the person. keep blameless postmortems genuinely blameless.

feedback, given and received situation, behaviour, impact: "in yesterday's review (situation) you rewrote asha's query without explaining (behaviour); she didn't learn why and felt sidelined (impact)." be specific and timely; praise in public, correct in private. receive feedback with "thank you" first, questions second, defence never. ask for feedback regularly, not just at review time.

conflict and disagreement assume good intent; most conflict is about unclear goals or information. restate the other view until they agree you understood it. find the shared goal, then disagree about the route. use data and small experiments to settle technical disagreements. disagree and commit: once decided, support the decision fully, or reopen it openly with new evidence. apologise well: name what you did, its effect, and what you will do differently, with no "but".

care for users and society build for everyone: accessibility, other languages, slow networks, older devices. treat user data as if it were your family's. be honest in what the product claims; never ship dark patterns that trick people. think about who could be harmed, not only who benefits. consider the environmental cost of compute you do not need.

care for yourself sustainable pace: long hours produce bugs, poor decisions and burnout. the who recognises burnout as an occupational phenomenon resulting from chronic workplace stress. sleep, movement, breaks: they are part of doing good work, not a reward for finishing it. boundaries: be reachable when on call; be off when you are off. ask for help early, technical or personal. life outside work: family, friends, interests and rest make you a better engineer and a happier person.

c.h: Run your day, or the day runs you
c.x: run your day, or the day runs you if you do not decide how your day starts, the inbox, the chat and whatever is on fire will decide for you. a small routine you keep every day is how you take the day back. move your body, every day. it does not matter what: a walk, a run, yoga, cycling, a swim, push-ups in the kitchen, dancing, playing with your children. the best exercise is the one you will actually do tomorrow. start small enough to keep. twenty minutes you look forward to becomes a habit; an hour you dread is easy to skip. build the habit first, then make it harder. anchor it to something you already do: after the first coffee, before you open the laptop, at lunch. a habit tied to a moment survives busy days. get up from the desk during the day too. stand, stretch, walk while you talk through a problem: a bug that will not give way at the desk often does on a walk. protect the basics around it: a regular time to sleep and wake, food that is not only snacks, and a few minutes with no screen. miss a day, not two. life will break the routine; just start again the next day, without guilt and without making up for it. discipline in small things carries into the work: the engineer who keeps a daily habit is the one who keeps the tests green and the runbook current. if you have a health condition, check with a doctor what kind of movement suits you.

mentoring and lifting others explain the why, not just the what. let people struggle a little before rescuing; then help them reflect. give stretch work with support. credit people by name for their work, especially when they are not in the room. remember who helped you, and pass it on.

a short daily check was i honest today, including about my mistakes? did i help someone, and thank someone? did i listen more than i spoke in at least one conversation? did i do work i would be proud to have the users see? did i move my body, and look after my own health?

levels: what to expect 1 foundation be honest about mistakes and what you do not know thank people specifically; review kindly look after your health and ask for help early 2 practitioner give and receive feedback well handle disagreement with respect and evidence build for all users, including accessibility 3 senior create psychological safety in your team mentor others and share credit generously raise ethical concerns and stand by them 4 expert shape a humane, inclusive culture across the organisation lead with integrity under pressure give back to the wider community each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

c.h: One life: make the journey beautiful
c.x: one life: make the journey beautiful your job is part of your life, not all of it. the habits on this page help whatever work you do, and they help most in the parts of life that are not work at all. notice the good things, however small: a conversation, a problem solved, a walk, a meal shared. noticing is a habit, and it can be practised. spend time on what you will be glad of later: the people you love, your health, learning, making something, helping someone. be kind to yourself as well as others. you will have bad days. a bad day is a day, not a verdict on you.

c.h: Your nervous system, in plain words
c.x: your nervous system, in plain words the central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord. the peripheral nervous system is the network of nerves that carries signals between them and the rest of the body. the autonomic nervous system runs what you do not think about: heartbeat, breathing, digestion. it has two main branches that balance each other. sympathetic: "fight or flight". heart faster, breathing quicker, muscles ready, digestion paused. useful in a real emergency. parasympathetic: "rest and digest". heart slower, breathing deeper, digestion and repair. this is where recovery happens. both are normal. the aim is not to switch one off, but to move between them, and not to stay stuck in alarm.

c.h: Stress: an alarm that should switch off
c.x: stress: an alarm that should switch off your body cannot tell a deadline from a danger. a page at 2am, a tense meeting, an angry message: each can start the same stress response, with adrenaline and cortisol. short bursts are fine, and can sharpen you. the harm comes when the alarm never switches off: sleep, mood, focus and health all suffer. notice your signals: a tight jaw or shoulders, shallow breathing, short temper, waking at night thinking about work. slow your breathing, with the out-breath longer than the in-breath. breathing is one of the few parts of the autonomic system you can change on purpose, and many people find a few slow breaths calming. move, sleep, and talk to someone. if stress or low mood lasts for weeks, speak to a doctor or a professional. asking for help is a strength.

c.h: Sleep is part of the work
c.x: sleep is part of the work sleep is when the brain consolidates what you learned during the day. cutting sleep to learn more works against you. most adults need at least seven hours, as the major health bodies advise. needs vary; how you feel during the day is a good guide. keep regular times for sleeping and waking, even at weekends where you can. your body clock likes routine. get daylight in the morning and dim the lights and screens in the evening. light is the main signal that sets your body clock. watch late caffeine. its effects can last for hours after the last cup. on-call nights are real costs. plan recovery after them, as you would after any hard physical shift.

your brain keeps changing the brain changes with what you do. learning and practice strengthen connections between neurons throughout life. this is called neuroplasticity, and it is why "i will learn it" is true at any age. spread practice out. studying in several shorter sessions over days is remembered better than one long cram. this is the spacing effect. test yourself rather than rereading. recalling something from memory strengthens it more than looking at it again. learn by doing. building the thing, breaking it and fixing it engages far more of you than watching someone else do it.

attention is a limited resource focus tires, like a muscle. plan your hardest thinking for the time of day you are sharpest. every interruption has a cost: getting back into a hard problem takes time. turn off notifications you do not need, and batch messages. work in blocks, then take a real break: stand up, look away from the screen, step outside. one thing at a time. switching between tasks feels productive and usually is not.

c.h: Look after the body you work in
c.x: look after the body you work in rest your eyes. eye-care bodies suggest the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look at something about 20 feet (6 metres) away for 20 seconds. remember to blink. change position often. no single posture is perfect for hours; the best posture is the next one. set the screen at eye level and keep your wrists relaxed. move every day (see being a good human ): it helps your heart, your mood, your sleep and your thinking. drink water, eat real food, and do not let the day run on snacks and caffeine. protect your hearing: keep headphones at a moderate volume. listen to pain. wrist, neck or back pain that keeps coming back is a signal to change something, and to see a professional.

mother nature we are part of nature, not visitors to it. the air, water, food and climate that every job depends on come from it, and we are the only ones who can look after it. go outside. time in green and blue spaces (parks, woods, rivers, the sea) is linked in research with better wellbeing. a walk outside is one of the cheapest good things you can do for yourself. nature is the original systems engineer. ecosystems run on feedback loops, recycle everything, spread risk through diversity and redundancy, and grow within limits. those are good lessons for any system you build. learn from its designs. engineers call this biomimicry: velcro came from burdock burrs catching on a dog's fur, and the nose of japan's 500 series shinkansen was shaped after a kingfisher's beak to reduce noise in tunnels. notice the seasons. energy, light and mood change through the year. planning with them, rather than against them, is kinder to people.

c.h: Care for the planet in your work
c.x: care for the planet in your work computing uses real energy and water. every server, model and stored copy has a footprint, even when nobody looks at it. turn off what you do not use: idle machines, forgotten environments, old snapshots, data nobody reads. it saves money and energy together. right-size: pick the smallest machine and the simplest design that does the job, and scale to zero where you can. choose cleaner regions where you have the choice. cloud providers publish how much of each region's electricity comes from carbon-free sources. use ai where it helps, not by reflex. a large model is a heavy tool; a query, a script or a small model is often enough. none of this is about guilt. it is about being a good guest on a planet we share, in the same spirit as being a good colleague.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain fight-or-flight and rest-and-digest in plain words keep regular sleep, daily movement and real breaks notice your own stress signals 2 practitioner plan hard thinking for your best hours; protect focus recover after on-call and crunch periods switch off idle resources you own 3 senior set a sustainable pace and humane on-call for a team spot burnout signals in others and act early design systems that are lean in energy and cost 4 expert shape a culture where health and rest are normal make sustainability part of architecture decisions model a full life, not only a full calendar each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

permissions & users ls -l f # -rwxr-x--- 1 app app ... owner / group / others chmod 640 f # rw- r-- --- (r=4 w=2 x=1) chmod u+x run.sh chmod -r g+rx dir/ # x: execute only on dirs chown app:app f; chown -r 1001:1001 /data id; whoami; groups sudo -u app ./run.sh sudo useradd -r -s /usr/sbin/nologin app # service account, no login umask # default permission mask private keys must not be readable by group or others ( 600 or 400 ), or ssh refuses them. a directory needs x to be entered and r to be listed.

safe bash scripts #!/usr/bin/env bash set -euo pipefail # stop on error, unset var, or failed pipe stage ifs=$'\n\t' usage() { echo "usage: $0 <env> <date>" >&2; exit 2; } [[ $# -eq 2 ]] || usage env="$1"; date="$2" [[ "$env" =~ ^(dev|prod)$ ]] || { echo "bad env: $env" >&2; exit 2; } tmp="$(mktemp -d)" trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' exit # always clean up log() { printf '%s %s\n' "$(date -u +%ft%tz)" "$*" >&2; } for f in data/*.csv; do [[ -e "$f" ]] || continue # glob matched nothing log "loading $f" done # capture an exit code without dying under set -e if ! out="$(some_command 2>&1)"; then log "failed: $out"; exit 1 fi # shellcheck script.sh ← run it quote every variable ( "$f" ). unquoted values split on spaces and expand globs.
