dns record means a / aaaa name → ipv4 / ipv6 cname name → another name (not allowed at the zone apex) mx mail servers for the domain txt free text: domain verification, spf, dkim ns / soa which servers are authoritative for the zone srv host + port for a service ptr ip → name (reverse lookup) caa which cas may issue certificates dig shop.example.com a +short dig example.com ns dig +trace example.com # follow delegation from the root dig @8.8.8.8 example.com # ask a specific resolver nslookup example.com ttl is how long resolvers cache an answer. lower it a day before a planned change, not at the moment of it.

http & tls status classes: 2xx ok, 3xx redirect, 4xx your request is wrong (401 no/invalid credentials, 403 authenticated but not allowed, 404 missing, 429 rate limited), 5xx the server failed (502 bad gateway, 503 unavailable, 504 upstream timeout). http/1.1 one request at a time per connection; http/2 multiplexes streams on one tcp connection (grpc uses it); http/3 runs over quic on udp. tls proves the server's identity with a certificate chain to a trusted root, then encrypts. sni sends the hostname so one ip can serve many certificates. mtls : the client also presents a certificate. common inside service meshes. a proxy that terminates tls can read and route on the request; one that passes it through (l4) cannot. openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com </dev/null \ | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates curl -vi https://example.com # handshake, headers curl -o /dev/null -s -w 'dns %{time_namelookup} connect %{time_connect} tls %{time_appconnect} ttfb %{time_starttransfer} total %{time_total}\n' https://example.com

troubleshooting commands ping -c 3 10.0.0.5 # icmp reachability (often blocked; not proof) nc -vz db.internal 5432 # is the tcp port open? traceroute -n host / mtr host # where packets stop curl -v http://svc:8080/health # app-level answer ss -tulpn # what is listening locally ip addr; ip route # my addresses and routes cat /etc/resolv.conf # which resolver am i using getent hosts db.internal # resolve the way apps do sudo tcpdump -i any -nn port 5432 -c 20 # see packets

"cannot connect": read the error could not resolve host / nxdomain: dns. wrong name, wrong resolver, or a private zone not visible from here. connection refused: the host answered but nothing listens on that port, or the app binds to 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0 . connection timed out: packets are dropped. firewall, security group, missing route, or no nat for egress. tls / certificate error: name mismatch, expired certificate, missing intermediate, or a corporate proxy re-signing traffic. 403 from a proxy or website: first suspect your own egress (datacentre ip, proxy policy) before blaming the far side. works locally, fails in the cloud: compare egress path, dns resolver and credentials, not code.

nat, proxies, load balancers nat lets private hosts reach the internet through a shared public ip. inbound connections are not possible through it. forward proxy acts for clients going out (egress control, allowlists). reverse proxy acts for servers taking traffic in (nginx, envoy, cloud lbs). load balancer health checks decide which backends get traffic. a failing check looks like a 502/503 to clients. stateful firewalls allow the reply to an allowed connection automatically; you write rules for the initiating direction only. bastion / iap tunnel reaches private hosts without giving them public ips.

gcp networking map piece what it does vpc global private network. subnets are regional and carry the ip ranges. firewall rules / policies stateful allow/deny, ingress or egress, targeted by network tag or service account. default: deny ingress, allow egress. cloud nat outbound internet for vms, gke nodes and cloud run (with vpc egress) that have no public ip. gives a fixed egress ip to allowlist. private google access lets private-only hosts reach google apis (bigquery, gcs) without a public ip. private service connect / private services access private ips for managed services such as cloud sql, reachable only from the vpc. direct vpc egress / serverless vpc access connector connects cloud run and cloud functions to private ips in the vpc. cloud load balancing global external http(s) (l7), regional internal, and network (l4) load balancers. managed certificates. cloud armor waf and ip allow/deny in front of an external http(s) load balancer. cloud dns public and private zones; private zones resolve only inside chosen vpcs. vpc service controls a perimeter around google apis so data cannot be copied out to another project. gcloud compute networks list gcloud compute networks subnets list --network=default gcloud compute firewall-rules list --format="table(name,direction,sourceranges.list(),allowed[].map().firewall_rule().list(),targettags.list())" gcloud compute routers nats list --router=my-router --region=asia-south1 gcloud compute ssh vm-1 --tunnel-through-iap # no public ip needed

c.h: What happens when you open a URL
c.x: what happens when you open a url parse the url and check the browser cache, including a cached hsts rule that forces https. dns resolves the host name to an ip address (browser cache → os → resolver → authoritative servers). connect: tcp handshake (or quic over udp for http/3), then the tls handshake proves the server's identity and agrees keys. http request with method, path, headers and cookies, usually reaching a cdn or load balancer first. server side: load balancer → reverse proxy → application → database or cache → response. http response : status, headers (caching, cookies, security), and the body (html, json, images). render: parse html into the dom, css into the cssom, run javascript, lay out, paint, and fetch the sub-resources the page references. after load: javascript calls apis ( fetch ), updates the page, and may open websockets or server-sent events. every step can fail or be slow. browser devtools (network tab: timing, headers, initiator) shows which.

anatomy of a url https://shop.example.com:443/v1/orders/123?store=1_05&page=2#items └─┬─┘ └──────┬───────┘└┬─┘└─────┬──────┘└───────┬────────┘└─┬──┘ scheme host port path query fragment origin = scheme + host + port. it is the browser's security boundary. path names the resource; query parameters filter or modify it. fragment ( #… ) never reaches the server; the browser uses it to scroll or route. encoding: special characters are percent-encoded ( space → %20 , + in a query can mean a space). encode parameters with a library, not by hand.

http request and response get /v1/orders/123 http/1.1 host: shop.example.com accept: application/json accept-encoding: br, gzip authorization: bearer eyj… if-none-match: "a1b2c3" http/1.1 200 ok content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8 content-encoding: br cache-control: private, max-age=60 etag: "a1b2c3" strict-transport-security: max-age=31536000; includesubdomains {"id":"123","order_ref":"ord-2024-000123", …} content negotiation: accept / content-type for format, accept-language for language, accept-encoding for compression. compression: brotli or gzip for text; never for already-compressed images or video. mime types tell the browser what it received; a wrong one breaks scripts or opens security holes.

status codes you will see code means 200 / 201 / 204 ok / created / ok with no body 301 / 308 moved permanently (308 keeps the method) 302 / 307 temporary redirect (307 keeps the method) 304 not modified: use your cached copy 400 malformed or invalid request 401 not authenticated (missing or bad credentials) 403 authenticated but not allowed 404 / 410 not found / gone for good 409 / 422 conflict / valid syntax but semantically invalid 429 too many requests; see retry-after 500 server error 502 / 503 / 504 bad gateway / unavailable / gateway timeout (usually a proxy talking to a sick backend)

cookies, sessions and tokens http is stateless. state across requests comes from cookies or tokens the client sends each time. cookie : set by set-cookie , sent back automatically to the same site. flags that matter: secure (https only), httponly (javascript cannot read it), samesite=lax|strict|none (whether it goes on cross-site requests), domain , path , max-age . server session: the cookie holds a random id; data lives on the server (or redis). easy to revoke. token (jwt): the client sends authorization: bearer … ; the server validates it without a lookup. harder to revoke; keep it short-lived. see oauth & oidc . browser storage: localstorage and sessionstorage are readable by any script on the page, so never keep secrets there; indexeddb for larger client data.

same-origin policy and cors by default, a script on https://app.example.com cannot read responses from another origin such as https://api.example.com . cors lets the api opt in with response headers: access-control-allow-origin: https://app.example.com . preflight: for non-simple requests (custom headers, json bodies, put/delete) the browser first sends options and checks access-control-allow-methods and -headers . credentials (cookies) cross-origin need access-control-allow-credentials: true and an exact origin, never * . cors protects users in browsers; it is not server-side access control. curl ignores it. serving the app and api from the same origin (e.g. /api on the same host) avoids cors entirely.

caching on the web header effect cache-control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable cache everywhere for a year; for fingerprinted assets like app.3f2a9c.js cache-control: private, max-age=60 only the user's browser may cache, for 60 s cache-control: no-cache may store, but must revalidate before each use cache-control: no-store never store (sensitive data) etag + if-none-match revalidate cheaply; server answers 304 if unchanged vary: accept-encoding cache separate copies per header value layers: browser cache → cdn → reverse proxy → application cache → database. fingerprint static files so you can cache them forever and still deploy changes instantly.

rendering models model how good for trade-offs server-side rendering (classic) server returns full html per request content sites, seo, simple apps full page reloads; server does the work single-page app (spa) browser loads js once, renders and routes on the client, calls json apis rich interactive tools (react, vue, angular) slower first load, seo effort, more client code ssr + hydration server renders html, then js takes over on the client fast first paint with interactivity (next.js, nuxt) complexity; double rendering work static site generation (ssg) html built at deploy time, served from a cdn docs, marketing, blogs content changes need a rebuild progressive web app (pwa) web app with a manifest and service worker for offline and install app-like experiences without an app store platform differences, caching complexity native wrapper web app inside a native shell (capacitor, cordova) store presence and device apis from one codebase native build and signing still required

how the browser renders html parsed into the dom ; css into the cssom . combined into a render tree; layout computes sizes and positions; paint draws pixels; composite layers them. render-blocking resources (css, synchronous scripts in <head> ) delay the first paint. use defer or type="module" for scripts. javascript runs on one main thread; long tasks block input. move heavy work to web workers.

performance: core web vitals metric measures good lcp (largest contentful paint) when the main content appears ≤ 2.5 s inp (interaction to next paint) how quickly the page responds to input ≤ 200 ms cls (cumulative layout shift) how much the layout jumps ≤ 0.1 serve from a cdn; compress; cache fingerprinted assets. send less javascript; split bundles by route; lazy-load below-the-fold images. size images correctly; use modern formats (webp, avif) and give width and height to avoid shifts. measure with lighthouse in the lab and real-user data in the field.

web security essentials https everywhere plus hsts , so browsers never fall back to http. xss (cross-site scripting): untrusted data rendered as html runs as script. escape output (frameworks do it by default), avoid innerhtml with user data, and add a content-security-policy . csrf : another site makes the user's browser send a cookie-authenticated request. use samesite cookies and csrf tokens for cookie-based sessions. clickjacking : your page framed invisibly. use frame-ancestors in csp. mixed content : http resources on an https page are blocked or warned. subresource integrity ( integrity= ) for scripts from cdns. more on the security tab. content-security-policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; frame-ancestors 'none' x-content-type-options: nosniff referrer-policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin

accessibility basics semantic html first: <button> , <nav> , <main> , headings in order, <label> for every input. keyboard: everything usable with tab, enter and space; visible focus outlines. text alternatives: alt on meaningful images; empty alt="" on decorative ones. contrast: at least 4.5:1 for normal text (wcag aa). aria only when html has no native element for the job. test with a screen reader and automated checks (axe, lighthouse); they catch different things.

servers on the web web server / reverse proxy (nginx, envoy): tls, static files, compression, routing to apps. application server : runs your code (spring boot with tomcat or netty, quarkus with vert.x, gunicorn or uvicorn for python). cdn : caches content near users and absorbs traffic spikes and attacks. real-time : websockets (two-way) and server-sent events (server to browser, simpler, works over http). http versions : http/1.1 (one request at a time per connection), http/2 (multiplexed streams), http/3 (over quic, better on lossy networks).

devtools habits network: status, timing waterfall, request and response headers, "disable cache", throttling, "copy as curl". console: javascript errors and cors failures, which say exactly which header is missing. application: cookies with their flags, storage, service workers. performance and lighthouse: long tasks, layout shifts, core web vitals. elements: live dom and css, accessibility tree.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain what happens from typing a url to seeing a page read requests, responses, headers and status codes in devtools know what cookies, sessions and cors are 2 practitioner set caching, cookie and security headers correctly debug cors, redirects, mixed content and caching problems choose a rendering model for a feature 3 senior design front-end delivery: cdn, caching, rendering, performance budgets lead web security (csp, session design) and accessibility for a product diagnose core web vitals problems with field data 4 expert set web platform standards across products know the http, tls and browser specs in depth lead large front-end architecture and performance programmes each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

mental model image: a read-only stack of layers plus metadata (entrypoint, env, user). built from a dockerfile, named registry/repo:tag , pinned exactly by @sha256:digest . container: a running process from an image, with its own filesystem layer, network and process namespace. not a vm: it shares the host kernel. layer cache: each instruction is a layer. a change invalidates that layer and every one after it, so put what changes least first. volume: storage that outlives the container. anything written elsewhere disappears with it. tag vs digest: a tag can be moved to a new image; a digest cannot. deploy by digest or by an immutable tag such as the commit sha.

everyday commands docker build -t api:dev . docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 -e app_profile=local api:dev docker run -d --name db -e postgres_password=pw -p 5433:5432 postgres:16 docker ps -a docker logs -f --tail=100 db docker exec -it db psql -u postgres docker stop db && docker rm db docker images docker image inspect api:dev --format '{{.config.user}} {{.size}}' docker history api:dev # layer sizes docker inspect db --format '{{.state.exitcode}} {{.state.oomkilled}}' docker stats # live cpu and memory docker tag api:dev asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/apps/api:3f2a9c1 gcloud auth configure-docker asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev docker push asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/apps/api:3f2a9c1 docker system df # what uses disk docker system prune # stopped containers, dangling images docker builder prune # build cache

a good dockerfile # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 from python:3.12-slim as base env pythonunbuffered=1 pythondontwritebytecode=1 workdir /app # dependencies first: cached until requirements change copy requirements.txt . run --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip pip install -r requirements.txt # then the code, which changes often copy src/ ./src/ run useradd --uid 1001 --no-create-home app user 1001 expose 8080 entrypoint ["python", "-m", "src.main"] # .dockerignore: keeps the build context small and secrets out .git .venv __pycache__/ *.pyc .env node_modules/ target/ build/

multi-stage builds # build with the full toolchain, ship only the result from eclipse-temurin:21-jdk as build workdir /src copy gradle/ gradle/ copy gradlew settings.gradle.kts build.gradle.kts ./ run ./gradlew dependencies --no-daemon # cache dependencies copy src/ src/ run ./gradlew bootjar --no-daemon -x test from gcr.io/distroless/java21-debian13 # no shell, no package manager copy --from=build /src/build/libs/app.jar /app.jar user nonroot entrypoint ["java", "-xx:maxrampercentage=75", "-jar", "/app.jar"] # build one stage only docker build --target build -t api:build . distroless images have no shell, which makes them smaller and safer but harder to debug. keep a -debug variant or use an ephemeral debug container.

instructions that trip people up entrypoint vs cmd : entrypoint is the program; cmd supplies default arguments that docker run image … replaces. exec form ["java","-jar","app.jar"] runs your process as pid 1 so it receives sigterm . shell form java -jar app.jar wraps it in /bin/sh , which may not forward signals. copy over add : add also unpacks archives and fetches urls, which surprises people. arg vs env : arg exists only at build time; env persists into the running container. neither is a safe place for secrets: use run --mount=type=secret . one run per logical step, cleaning up in the same command: apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* . pin base images to a version ( python:3.12-slim ) or a digest, never latest .

docker compose for local stacks # compose.yaml services: db: image: postgres:16 environment: postgres_password: pw postgres_db: shop ports: ["${db_port:-5433}:5432"] volumes: [dbdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data] healthcheck: test: ["cmd-shell", "pg_isready -u postgres"] interval: 5s retries: 10 api: build: . ports: ["${app_port:-8080}:8080"] environment: db_host: db # service name is the hostname depends_on: db: { condition: service_healthy } volumes: dbdata: docker compose up -d --build docker compose logs -f api docker compose exec db psql -u postgres shop docker compose down # keep volumes docker compose down -v # also delete volumes (data gone) docker compose -p wt2 up -d # second copy with its own project name

multi-platform & build secrets # apple silicon builds arm64 by default; cloud run and most servers need amd64 docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64 -t registry/api:3f2a9c1 --push . docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t registry/api:3f2a9c1 --push . docker image inspect api:dev --format '{{.os}}/{{.architecture}}' # secret available during one run, never stored in a layer docker build --secret id=pip_token,env=pip_token . run --mount=type=secret,id=pip_token \ pip_index_url="https://__token__:$(cat /run/secrets/pip_token)@pypi.example.com/simple" \ pip install -r requirements.txt

debugging containers symptom check exits immediately docker logs ; docker inspect … .state.exitcode . 137 = killed (often oom), 139 = segfault, 1 = app error, 127 = command not found. "exec format error" wrong cpu architecture: rebuild with --platform linux/amd64 . port works inside, not from host app binds to 127.0.0.1; bind 0.0.0.0. or a missing -p host:container . cannot reach another container use the service name on a shared network, not localhost . permission denied on a volume container user's uid does not own the host directory. image is huge docker history ; move build tools to a build stage; add a .dockerignore . build ignores code change cached layer: check copy order, or --no-cache once. docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh api:dev # look inside the image docker run --rm -it --network container:db nicolaka/netshoot # debug its network

image security run as a non-root user ( user 1001 ). start from a minimal base (slim, distroless, or alpine where musl is fine). fewer packages, fewer cves. scan images in ci: trivy image registry/api:tag , or artifact registry's built-in scanning. never bake secrets into an image or a layer; anyone who can pull it can read them with docker history or by unpacking layers. rebuild regularly so base-image security fixes reach you. generate an sbom ( docker buildx build --sbom=true or syft ) so you can answer "are we affected?" quickly.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation build, run, stop and inspect containers read a dockerfile and explain each instruction use docker compose for a local stack 2 practitioner write small multi-stage dockerfiles with good layer caching run as non-root; keep secrets out of layers build for linux/amd64; debug exit codes and oom kills 3 senior set image standards: base images, scanning, sboms, signing optimise image size and startup time for cloud run or kubernetes design local development environments for a team 4 expert own the organisation's container supply chain understand the oci image and runtime specs choose and govern registries, build systems and policies each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

c.h: Practice schema used on this tab
c.x: practice schema used on this tab orders(order_id string, order_ref string, store_id string, order_date date, order_year int64, items array<string>, raw_date string, _landed_at timestamp) stores(store_id string, name string, state string) practise for free in the bigquery sandbox (no billing account needed) against bigquery-public-data , for example bigquery-public-data.stackoverflow.posts_questions or bigquery-public-data.new_york_taxi_trips . always dry-run first and select only the columns you need.

c.h: The order SQL really runs in
c.x: the order sql really runs in from and join : build the row set where : filter rows group by : form groups aggregates computed having : filter groups window functions computed qualify : filter on window results select expressions, then distinct order by limit this explains most errors: you cannot use a window function in where (it does not exist yet; use qualify ), and where cannot filter on an aggregate (use having ).

c.h: Write it so it reads top to bottom
c.x: write it so it reads top to bottom with landed as ( -- 1. narrow the input early select order_id, store_id, order_date from `p.analytics.orders` where order_date between '2024-01-01' and '2024-12-31' ), per_store as ( -- 2. aggregate at one grain select store_id, count(*) as n from landed group by store_id ) select c.name, coalesce(p.n, 0) as n -- 3. join for labels last from `p.ref.stores` as c left join per_store as p using (store_id) order by n desc; one cte per step, named for what it holds. state each cte's grain in a comment when it is not obvious. filter and aggregate before joining wide tables.

c.h: NULL: the source of quiet bugs
c.x: null: the source of quiet bugs null = null is null, not true. use is null , or a is not distinct from b to compare nullable values. count(*) counts rows; count(col) skips nulls. avg , sum , min ignore nulls too. x not in (subquery) returns no rows if the subquery yields a single null. use not exists . where status != 'x' drops rows where status is null. sum of no rows is null, not 0: wrap in coalesce(…, 0) . safe_cast and safe.parse_date turn bad input into null. count those nulls, or the failure is invisible. select count(*) as total_rows, count(order_date) as with_date, countif(raw_date is not null and order_date is null) as failed_parse from `p.analytics.orders`;

joins without surprises know the grain of both sides before joining. joining one-to-many multiplies rows; a sum afterwards is inflated (fan-out). aggregate first, then join when you need totals from two child tables. a filter on the right table in where turns a left join into an inner join. put it in on . check row counts before and after each join while developing. -- wrong: stores with no 2024 orders disappear select c.store_id, count(o.order_id) n from stores c left join orders o using (store_id) where o.order_year = 2024 group by 1; -- right: the filter belongs to the join select c.store_id, count(o.order_id) n from stores c left join orders o on o.store_id = c.store_id and o.order_year = 2024 group by 1; -- did my join fan out? keys should be unique on the "one" side select store_id, count(*) from stores group by 1 having count(*) > 1;

semi-joins and anti-joins -- semi-join: stores that have at least one order (no duplicates) select * from stores c where exists (select 1 from orders o where o.store_id = c.store_id); -- anti-join: stores with no order select * from stores c where not exists (select 1 from orders o where o.store_id = c.store_id); -- same anti-join with left join select c.* from stores c left join orders o using (store_id) where o.store_id is null; -- set operations (columns by position) select order_ref from a except distinct select order_ref from b; -- in a, not in b select order_ref from a intersect distinct select order_ref from b; select order_ref from a union all select order_ref from b; -- keeps duplicates, cheaper

aggregation toolkit select store_id, count(*) as n, count(distinct order_ref) as orders_n, countif(order_date is null) as undated, safe_divide(countif(order_date is null), count(*)) as undated_share, min(order_date) as first_d, max(order_date) as last_d, any_value(order_ref having max order_date) as latest_order_ref, -- value at the max string_agg(distinct cast(order_year as string), ',' order by cast(order_year as string)) as years, approx_quantiles(date_diff(date(_landed_at), order_date, day), 100)[offset(50)] as median_lag_days, logical_and(order_date is not null) as all_dated from `p.analytics.orders` group by all; -- groups by every non-aggregated column -- subtotals in one pass select state, store_id, count(*) n from orders join stores using (store_id) group by rollup (state, store_id); -- per store, per state, grand total

window functions, properly a window function computes a value for each row from a set of related rows, without collapsing them . three parts: partition by (which rows are related), order by (their sequence), and the frame (which of them count for this row). select store_id, d, n, row_number() over w_date as rn, -- 1,2,3 no ties rank() over (partition by store_id order by n desc) as rnk, -- 1,1,3 dense_rank() over (partition by store_id order by n desc) as drnk,-- 1,1,2 lag(n) over w_date as prev_day, lead(n) over w_date as next_day, sum(n) over (partition by store_id order by d rows between unbounded preceding and current row) as running_total, avg(n) over (partition by store_id order by d rows between 6 preceding and current row) as avg_7_rows, avg(n) over (partition by store_id order by unix_date(d) range between 6 preceding and current row) as avg_7_days, n / sum(n) over (partition by store_id) as share_of_store, first_value(d) over w_date as first_day, last_value(d) over (w_date rows between unbounded preceding and unbounded following) as last_day from daily window w_date as (partition by store_id order by d); rows vs range: rows 6 preceding means six rows back, even if days are missing. range on a numeric day number means six calendar days back. fill gaps with a date spine or use range. default frame trap: with order by and no frame, the frame ends at the current row, so last_value returns the current row. give an explicit frame. ties: row_number picks arbitrarily among ties. add a tie-breaker column to order by so results are repeatable.

pattern: top n per group -- 3 most recent orders per store select store_id, order_ref, order_date from `p.analytics.orders` where order_date is not null qualify row_number() over ( partition by store_id order by order_date desc, order_id -- tie-breaker ) <= 3; use rank instead of row_number if ties should all be included. if bigquery complains that qualify needs a where , group by or having clause, add where true .

pattern: deduplicate -- find duplicates first: never dedupe blind select order_ref, count(*) as copies, count(distinct _landed_at) as loads from `p.raw.orders` group by order_ref having count(*) > 1 order by copies desc limit 20; -- keep the latest copy of each key select * from `p.raw.orders` qualify row_number() over (partition by order_ref order by _landed_at desc) = 1; -- exact duplicate rows only select distinct * except (_run_id) from t; -- distinct * fails on array columns

c.h: Pattern: date spine and missing days
c.x: pattern: date spine and missing days with days as ( select d from unnest(generate_date_array('2025-01-01', '2025-03-31')) as d ), grid as ( -- every store × every day select c.store_id, days.d from `p.ref.stores` c cross join days ), actual as ( select store_id, order_date as d, count(*) as n from `p.analytics.orders` where order_date between '2025-01-01' and '2025-03-31' group by 1, 2 ) select g.store_id, g.d, coalesce(a.n, 0) as n from grid g left join actual a using (store_id, d) order by 1, 2; without the spine, days with zero rows simply do not appear, and averages and lags are computed over the wrong set.

pattern: gaps and islands -- streaks of consecutive days on which a store took orders with d as ( select distinct store_id, order_date from `p.analytics.orders` where order_date is not null ), tagged as ( select *, date_sub(order_date, interval row_number() over (partition by store_id order by order_date) day ) as island -- constant within a run of consecutive days from d ) select store_id, min(order_date) as start_d, max(order_date) as end_d, count(*) as days from tagged group by store_id, island order by days desc; the trick: a date minus its row number stays the same while dates are consecutive and jumps at each gap.

pattern: change vs previous period with yearly as ( select store_id, order_year, count(*) as n from `p.analytics.orders` group by all ) select * from ( select *, lag(n) over (partition by store_id order by order_year) as prev_n from yearly ) where safe_divide(n - prev_n, prev_n) < -0.2; -- fell by more than 20% lag takes the previous row . if a year is missing for a store, "previous" is two years back. use a spine when that matters.

pattern: arrays (one-to-many in one row) -- top 3 items per store by number of orders with per_item as ( select store_id, trim(item) as item, count(*) as n from `p.analytics.orders`, unnest(items) as item group by all ) select * from per_item qualify row_number() over (partition by store_id order by n desc, item) <= 3; -- filter rows by array content without exploding select order_ref from `p.analytics.orders` where exists (select 1 from unnest(items) i where i like '%umbrella%'); -- array size, and rows whose array is empty or null select array_length(items) as n_items from t; select countif(array_length(items) = 0 or items is null) from t; the comma before unnest is a cross join: rows with an empty array vanish. use left join unnest(items) as item to keep them.

pattern: pivot and unpivot -- one row per store, a column per year select * from ( select store_id, order_year, order_id from `p.analytics.orders` where order_year between 2023 and 2025 ) pivot (count(order_id) for order_year in (2023 as y2023, 2024 as y2024, 2025 as y2025)); -- the portable way, works in any sql select store_id, countif(order_year = 2023) as y2023, countif(order_year = 2024) as y2024, countif(order_year = 2025) as y2025 from `p.analytics.orders` group by store_id; -- columns back to rows select * from wide unpivot (n for year in (y2023, y2024, y2025));

pattern: recursive hierarchy -- every category under x, directly or through a chain (max depth 5) with recursive chain as ( select category_id, parent_id, 1 as depth from `p.analytics.categories` where parent_id = 'x' union all select c.category_id, c.parent_id, chain.depth + 1 from `p.analytics.categories` c join chain on c.parent_id = chain.category_id where chain.depth < 5 -- always bound the recursion ) select category_id, min(depth) as depth from chain group by category_id;

pattern: point-in-time join (scd type 2) -- which store name was valid on the order date? select o.order_ref, o.order_date, s.name from `p.analytics.orders` o join `p.snapshots.store_snapshot` s on s.store_id = o.store_id and o.order_date >= date(s.dbt_valid_from) and (s.dbt_valid_to is null or o.order_date < date(s.dbt_valid_to)); half-open intervals ( >= from and < to ) never match two versions for one date.

reusable logic -- temporary sql function for this script create temp function parse_any_date(s string) as ( coalesce(safe.parse_date('%y-%m-%d', s), safe.parse_date('%d-%m-%y', s)) ); select raw_date, parse_any_date(raw_date) from t; -- persistent function in a dataset create or replace function `p.util.safe_ratio`(a float64, b float64) as ( if(b = 0 or b is null, null, a / b) ); -- table function: a parameterised view create or replace table function `p.util.store_year`(c string, y int64) as select * from `p.analytics.orders` where store_id = c and order_year = y; select count(*) from `p.util.store_year`('1_05', 2024);

making bigquery fast and cheap habit why select named columns bytes billed = bytes of the columns you read. one wide text column can be most of a table. filter on the partition column with literals or parameters lets bigquery skip partitions before reading. wrapping the column in a function can prevent it. filter on clustered columns skips blocks inside partitions; benefit shows in "bytes processed" after the run. dry-run before running shows bytes to be scanned for free. set a maximum bytes billed on risky jobs. aggregate early, join late shuffling fewer rows between stages is the main cost in slot time. avoid order by without limit on huge results a global sort runs on one worker at the end. use approx_count_distinct for exploration exact distinct counts on billions of rows are expensive; the approximate version has a small, documented error and is far cheaper. materialise reused intermediate results a cte referenced several times may be computed several times. write it to a table (or temp table in a script) when it is big. read the execution graph in the console's execution details: look for a stage with skewed time (one huge key), large shuffle, or spill to disk. avoid self-joins for running totals a window function does in one pass what a self-join does quadratically.

c.h: Mistakes that give wrong answers quietly
c.x: mistakes that give wrong answers quietly fan-out from a one-to-many join before a sum . a right-table filter in where after a left join . not in against a column that contains null. integer division in other engines ( 1/2 = 0 ); bigquery's / returns float64, but div() is integer. between on timestamps: between '2025-01-01' and '2025-01-31' misses most of the 31st. use >= start and < next_day . time zones: date(ts) is utc unless you pass a zone ( date(ts, 'asia/kolkata') ). row_number without a tie-breaker: a different row "wins" on each run. limit without order by : an arbitrary sample, not the top rows. averaging averages, or averaging percentages, instead of recomputing from totals. safe-parsing into null and never counting the nulls.

check your own query grain: what does one output row mean? is the key unique? ( count(*) vs count(distinct key) ) totals: does the sum across groups equal the ungrouped total? rows in vs out: did a join drop or multiply rows you did not expect? edges: empty groups, nulls, the first and last day, ties. one example by hand: pick one key and check its row against the source. cost: dry-run bytes reasonable for the question?

exercises (open each for a solution) try each on the practice schema, or adapt it to a public dataset. solutions are one good answer, not the only one. 1. orders per store in 2024, including stores with none. select c.store_id, c.name, count(o.order_id) as n from `p.ref.stores` c left join `p.analytics.orders` o on o.store_id = c.store_id and o.order_year = 2024 group by all order by n desc; filter in on , and count a column from the right table so empty stores give 0. 2. the most recent order per store, with ties broken consistently. select store_id, order_ref, order_date from `p.analytics.orders` where order_date is not null qualify row_number() over (partition by store_id order by order_date desc, order_id) = 1; 3. what share of each store's rows failed to parse their date? only stores above 1%. select store_id, count(*) as n, countif(raw_date is not null and order_date is null) as failed, safe_divide(countif(raw_date is not null and order_date is null), count(*)) as failed_share from `p.analytics.orders` group by store_id having safe_divide(countif(raw_date is not null and order_date is null), count(*)) > 0.01 order by failed_share desc; 4. daily counts for one store with a 7-day moving average, including days with zero. with days as ( select d from unnest(generate_date_array('2025-01-01', '2025-06-30')) d ), daily as ( select order_date as d, count(*) n from `p.analytics.orders` where store_id = '1_05' and order_date between '2025-01-01' and '2025-06-30' group by 1 ) select days.d, coalesce(n, 0) as n, avg(coalesce(n, 0)) over (order by days.d rows between 6 preceding and current row) as ma7 from days left join daily using (d) order by d; the spine makes rows equal to days, so the moving average is over seven calendar days. 5. stores whose yearly count fell by more than 20% compared with the previous year. with y as ( select store_id, order_year, count(*) n from `p.analytics.orders` group by all ), c as ( select *, lag(n) over (partition by store_id order by order_year) as prev_n, lag(order_year) over (partition by store_id order by order_year) as prev_year from y ) select *, safe_divide(n - prev_n, prev_n) as change from c where prev_year = order_year - 1 -- only compare adjacent years and safe_divide(n - prev_n, prev_n) < -0.2; 6. find duplicate keys, then build the deduplicated table keeping the latest load. select order_ref, count(*) copies from `p.raw.orders` group by order_ref having count(*) > 1; create or replace table `p.scratch.orders_dedup` as select * from `p.raw.orders` qualify row_number() over (partition by order_ref order by _landed_at desc) = 1; -- verify: should return 0 select count(*) - count(distinct order_ref) from `p.scratch.orders_dedup`; 7. the longest run of consecutive trading days for each store. with d as ( select distinct store_id, order_date from `p.analytics.orders` where order_date is not null ), t as ( select *, date_sub(order_date, interval row_number() over (partition by store_id order by order_date) day) as grp from d ), runs as ( select store_id, min(order_date) s, max(order_date) e, count(*) len from t group by store_id, grp ) select * from runs qualify row_number() over (partition by store_id order by len desc, s) = 1; 8. each store's share of all 2024 orders, and its rank within its state. with n as ( select c.state, o.store_id, count(*) n from `p.analytics.orders` o join `p.ref.stores` c using (store_id) where o.order_year = 2024 group by all ) select *, n / sum(n) over () as share_all, rank() over (partition by state order by n desc) as rank_in_state from n order by state, rank_in_state; 9. stores present in the reference table but absent from the landed data, and the reverse. (select 'missing_data' as issue, store_id from `p.ref.stores` except distinct select 'missing_data', store_id from `p.analytics.orders`) union all (select 'unknown_store', store_id from `p.analytics.orders` except distinct select 'unknown_store', store_id from `p.ref.stores`); parenthesise when mixing different set operators; bigquery requires it. 10. median, 90th percentile and maximum lag (days) between order and landing, per store. select store_id, approx_quantiles(lag_d, 100)[offset(50)] as p50, approx_quantiles(lag_d, 100)[offset(90)] as p90, max(lag_d) as max_lag from ( select store_id, date_diff(date(_landed_at), order_date, day) as lag_d from `p.analytics.orders` where order_date is not null ) group by store_id order by p90 desc; 11. upsert a day's new rows into a target table without creating duplicates. merge `p.mart.serving` t using ( select * from `p.analytics.orders` where date(_landed_at) = @run_date qualify row_number() over (partition by order_id order by _landed_at desc) = 1 ) s on t.order_id = s.order_id when matched then update set order_date = s.order_date, order_ref = s.order_ref when not matched then insert row; deduplicate the source first: merge fails if two source rows match one target row. 12. explain why this returns no rows: select * from stores where store_id not in (select store_id from orders) . if any orders.store_id is null, x not in (…, null) evaluates to null for every x, never true, so no row passes. use not exists , or add where store_id is not null inside the subquery.

a plan to get better week 1: the evaluation order, nulls and joins. redo exercises 1, 9 and 12 until they feel obvious. week 2: window functions. exercises 2, 4, 5 and 8; then rewrite one self-join you have seen as a window. week 3: patterns. gaps and islands, date spines, dedup, pivots (6, 7). week 4: bigquery cost and plans. dry-run everything, read the execution graph of your slowest query, and cut its bytes in half. ongoing: before sharing any number, run the self-check list on this tab. read other people's sql: dbt models in your repo, and the queries behind dashboards you use. ask "what is the grain?" of each.

modelling rules start normalised (third normal form): each fact stored once, in the table it describes. denormalise later, on purpose, for a measured read need. every table has a primary key. surrogate ( bigint identity or uuid) for internal identity; natural keys (order reference, email) get a unique constraint. never reuse or renumber a key that others store: urls, foreign systems, legal records. constraints are free correctness: not null , unique , check , foreign key . the database enforces them for every writer, including the one you forgot. right types: date / timestamptz not strings; numeric for money, never float; text over arbitrary varchar(n) ; jsonb for truly variable attributes, not as a substitute for columns. name things plainly and consistently: snake_case , singular or plural but one choice, _at for timestamps, _id for keys.

a schema example create table store ( store_id text primary key, name text not null ); create table orders ( -- "order" is a reserved word id bigint generated always as identity primary key, order_id text not null unique, -- stable natural key order_ref text not null, -- what the customer sees store_id text not null references store, order_date date, status text not null check (status in ('paid','pending')), notes text, created_at timestamptz not null default now(), updated_at timestamptz not null default now() ); -- many-to-many through a join table create table order_item ( order_id text not null references orders (order_id) on delete cascade, product_id text not null references product, quantity int not null check (quantity > 0), primary key (order_id, product_id) );

index types (postgresql) type good for example b-tree (default) equality, ranges, sorting, prefix like 'abc%' (with c collation, or an index using text_pattern_ops ) create index on orders (order_date); composite filters on several columns; column order matters (store_id, order_date desc) covering ( include ) answering a query from the index alone (index-only scan) (store_id) include (order_ref, order_date) partial indexing only the rows you query; small and fast (id) where status = 'pending' expression queries on a computed value (lower(email)) unique enforcing uniqueness, and lookups unique (store_id, order_ref) gin full-text search ( tsvector ), jsonb containment, arrays using gin (to_tsvector('english', notes)) brin huge tables physically ordered by a column (append-only by time); tiny index using brin (created_at) hnsw / ivfflat (pgvector) approximate nearest-neighbour search on embeddings using hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)

index rules of thumb index for your queries, not your columns. start from the slow query's where , join and order by . composite order: equality columns first, then the range or sort column. (store_id, order_date) serves store_id = ? and order_date > ? ; the reverse order serves it poorly. leftmost prefix: an index on (a, b, c) helps queries on a , a,b , a,b,c , not on b alone. foreign keys usually need an index on the referencing column, or deletes and joins scan. every index slows writes and uses disk. drop unused ones ( pg_stat_user_indexes.idx_scan = 0 ). low-selectivity columns (a boolean, a status with 3 values) rarely help alone; use a partial index instead. functions on columns ( where date(created_at) = … ) skip a plain index; write a range or index the expression. build on live tables with create index concurrently , then confirm it is valid: an interrupted build leaves an invalid index.

reading a query plan explain (analyze, buffers) select order_ref, order_date from orders where store_id = '1_05' and order_date >= '2024-01-01' order by order_date desc limit 20; -- look for: -- seq scan on a big table → missing or unusable index -- rows=10 (estimated) vs actual rows=500000 → stale stats: analyze -- sort … external merge disk → work_mem too low, or index the sort -- nested loop with huge inner loops → join order or missing index -- index only scan, heap fetches: 0 → ideal -- check index validity after a concurrent build select indexrelid::regclass, indisvalid from pg_index where not indisvalid; -- slowest queries (pg_stat_statements extension) select query, calls, mean_exec_time from pg_stat_statements order by total_exec_time desc limit 10;

partitioning (one database) create table event ( id bigserial, -- fine here; generated … as identity on a partitioned table needs postgresql 17+ event_date date not null, payload jsonb, primary key (id, event_date) -- must include the partition key ) partition by range (event_date); create table event_2025 partition of event for values from ('2025-01-01') to ('2026-01-01'); create table event_2026 partition of event for values from ('2026-01-01') to ('2027-01-01'); create table event_default partition of event default; -- retire old data instantly instead of a slow delete alter table event detach partition event_2025; drop table event_2025; -- other kinds: partition by list (region) partition by hash (customer_id) why: queries that filter on the key skip other partitions (pruning); old data drops in one statement; maintenance runs per partition. when: very large tables (tens of millions of rows and up) with a natural time or category filter. small tables only get slower. cost: unique constraints must include the partition key; queries without it scan every partition.

sharding (many databases) what: split rows across separate database servers by a shard key, so each holds part of the data and load. shard key choice is the whole design: high cardinality, evenly spread, present in almost every query (tenant id, user id). hash sharding spreads load evenly but makes range queries hit every shard. range sharding keeps ranges together but creates hot shards (all of today's writes on one). directory / lookup sharding maps keys to shards in a table: flexible, but the directory becomes critical. costs: cross-shard joins and transactions become application problems; resharding is a migration project; operations multiply. try first: better indexes, read replicas, caching, partitioning, a bigger instance, archiving cold data. shard when one primary truly cannot take the writes. managed or distributed options do it for you: spanner, cockroachdb, citus (postgres), vitess (mysql). alloydb read pools scale reads only; they do not shard.

replication & scaling reads read replicas copy the primary asynchronously. scale reads; accept replica lag (a user may not see their own write). synchronous replicas confirm writes before commit: no data loss on failover, at the cost of write latency. high availability (cloud sql ha, patroni) promotes a standby when the primary fails. connection pooling (pgbouncer, hikaricp, r2dbc pool): postgres connections are expensive. size pools so instances × pool size stays under max_connections . caching (redis) for hot, read-heavy data, with a deliberate invalidation rule.

transactions, isolation, locking isolation prevents read committed (postgres default) dirty reads. each statement sees data committed before it began. repeatable read non-repeatable reads (and, in postgresql, phantom reads): the transaction sees one snapshot throughout. serializable all anomalies; transactions behave as if run one by one. retry on serialization failure. -- pessimistic: lock the row you will change select * from account where id = 7 for update; -- job queue: each worker claims different rows select id from job where state = 'ready' order by created_at limit 10 for update skip locked; -- optimistic: version column, fail if someone else changed it update doc set body = $1, version = version + 1 where id = $2 and version = $3; -- 0 rows → conflict, reload and retry keep transactions short. a long one holds locks and stops vacuum cleaning up dead rows.

c.h: Safe schema changes on live data
c.x: safe schema changes on live data additive first: add a nullable column, a new table, a new index (concurrently). safe and reversible. expand / contract for renames and type changes: add the new column, write to both, backfill in batches, switch reads, stop writing the old, drop it in a later release. avoid long locks: some alter table forms rewrite the whole table. set lock_timeout so a migration fails fast instead of blocking traffic. backfill in batches (by id range), committing as you go, not one giant update. version every change with a migration tool (liquibase, flyway, alembic), and never edit a migration that has already run in production. test on a production-sized copy; a change that takes 30 s on 10k rows can take hours on 20m.

anti-patterns entity-attribute-value tables ( key , value rows for everything): no types, no constraints, painful queries. comma-separated lists in a column: use a join table or an array with a gin index. floats for money and strings for dates. no foreign keys "for speed": orphans and silent corruption cost more. n+1 queries from an orm loop: one query per row instead of one join. select * in application code: breaks when columns change, fetches what you do not need. offset pagination on deep pages: use keyset pagination ( where (date, id) < ($1, $2) order by date desc, id desc limit 20 ). unbounded growth with no retention or archiving plan.

oltp vs olap design oltp (postgres) olap (bigquery) workload many small reads/writes by key few large scans and aggregates storage row-oriented column-oriented schema normalised, constraints denormalised, nested, wide speed comes from indexes partitioning, clustering, reading fewer columns updates row by row, transactional batch loads and merge; avoid row-by-row dml

levels: what to expect 1 foundation design a normalised table with a primary key and constraints add an index for a slow lookup understand what a transaction guarantees 2 practitioner read explain analyze and fix the plan choose composite, partial and covering indexes write safe, additive migrations 3 senior partition large tables; plan retention and archiving choose isolation levels and locking strategies plan replicas, pooling and capacity 4 expert decide between scaling up, partitioning, sharding or a distributed database run zero-downtime migrations on very large tables set database standards and review all schema changes each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

match (structural pattern matching) match event: case {"state": "succeeded", "rows": int(n)} if n == 0: warn("succeeded with zero rows") case {"state": "succeeded", "rows": int(n)}: ok(n) case {"state": "failed", "error": str(msg)}: fail(msg) case {"state": state}: unknown(state) case _: raise valueerror(f"bad event: {event!r}") match path.split("/"): case ["data", y, *rest] if y.startswith("year="): ... patterns match structure and types; they do not do string prefix matching. use a guard ( if ) for that.

errors, logging, context managers import logging, contextlib, time log = logging.getlogger(__name__) logging.basicconfig(level=logging.info, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s") try: load(uri) except notfound: log.warning("missing %s", uri) # lazy formatting except exception: log.exception("load failed for %s", uri) # includes traceback raise else: log.info("loaded %s", uri) @contextlib.contextmanager def timed(label): t = time.perf_counter() try: yield finally: log.info("%s took %.2fs", label, time.perf_counter() - t) with timed("orders load"): run()

concurrency # threads for blocking i/o (gcs, bq, http) from concurrent.futures import threadpoolexecutor, as_completed with threadpoolexecutor(max_workers=16) as ex: futs = {ex.submit(copy, uri): uri for uri in uris} for f in as_completed(futs): try: f.result() except exception as e: log.error("%s: %s", futs[f], e) # asyncio with structured cancellation (3.11) import asyncio async def main(): async with asyncio.taskgroup() as tg: tasks = [tg.create_task(fetch(u)) for u in urls] return [t.result() for t in tasks] asyncio.run(main()) # processes for cpu-bound work from concurrent.futures import processpoolexecutor

levels of testing level checks speed tools unit one function or class in isolation; logic, edge cases, errors ms junit + assertj, pytest, dbt unit tests integration your code with a real database, queue or http layer seconds testcontainers, wiremock, @springboottest, @quarkustest, bigquery emulator contract producer and consumer agree on an api or schema seconds pact, spring cloud contract, schema tests, dbt contracts end to end a user journey through the deployed system minutes playwright, selenium, scripted api checks data tests the data itself: keys, nulls, ranges, freshness, row counts per run dbt data tests, assertions in pipelines non-functional load, latency, resilience, security minutes–hours k6, gatling, locust, chaos tests, zap most tests should be fast unit and integration tests; a few end-to-end tests cover the critical journeys. a suite nobody runs because it is slow protects nothing.

what makes a good test fails for the right reason: write it first, or break the code on purpose, and watch it go red. a test only ever seen green is unproven. tests behaviour, not implementation: inputs and outputs, not which private method was called. refactors should not break it. one reason to fail, with a name that says what it checks: rejectsunparseabledate . arrange, act, assert: set up, do one thing, check the result. independent: no shared state or order between tests; unique test data per test. deterministic: fixed clock, fixed seed, no real network, no sleeps. covers the edges: empty, null, one, many, boundary values, bad input, the dependency being down.

tdd in one loop red: write a small failing test for the next behaviour. green: write the least code that makes it pass. refactor: clean up with the tests as a safety net. for a bug: first write a test that reproduces it and fails, then fix. the test stays, so the bug cannot return. this is also the best way to brief an ai assistant: give it the failing test as the definition of done.

java: junit + assertj + mockito class orderdateparsertest { @parameterizedtest(name = "{0} → {1}") @csvsource({ "05-05-1959, 1959-05-05", // day-first, from one source "2024-01-31, 2024-01-31", // iso, from the others }) void parsesbothformats(string raw, localdate expected) { assertthat(orderdateparser.parse(raw)).isequalto(expected); } @parameterizedtest @valuesource(strings = {"", "31-31-2024", "yesterday"}) void rejectsunparseable(string raw) { assertthatthrownby(() -> orderdateparser.parse(raw)) .isinstanceof(illegalargumentexception.class) .hasmessagecontaining("does not parse"); } } @extendwith(mockitoextension.class) class loadertest { @mock blobstore store; @injectmocks loader loader; @test void reportsunknownwhenlistingfails() { when(store.list(any())).thenthrow(new runtimeexception("403 forbidden")); assertthat(loader.run().state()).isequalto(state.unknown); // not "0 objects" verify(store, never()).copy(any(), any()); } } this code runs on junit 5 and junit 6 alike. junit 6 needs java 17 or newer.

test doubles: pick the lightest double is dummy passed but never used stub returns canned answers fake a working lightweight version (in-memory store) spy records how it was called mock pre-programmed with expectations it verifies mock what you do not own only at the boundary; prefer a fake or a real container. build stubs from captured real responses , never from a guess. a stub shaped from the docs confirms the guess. too many mocks means the test checks wiring, not behaviour.

testing data pipelines idempotency: run the same input twice; the output must be identical (row count and content). incremental vs full: an incremental run on top of yesterday equals a full rebuild. edge data: empty partition, one row, duplicates, late rows, a new source column, a malformed date. reconciliation: rows in = rows loaded + rows rejected + rows skipped, every run. run records: assert the counters written to the ledger, not only the log line. "source down": the run must end failed or unknown, never succeeded with zero. real dialect: a sql string checked against a mock proves its shape, not that bigquery accepts it. run it on the emulator or a dry run. # dbt dbt build -s my_model+ # models + their tests, in order dbt test -s test_type:unit # logic on fixed inputs dbt test -s test_type:data # assertions on built tables

property-based testing instead of hand-picked examples, state a property that must hold for all inputs and let the tool generate hundreds, shrinking any failure to the smallest case. # python: hypothesis from hypothesis import given, strategies as st @given(st.dates(min_value=date(1950,1,1), max_value=date(2030,12,31))) def test_format_then_parse_roundtrips(d): assert parse_order_date(d.strftime("%d-%m-%y")) == d @given(st.lists(st.text())) def test_dedupe_is_idempotent(xs): assert dedupe(dedupe(xs)) == dedupe(xs) java: jqwik ( @property , @forall ). good properties: round trips, idempotency, invariants (sorted output stays sorted), and "never throws".

load and performance tests // k6: ramp to 60 searches/s and check p95 latency import http from 'k6/http'; import { check } from 'k6'; export const options = { scenarios: { search: { executor: 'ramping-arrival-rate', startrate: 5, timeunit: '1s', preallocatedvus: 50, stages: [{ target: 60, duration: '5m' }, { target: 60, duration: '10m' }] } }, thresholds: { http_req_duration: ['p(95)<500'], http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'] }, }; export default function () { const r = http.get(`${__env.base}/api/search?q=land+acquisition`); check(r, { '200': (x) => x.status === 200 }); } // k6 run -e base=https://staging.example.com search.js test against production-sized data in a production-like environment. measure percentiles (p95, p99), not averages. find the breaking point, then decide the alert threshold below it.

flaky tests, coverage, ci flaky test: passes and fails on the same code. causes: time, ordering, shared state, real network, async waits. fix or delete it; never retry it into green or quarantine it forever. coverage shows what was executed , not what was checked . 100% coverage with weak assertions proves little. use it to find untested code, not as a target. mutation testing (pit for java, mutmut for python) changes your code and checks that some test fails. it measures test strength. ci runs every test on every pr, on a clean checkout. a local green and a ci red on the same commit usually mean untracked files or a different environment. never skip, disable or weaken a test to get green. if a test is wrong, fix it in its own reviewed change.

testing ai features unit-test everything around the model: prompt building, parsing, retries, fallbacks. validate structured outputs against the schema, and the values against your data. run an eval set in ci and track the score; fail the build on a regression beyond a threshold. include adversarial cases: prompt injection in documents, empty retrieval, the model refusing. mock the model in unit tests with recorded real responses; run the eval against the real model.

one we build: enrich-test-api enrich-test-api is a java test library for exercising real cloud service semantics against local emulators, so a test names no cloud provider. it is an early alpha: aws only, emulator only. it is open source (apache 2.0). it is ours, so we are not neutral: compare it with testcontainers and the other tools on this page.

principles least privilege: every person, service and token gets only the access it needs, for only as long as it needs it. defence in depth: several independent layers (network, identity, application, data), so one failure is not a breach. secure by default: private unless opened, denied unless allowed, encrypted unless there is a reason not to be. never trust input: anything from a user, another service, a file, a web page or a model's output is validated before use. no secrets in code, images, logs or chat. they live in a secret manager and are injected at runtime. fail closed: when an auth or permission check cannot run, deny. a gate that opens on error is not a gate. assume breach: log and alert so that a compromise is noticed and contained quickly.

owasp top 10 (2025 edition) risk looks like prevent with a01 broken access control get /api/orders/123 returns another user's order; the server fetches a user-supplied url that points to an internal service or metadata endpoint (ssrf, now part of this category) check ownership on every request, server side; deny by default; test it. for urls: allow-list destinations, block internal ranges, separate egress a02 security misconfiguration public bucket, debug endpoints on, default passwords, open cors infrastructure as code, reviewed; secure defaults; scanners a03 software supply chain failures an old library with a known cve; a compromised dependency or build tool an sbom, dependency updates, sca scanning, components from trusted sources only, protected ci a04 cryptographic failures plain http, passwords hashed with md5, keys in the repo tls everywhere, argon2id/bcrypt for passwords, managed keys a05 injection sql built by string concatenation; shell commands with user input parameterised queries, no shell with input, allow-lists a06 insecure design no rate limit on login; reset tokens that never expire threat model at design time; abuse cases as requirements a07 authentication failures weak passwords allowed, no mfa, session never expires use a proven identity provider; mfa; short-lived tokens a08 software or data integrity failures unsigned build artefacts; deserialising untrusted data signed images, pinned dependencies, verified artefacts a09 security logging & alerting failures a breach discovered months later; logs nobody is alerted on audit logs, alerts on suspicious patterns, retained logs a10 mishandling of exceptional conditions an error path that fails open, leaks a stack trace, or leaves a transaction half done handle errors where they happen and in one global handler; fail closed and roll back; rate limits and quotas the 2021 edition numbered these differently and had ssrf as its own a10. owasp revises the list every few years; check owasp.org for the latest edition. the api security top 10 is the companion list for apis.

injection: always parameterise // java jdbc // wrong: "select * from orders where order_ref = '" + orderref + "'" preparedstatement ps = conn.preparestatement( "select * from orders where order_ref = ?"); ps.setstring(1, orderref); // spring jdbcclient jdbc.sql("select * from orders where order_ref = :order_ref").param("order_ref", orderref)... # python psycopg cur.execute("select * from orders where order_ref = %s", (order_ref,)) # never f-strings # bigquery bigquery.queryjobconfig(query_parameters=[ bigquery.scalarqueryparameter("order_ref", "string", order_ref)]) # where order_ref = @order_ref identifiers (table and column names) cannot be parameters: pick them from an allow-list. never pass user input to a shell. use the library call, or an argument list without a shell. escape output for its context (html, json, urls) to prevent xss. use the framework's templating, not string building.

authentication & authorisation authentication is who you are; authorisation is what you may do. most breaches are authorisation bugs. use oidc / oauth 2.0 with a proven provider rather than building login yourself. for browser apps, the authorisation code flow with pkce. jwts: verify the signature, issuer, audience and expiry on every request; keep them short-lived; never accept alg: none ; never put secrets in them (they are only encoded). refresh tokens rotate on use and are revocable; in browsers keep them in httponly; secure; samesite cookies. check permissions on the server for every request and every object: "is this user allowed this order?", not just "is the user logged in?". load roles from the source of truth on each authentication; do not trust roles a client sends. passwords: argon2id or bcrypt, rate-limited login, breached-password checks, mfa for admins.

spring security: a stateless api @bean securityfilterchain api(httpsecurity http) throws exception { return http .authorizehttprequests(a -> a .requestmatchers("/actuator/health/**").permitall() .requestmatchers("/api/admin/**").hasrole("admin") .anyrequest().authenticated()) // deny by default .oauth2resourceserver(o -> o.jwt(customizer.withdefaults())) .sessionmanagement(s -> s.sessioncreationpolicy(sessioncreationpolicy.stateless)) .csrf(c -> c.disable()) // only safe when auth is a bearer header, not a cookie .build(); } // object-level check in the service, not only the url rule if (!casefile.ownerid().equals(currentuserid)) throw new accessdeniedexception("not yours");

web & api hardening https only, with hsts ( strict-transport-security ). content-security-policy to limit where scripts load from; x-content-type-options: nosniff ; frame-ancestors against clickjacking. cors: list exact origins; never reflect any origin with credentials allowed. csrf: needed when the browser sends cookies automatically; use tokens or samesite cookies. rate limits on login, signup, password reset and expensive endpoints. validate request bodies (types, lengths, ranges) and reject unknown fields where it matters. errors: generic messages to the client, details to the logs. no stack traces in responses. uploads: check type and size, store outside the web root, scan if users share them.

secrets # store echo -n "$value" | gcloud secrets create db-password --data-file=- # grant one workload access to one secret gcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding db-password \ --member=serviceaccount:api@p.iam.gserviceaccount.com \ --role=roles/secretmanager.secretaccessor # rotate: add a version, roll the workload, then disable and destroy the old one gcloud secrets versions add db-password --data-file=new.txt gcloud secrets versions destroy 1 --secret=db-password no service account json keys: workload identity federation for ci, attached service accounts for workloads. a rotation is not finished until old versions are destroyed. scan commits for secrets (gitleaks, github secret scanning). a leaked secret is rotated, not just deleted from git: history and forks keep it. never print secrets in logs, ci output, error messages or ai prompts.

cloud security on gcp iam: one service account per workload; predefined narrow roles; no owner or editor for services; grant to groups, not individuals. organisation policies: block public buckets, service account key creation, and external ips where not needed. network: private ips for databases; ingress limited to the load balancer; cloud armor in front of public apps. data: encryption at rest is on by default; cmek when you must control keys; vpc service controls around sensitive datasets. audit logs: admin activity is always on; enable data access logs for sensitive services so reads are attributable. security command center surfaces misconfigurations and threats across the project. separate projects for dev and prod; nobody's laptop has standing prod write access.

threat modelling in 30 minutes draw the data flow: users, services, stores, and the trust boundaries between them. for each boundary, ask stride questions. list the threats, rate likelihood and impact, and pick mitigations. turn mitigations into tickets and tests. stride question spoofing can someone pretend to be another user or service? tampering can data be changed in transit or at rest? repudiation can someone deny an action because nothing recorded it? information disclosure can data leak to someone not entitled to it? denial of service can someone exhaust a resource or the budget? elevation of privilege can someone gain rights they should not have?

data protection & privacy know where personal data is: tag columns and datasets; keep an inventory. collect less, keep less: only what the purpose needs, with a retention period. mask or tokenise personal data in non-production environments and analytics. honour legal obligations: deletion requests, legal holds, consent. apply them on every read path, not only in one table. know the law that applies: for india, the digital personal data protection act, 2023; gdpr for eu residents. logs are data too: no personal data or tokens in log lines unless necessary and protected.

supply chain & ci pin dependencies with lockfiles; review what new dependencies bring. automated updates (dependabot, renovate) gated by tests. scan: sast (codeql, semgrep), sca (dependabot alerts, osv), images (trivy), secrets (gitleaks). pin third-party github actions to a commit sha; give workflows the minimum permissions: . protect main and deploy tags; require reviews and checks; restrict who can push release tags. sign images and generate sboms so you can prove what is running.

security testing unit and integration tests for access control: user a cannot read user b's object; an expired token is refused; a missing role gets 403. sast reads code for dangerous patterns; dast (owasp zap) probes the running app. dependency and image scans on every build. fuzzing parsers and file handlers with malformed input. penetration test before launch and after major changes, by someone independent. prove each guard red: try the forbidden action in a test and watch it fail.

c.h: Cryptography: use it, do not invent it
c.x: cryptography: use it, do not invent it know the three jobs: hashing proves something has not changed and cannot be reversed; encryption hides data and can be reversed with the key; signing proves who produced something. passwords are hashed, never encrypted, with a slow, salted algorithm. the owasp password storage cheat sheet recommends argon2id (at least 19 mib of memory, 2 iterations, parallelism 1); scrypt if argon2id is not available; bcrypt (work factor 10 or more, 72-byte password limit) for legacy systems; pbkdf2 with hmac-sha-256 and 600,000 or more iterations where fips-140 is required. fast hashes such as sha-256 alone are not suitable. use a vetted library and its defaults. never write your own algorithm or protocol. random means a secure generator: securerandom in java, the secrets module in python, never math.random or random for tokens. encrypt in transit (tls 1.2 or 1.3 everywhere, inside the network too) and at rest, and keep keys in a key management service, apart from the data, with rotation.

containers and kubernetes small images: a minimal or distroless base has fewer packages to patch. scan images in ci, pin them by digest, and sign them. never bake secrets into an image ; mount them at run time from a secret manager. pod security standards define three cumulative profiles: privileged, baseline and restricted. aim for restricted, and enforce it per namespace with the label pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted . least privilege in the cluster: narrow rbac roles, no service-account token where a pod does not call the api, and networkpolicies that deny by default. # container securitycontext that meets restricted securitycontext: runasnonroot: true allowprivilegeescalation: false capabilities: drop: ["all"] seccompprofile: type: runtimedefault readonlyrootfilesystem: true # good practice too

networks and zero trust zero trust: being inside the network earns no trust. every call is authenticated and authorised, service to service as well as user to service (mtls and tokens; see service mesh ). deny by default: firewalls and security groups open only the ports and sources a service needs. control outbound traffic too: a compromised service that cannot reach the internet cannot send your data out. keep databases and internal services off the public internet; use private networking and private endpoints. protect the edge: a waf and ddos protection in front of public endpoints, rate limits on apis (see apigee ). segment: a breach in one area should not open every other one.

ai and llm security the owasp genai llm top 10 (2026 edition, published august 2026) lists the main risks for applications built on language models: llm01 prompt injection. treat every input, including retrieved documents, web pages and tool results, as possibly carrying instructions. separate instructions from data; never let content alone trigger an action. llm02 sensitive information disclosure. do not put data in a prompt that the user may not see; filter outputs; check what your provider keeps. llm03 excessive agency. give tools the least privilege they need, and require a person's approval for actions that change things. llm04 supply chain. vet models, datasets, plugins and mcp servers as you would any dependency. llm05 data and model poisoning. know where training and retrieval data come from, and who can write to them. llm06 unbounded consumption. rate limits, token budgets and timeouts per user and per job. llm07 misinformation. ground answers in sources, cite them, and evaluate; never present a guess as fact. llm08 hidden context exposure. assume the system prompt and tool schemas can be extracted: never put secrets or security rules only there. llm09 vector and embedding weaknesses. apply access control in retrieval, so a user can only retrieve what they may read. llm10 improper output handling. treat model output as untrusted input: validate, escape and parameterise it before it reaches a browser, a shell or a query. more in ai for engineers , rag , mcp and agent harness .

c.h: People: the most targeted part of any system
c.x: people: the most targeted part of any system most attacks start with a person, not a server: a convincing email, message or call. urgency is the warning sign. "pay this now", "reset my access", "send me the file": check through another channel you already trust before acting. voices and video can now be faked convincingly. use phishing-resistant sign-in where you can (passkeys or hardware security keys), a password manager with a unique password everywhere, and multi-factor authentication on every account that offers it. keep devices updated and locked, and never leave a logged-in laptop unattended. report mistakes at once, without blame. a clicked link reported in five minutes is a small incident; hidden for a week, it is a big one.

security logging and detection log what an investigator will need: sign-ins that succeed and fail, permission and role changes, admin actions, data exports, and access denied. never log secrets, tokens, passwords or full card numbers, and mask personal data. protect the logs: separate access, append-only or write-once storage, kept long enough to investigate. alert on what matters: many failed sign-ins, access from somewhere new, a sudden large export, a disabled control. see observability .

backups and ransomware a common rule of thumb is 3-2-1: three copies of your data, on two different kinds of storage, with one copy off-site. keep one copy immutable or offline, with separate credentials, so an attacker who gets in cannot delete or encrypt the backups too. a backup you have not restored is a hope. test restores on a schedule and time them. agree the targets: how much data you can lose (rpo) and how long you can be down (rto), then design to meet them.

compliance frameworks you will meet iso/iec 27001: an information security management system, certified by audit. soc 2: an auditor's report on a service organisation's controls, common with us customers. pci dss: rules for handling payment card data (see payment gateways ). data protection law: the gdpr in the eu, the uk gdpr, india's digital personal data protection act, and others where your users live. compliance is not security. a certificate shows controls existed when audited; good engineering keeps them working every day.

c.h: Security checklist for a pull request
c.x: security checklist for a pull request is every new endpoint authenticated, and does it check ownership of each object? is all input validated, and every query parameterised? any new secret? is it in the secret manager, not in code or config? any new permission or iam role? is it the narrowest that works? does anything new get logged that should not be (tokens, personal data)? new dependency: maintained, licensed acceptably, no known cves? what happens on error: does it fail closed? is there a test that proves the forbidden case is refused?

when something goes wrong contain: revoke the leaked key, disable the account, block the ip, take the endpoint down. preserve evidence: keep logs and snapshots before cleaning up. assess: what was accessed, since when, whose data. notify: security lead, then customers and regulators as the law requires and within its deadlines. fix the cause and add a guard (test, policy, alert) so it cannot recur.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation spot phishing; use a password manager and passkeys parameterise every query; never commit secrets check that users can only reach their own data apply the pr security checklist 2 practitioner hash passwords correctly and run containers to the restricted profile implement oauth 2.0 / oidc with a provider and validate tokens properly use least-privilege iam and a secret manager fix findings from sast, sca and image scans 3 senior threat-model a system and turn threats into tests design authentication, authorisation and audit for a product respond to and contain a security incident 4 expert own the security architecture and policies across teams lead compliance (dpdp, gdpr, soc 2) and external testing build a security culture and secure-by-default platforms each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.
