c.h: The roles and the two standards
c.x: the roles and the two standards role is example resource owner the user who owns the data a customer client the app that wants access the web app, a mobile app, a partner's server authorisation server authenticates the user and issues tokens google identity, okta, auth0, keycloak, entra id resource server the api that accepts tokens the search api, or apigee in front of it oauth 2.0 is about authorisation : giving a client an access token to call an api on someone's behalf, limited by scopes . openid connect (oidc) adds authentication on top: an id token (a jwt) that says who the user is. "sign in with google" is oidc. access token goes to apis. id token is for the client to learn who logged in; never send it to apis as an access token. refresh token gets new access tokens without a new login.

which flow for which client client flow notes web app with a server authorisation code + pkce confidential client: the server holds the secret and tokens single-page app (browser) authorisation code + pkce, ideally through a backend-for-frontend the bff keeps tokens server-side and gives the browser a secure cookie mobile / desktop app authorisation code + pkce via the system browser public client: no secret can be kept safe in the app service to service client credentials no user; the service authenticates as itself tv, cli, device without a browser device authorisation grant user approves on another device with a code workloads on gcp service account identity (google-signed tokens) no secrets at all; workload identity federation from outside gcp implicit , password do not use deprecated by current best practice (rfc 9700, oauth 2.1 draft)

c.h: Authorisation code + PKCE, step by step
c.x: authorisation code + pkce, step by step 1. client makes a random code_verifier and its hash: code_challenge = base64url(sha256(code_verifier)) 2. browser is sent to the authorisation server: get /authorize?response_type=code &client_id=shop-web &redirect_uri=https://shop.example.com/callback &scope=openid%20profile%20email%20search.read &state=random (csrf protection) &nonce=random (id-token replay protection) &code_challenge=…&code_challenge_method=s256 3. user logs in and consents; server redirects back: https://shop.example.com/callback?code=auth_code&state=random (client checks state matches) 4. client exchanges the code at the token endpoint (from the server for a web app or bff; from the device for a mobile or desktop app): post /token grant_type=authorization_code&code=auth_code &redirect_uri=…&client_id=shop-web&code_verifier=original 5. response: access_token, id_token, refresh_token, expires_in 6. client calls the api: authorization: bearer access_token pkce proves the party redeeming the code is the one that started the flow, so a stolen code is useless.

client credentials (machine to machine) curl -s https://auth.example.com/oauth2/token \ -u "$client_id:$client_secret" \ -d grant_type=client_credentials \ -d scope=orders.read # → {"access_token":"…","token_type":"bearer","expires_in":3600} curl -h "authorization: bearer $token" https://api.example.com/v1/orders/123 cache the token until shortly before it expires; do not fetch one per call. prefer private-key jwt or mtls client authentication over shared secrets where supported. on gcp, prefer service account identity over client secrets.

validating an access token (jwt) fetch the issuer's keys from its jwks url (from /.well-known/openid-configuration ); cache them. verify the signature with the key matching the token's kid ; accept only the expected algorithm (e.g. rs256 or es256). never none . check iss equals your issuer exactly. check aud contains your api's identifier. check exp (and nbf ) with small clock skew. check required scopes for the operation. then check object-level permission in your own code. # python (pyjwt) jwks = jwt.pyjwkclient("https://auth.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json") key = jwks.get_signing_key_from_jwt(token) claims = jwt.decode(token, key.key, algorithms=["rs256"], audience="https://api.example.com", issuer="https://auth.example.com/") # spring boot resource server spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri: https://auth.example.com/ spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.audiences: https://api.example.com # quarkus quarkus.oidc.auth-server-url=https://auth.example.com/ quarkus.oidc.token.audience=https://api.example.com opaque (non-jwt) tokens are validated by calling the server's introspection endpoint (rfc 7662).

scopes, claims and roles scopes limit what a client may do on the user's behalf ( orders.read ). they are about the app, not the user's own rights. claims are facts in the token: sub (stable user id), email , groups , custom claims. roles and permissions are your application's rules. load them from your source of truth; do not trust a role the client could have influenced. key users by sub plus issuer, not by email, which can change or be reused. keep tokens small; large claim sets slow every request.

tokens in browsers and apps best for spas: a backend-for-frontend does the oauth flow and keeps tokens; the browser gets an httponly; secure; samesite session cookie. avoid localstorage for tokens: any xss can read it. short access tokens (minutes) and rotating refresh tokens that are revoked if reused. mobile: store refresh tokens in the platform keychain / keystore; use the system browser, not an embedded web view, for login. logout revokes refresh tokens and ends the provider session if needed.

common mistakes accepting a token without checking audience: a token for another api works on yours. using the id token to call apis. loose redirect uris (wildcards, prefix matching): codes get sent to an attacker. missing or unchecked state : login csrf. implicit flow or tokens in urls, where they leak through logs and referrers. long-lived access tokens with no revocation. trusting scopes alone and skipping object-level checks. rolling your own authorisation server instead of using a maintained one.

beyond the basics sender-constrained tokens (dpop or mutual tls) make a stolen token useless to anyone else. pushed authorisation requests (par) send the request parameters server to server first. token exchange (rfc 8693) for a service calling another on the user's behalf. oauth 2.1 (draft) consolidates current best practice: pkce everywhere, no implicit or password grants. oauth for ai agents and mcp servers: agents act with delegated, scoped, revocable tokens, never the user's password.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain access, id and refresh tokens and scopes protect an api with a jwt resource server configuration use the authorisation code flow with pkce through a library 2 practitioner validate tokens fully: signature, issuer, audience, expiry, scopes choose the right flow per client type store tokens safely in web and mobile apps 3 senior design identity for a product: providers, bff, service-to-service, token lifetimes review oauth implementations for the common mistakes integrate gateways (apigee) and workload identity 4 expert own identity architecture across the organisation apply advanced specs (dpop, par, token exchange) lead identity incidents and provider migrations each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

in one paragraph data engineering is building and running the systems that move data from where it is produced to where it is used, and making it correct, current, documented and affordable on the way. source systems (apps, files, apis, sensors, public datasets) produce data in their own shapes and at their own pace. analysts, dashboards, machine-learning models, ai features and products need it in a shape they can query and trust. the data engineer owns the path between them: getting it in, keeping a faithful copy, reshaping it, checking it, delivering it, and knowing at any moment whether it is right. a pipeline that runs is not the goal. the goal is data that people can rely on without asking the data engineer first.

who does what role focus typical output data engineer ingestion, storage, pipelines, platform, reliability landed raw data, loaded tables, orchestrated jobs, a working platform analytics engineer modelling data for use, mostly in sql and dbt clean, tested, documented models and metrics data analyst answering business questions queries, dashboards, reports data scientist statistics, experiments, predictive models analyses, models, experiment results ml / ai engineer putting models into products and running them features, training and inference pipelines, evals, ai features backend engineer applications that create and serve data apis and services, the source systems data engineers read from in small teams one person covers several rows. the boundaries matter less than knowing who owns each table.

the lifecycle every pipeline follows stage question it answers on gcp, for example tab generation where does the data come from, how often, in what shape, under what licence? app databases, partner files, public mirrors, event streams — ingestion how do we get a faithful copy without losing or duplicating anything? storage transfer service, cloud run jobs, pub/sub, datastream (cdc) cloud run storage where does each version live, for how long, at what cost? gcs (files), bigquery (tables), cloud sql (serving) bigquery transformation how do raw records become clean, conformed, useful tables? dbt on bigquery, dataflow (beam), dataproc (spark) dbt serving how do consumers read it, fast enough and safely? bigquery views, postgres for an api, looker, exports, vector indexes for ai spring running underneath every stage: orchestration ( dags ), data quality and observability, security and access, data management (catalog, lineage, retention), infrastructure as code ( terraform ), and ordinary software engineering ( tests, ci, reviews ). this stage model follows fundamentals of data engineering by joe reis and matt housley, a good first book on the subject.

batch vs streaming batch: process a bounded chunk (yesterday, one file, one partition) on a schedule. simple, cheap, easy to rerun. latency of minutes to a day. streaming: process events continuously as they arrive. latency of seconds, but harder: ordering, late events, state, exactly-once. micro-batch: small batches every few minutes. often the practical middle. choose by the consumer's need, not by fashion. most reporting is fine with daily or hourly batch.

etl vs elt etl: extract, transform in a separate engine, then load the result. common when the warehouse was expensive or small. elt: extract, load the raw data into the warehouse, transform there with sql (dbt). the modern default on bigquery and similar. why elt wins today: you keep the raw data, so a bug in a transform is fixed by rerunning it, not by re-ingesting from a source that may have changed or gone. heavy non-sql work (parsing pdfs, images, large joins outside the warehouse) still goes to an engine built for it, such as dataflow or spark.

where data lives store good at oltp database (postgres) many small reads and writes by key; serving an app warehouse / olap (bigquery) scanning and aggregating billions of rows; analytics data lake (gcs) cheap storage of any file, raw and forever lakehouse (iceberg / delta on object storage) warehouse-style tables over lake files, readable by several engines vector index similarity search for ai retrieval file formats: csv and json are easy but untyped and slow to scan. parquet and orc are columnar, compressed and typed, best for analytics. avro suits row-by-row streams with schema evolution.

c.h: Layers: each one has one job
c.x: layers: each one has one job layer also called rule raw / landing bronze, raw byte-for-byte copy of what the source published. never edited. lets you replay everything. operational / staging odp, staging the raw data as typed tables, as published. renamed and cast, not reinterpreted. foundation / conformed silver, fdp, intermediate cleaned, deduplicated, keyed, versioned, joined to reference data. structure added once, reused by many. consumable / marts gold, cdp, marts shaped for one named use: a dashboard, an api, a model's features. derivation runs one way: each layer reads only the layer below. a product that reads from a downstream serving database creates a cycle and should be refused.

modelling basics grain: what one row means ("one order", "one order line per day"). state it for every table; most bugs are grain confusion. keys: a natural key from the source and, where needed, a surrogate key you generate. never reuse or renumber a key that others store. normalised (many narrow tables, no repetition) suits oltp. dimensional (facts plus dimensions, a star schema) suits analytics. one big table is fine on bigquery for a single use. facts are events with measures (an order, a payment). dimensions describe them (store, product, date). slowly changing dimensions: type 1 overwrites; type 2 keeps history with valid-from/valid-to rows (dbt snapshots).

properties of a good pipeline idempotent: running it twice for the same input gives the same result. overwrite a partition or merge on a key; never blindly append. incremental: processes only what is new or changed, decided from evidence (a watermark, etag or ledger), not "we visited it". backfillable: any past period can be rerun on purpose. late data aware: records can arrive after their period; reprocess a lookback window. schema-change safe: a new or renamed source column fails loudly or is handled deliberately, never silently dropped. observable: every run records what it read, wrote, skipped and failed, with counts. resumable: a failure midway restarts from where it stopped, not from zero.

data quality dimension example check completeness row count matches the source; no unexpected nulls validity dates parse; codes are in the allowed set uniqueness one row per key at the stated grain consistency every store code exists in the store table freshness newest record is within the expected age accuracy values match the source on a sample the worst quality failure is a silent one: a parse that turns bad dates into null, or a monitor that reports 0 when its source was unreachable. reject or count what you cannot read, and report "unknown" rather than a confident zero.

ingestion patterns full snapshot: copy everything each time. simple; fine for small tables. incremental by watermark: fetch rows changed since the last updated_at or id. change data capture (cdc): read the source database's change log for inserts, updates and deletes (datastream, debezium). file drops: compare source and destination listings (names, sizes, etags) and copy only the difference. events: producers publish to a queue (pub/sub, kafka); consumers process at-least-once, so handle duplicates. apis: paginate, respect rate limits, keep the raw response, and record the error body when a call fails.

governance & responsibility ownership: every table has a named owner and a description. lineage: you can say which sources feed a column and which products a change will affect. access: least privilege per dataset; serving systems get read-only access. personal and sensitive data: know where it is, mask or restrict it, honour deletion requests and legal holds. licences: respect source terms; carry attribution (for example cc-by) into every published output. retention and cost: decide how long each layer is kept and who pays for scans. contracts: agree the schema and meaning of anything another team reads, and change it on purpose.

c.h: A worked example, end to end
c.x: a worked example, end to end an online shop's orders, exported daily by its stores and served to the shop's staff through a reporting api. source: two order systems (the website and the store tills) export orders as parquet and json files to object storage, partitioned by year. files are sometimes re-exported in place. ingest (land): a cloud run job compares the source bucket's listing with the gcs landing bucket and copies only new or changed objects. it records examined, copied, already-current and failed counts. raw: the bucket keeps the originals byte for byte, so anything later can be replayed. load (raw): each landed file becomes rows in bigquery tables, with run id and load time, exactly as exported. transform (analytics): dbt cleans and conforms: parses two date formats (and rejects what does not parse), computes a stable order key, deduplicates re-exported rows, joins store reference data, and runs tests. consumable (mart): a dbt model shapes exactly what the reporting api needs, with a contract on its columns. serve: a loader upserts that table into postgres on the stable key, without renumbering existing ids that links, invoices and refunds depend on. the api reads postgres read-only. orchestrate and observe: a scheduler ticks daily; an orchestrator runs each stage when its input is ready and appends every state change to a ledger, so "what happened on 2026-09-19?" has an answer. every tab in this guide appears somewhere in that path. that is why a data engineer needs breadth.

c.h: Questions a data engineer always asks
c.x: questions a data engineer always asks what does one row mean, and what is its key? what happens if this runs twice? if it fails halfway? what does this return when the source is down, and can anyone tell that apart from "no data"? how will i know it is late or wrong before a user does? who reads this table, and what breaks for them if i change it? how much does a run cost, and what makes it grow? can i rebuild it from raw if i have to?

glossary partition: a slice of a table (by date or year) that queries can skip. watermark: the point up to which data is known to be processed. backfill: deliberately reprocessing a past period. upsert / merge: insert new rows, update existing ones, by key. lineage: the graph of which data feeds which. data contract: an agreed schema and meaning between producer and consumer. freshness: how old the newest data is. scd: slowly changing dimension, how history of descriptive attributes is kept. cdc: change data capture, streaming a database's changes. dag: directed acyclic graph, the dependency order of tasks. ledger: an append-only record of every run and state change.

choosing by situation data already in bigquery: sql or dbt first; bigframes if you need a dataframe api. do not pull it out to process it. files up to a few gb on one machine: polars or duckdb; pandas if a library you need expects it. tens to low hundreds of gb on one large machine: polars (lazy, streaming) or duckdb. beyond one machine, batch: bigquery, dataflow (beam) or spark on dataproc. streaming: dataflow (beam), flink, or kafka streams inside a service. inside a java service: plain java streams for small sets; beam for pipelines; spring batch for restartable business jobs. reading and writing parquet in python: pyarrow underneath, whatever dataframe you use on top.

validation libraries pandera: schemas for pandas and polars dataframes (types, ranges, nullability) checked in code and tests. great expectations: expectation suites and data docs for pipelines. pydantic: validating individual records and api payloads in python. dbt tests: keys, relationships and accepted values in the warehouse. jakarta bean validation: record validation in java. whatever the tool: reject or quarantine what does not parse, and count it. never coerce failures to null silently.

c.h: The same task in five libraries
c.x: the same task in five libraries count orders per store since 2020 from parquet files partitioned by year. # pandas: reads into memory, eager import pandas as pd df = pd.read_parquet("data/", columns=["store", "year"], filters=[("year", ">=", 2020)]) # pushdown; partition columns arrive as category out = (df.groupby("store", observed=true).size() .sort_values(ascending=false)) # polars: lazy; filters and column selection pushed into the scan import polars as pl out = (pl.scan_parquet("data/year=*/*.parquet", hive_partitioning=true) .filter(pl.col("year") >= 2020) .group_by("store").agg(pl.len().alias("n")) .sort("n", descending=true) .collect()) # duckdb: sql straight over the files import duckdb out = duckdb.sql(""" select store, count(*) as n from read_parquet('data/year=*/*.parquet', hive_partitioning = true) where year >= 2020 group by store order by n desc """).df() # pyspark: distributed, writes results back to gcs from pyspark.sql import sparksession, functions as f spark = sparksession.builder.getorcreate() (spark.read.parquet("gs://landing/data/") .where(f.col("year") >= 2020) .groupby("store").count() .orderby(f.desc("count")) .write.mode("overwrite").parquet("gs://out/store_counts/")) # bigquery dataframes: pandas-like code, executed inside bigquery import bigframes.pandas as bpd df = bpd.read_gbq("my-proj.analytics.orders") out = df[df["order_year"] >= 2020].groupby("store_id").size()

arrow and parquet in python import pyarrow.dataset as ds import pyarrow.parquet as pq dataset = ds.dataset("data/", format="parquet", partitioning="hive") table = dataset.to_table(columns=["order_ref", "store", "order_date"], filter=ds.field("year") >= 2020) # pushdown print(table.schema) # check types before trusting them pq.write_table(table, "out.parquet", compression="zstd", coerce_timestamps="us", # many readers expect microseconds allow_truncated_timestamps=true) timestamp units are a classic trap: parquet written with nanosecond timestamps can be read wrongly or refused by some engines, especially for dates before 1970. check the schema and write the unit the reader expects.

java options java streams and collectors for in-memory work ( java tab ). apache beam (java) for pipelines on dataflow, flink or spark. spark (java/scala) on dataproc or databricks. spring batch for chunked, restartable jobs with skip and retry policies. parquet-java and arrow java for columnar file io. jackson (json), apache commons csv or fastcsv for text formats; stream rather than loading whole files. duckdb jdbc for sql over local or remote parquet from java.

c.h: Habits that make any library fast
c.x: habits that make any library fast columnar formats (parquet) over csv and json for anything read more than once. read only the columns and rows you need (projection and predicate pushdown). lazy evaluation (polars, spark, beam) lets the engine optimise the whole plan. no row-by-row loops ( apply , iterrows ); use vectorised expressions. right types: categoricals for repeated strings, arrow-backed strings, proper dates. partition by the common filter (date, year); avoid thousands of tiny files. stream or chunk data larger than memory. push work to the warehouse when the data is already there.

correctness traps silent type coercion: integers with nulls become floats in classic pandas; ids with leading zeros become numbers. set dtypes explicitly. date parsing: mixed formats ( dd-mm-yyyy and yyyy-mm-dd ) parse wrongly or to null; specify the format and count failures. time zones: naive vs aware timestamps compared silently. joins: duplicate keys multiply rows, just as in sql. floating-point money: use decimals or integer minor units. schema drift: a new or renamed source column must fail loudly or be mapped on purpose.

the idea pipelines are defined once against a language-neutral contract set (sixteen contracts plus a metrics record: blobstore , warehouse , source , sink , jobcontrolrepository and eleven more), realised as java interfaces and python protocols. adapters implement the contracts for each cloud, and every adapter must pass the same conformance suite , or it is not an adapter. swap the cloud, keep the logic. layer is your business logic written once; depends only on the contracts, never on a cloud sdk the contracts java interfaces and python protocols from one spec cloud adapters swappable implementations that pass the shared conformance suite this is the "framework, not generated boilerplate" argument from the frameworks vs ai tab made concrete: one contract and one test suite instead of a hand-written cloud integration in every pipeline.

design choices java owns beam: the dataflow/beam execution layer is java; legacy python beam is not carried forward. the two languages deliberately do different jobs. dbt, reused: transformation is sql and macros, packaged once; there is deliberately no java transform module. local-first: the whole stack runs against emulators, so you can develop and test without a cloud account. no silent defaults: warehouse.loadfromuri requires a loadoptions , because a defaulted write disposition let a re-run silently double its data. honest failure: reconciliation runs before the target is written, so a failed load cannot be reported as succeeded. not a replacement for beam, airflow or dbt: they are engines, and culvert is a framework around them.

install (python) # core contracts only, no cloud sdks pip install culvert # + bigquery, gcs, pub/sub, secret manager, observability pip install 'culvert[gcp]' # + airflow-side dag factory / operators / sensors, or dbt pip install 'culvert[orchestration]' pip install 'culvert[transform]' # + stageclaim on postgresql pip install 'culvert[postgres]' # test fixtures, and the conformance suite for your own adapters pip install 'culvert[tester]' pip install 'culvert[contract-tests]' # gcp + orchestration + transform pip install 'culvert[all]' # adapters are discovered through entry points from data_pipeline_core import autoconfig blob_store = autoconfig.discover().first("blob_store") # -> gcsblobstore, when culvert[gcp] is installed python 3.10 or newer.

what runs where contract gcp aws azure blobstore gcs s3 skeleton warehouse bigquery athena roadmap source · sink pub/sub sqs roadmap jobcontrolrepository bigquery dynamodb · athena roadmap observability cloud monitoring cloudwatch roadmap secrets secret manager secrets manager roadmap gcp is the full implementation; aws has the java adapter family; azure has a blob storage skeleton and is otherwise roadmap. jobcontrolrepository also has a postgresql implementation.

features worth knowing job control: run state through jobcontrolrepository on bigquery, dynamodb, athena or postgresql; a read-only culvert command line ( runs , run , entities , failures , adapters ). stageclaim (postgresql): one stage of one unit for one period cannot start twice. inputreadiness (postgresql): names each expected input that is missing, failed or still running, rather than counting rows. orchestration: a cloud-neutral dag model rendered to airflow/composer or cloud run jobs, with stage gates and a concurrency ceiling. schema files: an entity's columns, types, required flags, classification, masking, ranges and allowed values in yaml or json, loaded with the same rules in java and python. blobstore.head(uri) : size, version token and metadata without reading the object, for loaders that must be idempotent by object version. bigquerywarehouse.merge() : upserts with one merge and refuses a key that is not a target column.

status, stated plainly released in both languages on maven central and pypi, under apache 2.0 (the earliest releases were mit). ran end to end on a real gcp project (cloud run to bigquery, event-driven) before release; that run caught eight production-only bugs every local test had passed. culvert is pre-1.0: read the changelog's upgrade notes before moving between versions. a book on its design is in progress. pin a version in your build, and verify any api against that version's sources, not against main .

model config for bigquery {{ config( materialized = 'table', partition_by = { 'field': 'order_date', 'data_type': 'date', # date | timestamp | datetime | int64 'granularity': 'month' # day | hour | month | year }, cluster_by = ['store_id', 'order_ref'], # up to 4 columns require_partition_filter = true, partition_expiration_days = none, labels = {'layer': 'analytics'}, tags = ['daily'] ) }} -- integer-range partition partition_by = {'field': 'order_year', 'data_type': 'int64', 'range': {'start': 1995, 'end': 2030, 'interval': 1}}

incremental: merge {{ config( materialized = 'incremental', incremental_strategy = 'merge', unique_key = 'order_id', # or a list on_schema_change = 'append_new_columns',# ignore | fail | sync_all_columns partition_by = {'field': 'order_date', 'data_type': 'date'}, incremental_predicates = [ "dbt_internal_dest.order_date >= date_sub(current_date(), interval 30 day)" ] ) }} select * from {{ ref('int_orders') }} {% if is_incremental() %} where _landed_at > (select max(_landed_at) from {{ this }}) {% endif %} incremental_predicates prunes the target side of the merge. without it bigquery scans the whole destination on every run.

incremental: insert_overwrite {% set partitions_to_replace = [ 'current_date()', 'date_sub(current_date(), interval 1 day)' ] %} {{ config( materialized = 'incremental', incremental_strategy = 'insert_overwrite', partition_by = {'field': 'event_date', 'data_type': 'date'}, partitions = partitions_to_replace # static: cheapest ) }} select * from {{ ref('stg_events') }} {% if is_incremental() %} where event_date in ({{ partitions_to_replace | join(',') }}) {% endif %} replaces whole partitions, no row matching. leave out partitions for "dynamic" mode: dbt finds the partitions in the new data, at the cost of an extra query.

incremental: microbatch 1.9 {{ config( materialized = 'incremental', incremental_strategy = 'microbatch', event_time = 'order_date', batch_size = 'day', # hour | day | month | year begin = '2023-01-01', lookback = 2, partition_by = {'field': 'order_date', 'data_type': 'date', 'granularity': 'day'} ) }} -- no is_incremental() block: dbt filters each batch for you, -- and filters upstream refs that declare their own event_time select * from {{ ref('stg_orders') }} dbt run -s fct_orders --event-time-start 2024-01-01 --event-time-end 2024-02-01 dbt retry # re-runs only failed batches

reliability checklist idempotent tasks: a rerun of the same interval gives the same result. use write_truncate on a partition ( table$20250131 ) or a merge, never a blind append. no heavy work at parse time: top-level code runs on every scheduler parse. no api calls or db queries outside tasks. small xcoms: pass uris and counts, not dataframes. deferrable operators and sensors ( deferrable=true ) free worker slots while waiting. pools cap concurrency against a shared resource: pool="bq_slots" . alert on failure: on_failure_callback in default_args . pin provider versions in your composer/requirements; operator args change between majors.

airflow 2 → 3 gotchas authoring imports move to airflow.sdk ( dag , task , asset , variable ). schedule_interval and timetable args are removed: use schedule . catchup now defaults to false . context keys execution_date , next_ds , prev_ds , tomorrow_ds are removed. bash, python and empty operators live in the apache-airflow-providers-standard package. tasks no longer get direct metadata-db access; use the rest api or the sdk. subdagoperator and slas are gone; use task groups and deadline alerts. run ruff check --select air3 dags/ to find most of these.

what an api is an api (application programming interface) is a contract: the operations a system offers, the inputs they take, the outputs and errors they return, and the rules for calling them. the contract is what other teams build against; the implementation behind it can change freely as long as the contract holds. public / partner / internal: who may call it, and so how strict versioning, security and documentation must be. synchronous: the caller waits (rest, grpc, graphql). asynchronous: the caller sends and moves on; the result arrives later (queues, events, webhooks). spec first: write the contract (openapi, protobuf, asyncapi) before the code; generate clients and docs from it.

rest in practice resources are nouns with urls: /orders , /orders/{id} , /stores/{code}/orders . http methods are the verbs: get reads, post creates, put replaces, patch updates part, delete removes. stateless: each request carries everything needed (including auth); no server session required. status codes carry meaning: 200, 201 created (+ location ), 204, 400, 401, 403, 404, 409 conflict, 422, 429, 500, 503. errors as problem details (rfc 9457): type , title , status , detail . pagination with a cursor ( ?cursor=…&limit=50 ) rather than deep offsets. filtering and sorting by query parameters: ?store=1_05&from=2024-01-01&sort=-order_date . caching with etag / if-none-match and cache-control . method safe idempotent get, head yes yes put, delete no yes post no no: use an idempotency-key header patch no not guaranteed

an openapi contract openapi: 3.1.0 info: { title: shop api, version: 1.2.0 } paths: /v1/orders/{id}: get: operationid: getorder parameters: - { name: id, in: path, required: true, schema: { type: string } } responses: "200": description: the order content: application/json: schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/order" } "404": description: not found content: application/problem+json: schema: { $ref: "#/components/schemas/problem" } components: schemas: order: type: object required: [id, orderref, store] properties: id: { type: string } orderref: { type: string } store: { type: string } orderdate: { type: [string, "null"], format: date } securityschemes: bearer: { type: http, scheme: bearer, bearerformat: jwt } security: [ { bearer: [] } ]

api styles compared style shape strengths weaknesses use for rest / json over http resources + http verbs universal, cacheable, easy to debug over- or under-fetching; loose typing unless specified public and partner apis, most web services grpc protobuf messages over http/2, generated clients fast, strongly typed, streaming both ways not browser-native; harder to inspect internal service-to-service calls graphql one endpoint; client asks for exactly the fields it needs flexible for uis; one round trip for nested data caching, query cost control, authorisation per field front ends combining many sources webhooks your server calls the client's url when something happens no polling delivery retries, signature checks, client downtime notifying partners (payments, git events) messaging / events publish to a topic; subscribers consume decoupling, buffering, fan-out eventual consistency, duplicates, debugging integration between domains, pipelines websockets / sse long-lived connection for pushes real-time updates, streaming responses connection management at scale live dashboards, chat, streaming ai output soap / xml envelope with wsdl contract strict contracts, ws-* standards verbose, legacy tooling integrating older enterprise systems file exchange csv/parquet drops on sftp or buckets simple, bulk latency, partial files, schema drift bulk data between organisations

grpc contract syntax = "proto3"; package shop.v1; service orderservice { rpc getorder(getorderrequest) returns (order); rpc streamnew(streamnewrequest) returns (stream order); // server streaming } message getorderrequest { string id = 1; } message streamnewrequest { string store = 1; } message order { string id = 1; string order_ref = 2; string store = 3; string order_date = 4; // iso date; field numbers never reused } compatibility rules: add fields with new numbers; never change or reuse a field number; reserve removed ones.

api versioning and evolution additive changes are safe: new endpoints, new optional fields, new enum values clients are told to tolerate. breaking changes (removing or renaming fields, changing types or meaning) need a new version. where to version: in the path ( /v1/ ) is the most visible and the easiest to route at a gateway; headers are cleaner but harder to test. deprecate politely: announce, add deprecation and sunset headers, measure who still calls, then remove. meaning can break without a schema change: a field whose values change meaning is a breaking change even if its type is the same. contract tests in ci catch accidental breaks.

reliable integration timeouts on every call; retries only for idempotent operations, with backoff and jitter. idempotency keys for posts that create or charge. long-running work: return 202 accepted with a status url, or emit an event when done. webhooks you send: sign the payload (hmac), retry with backoff, let clients replay. webhooks you receive: verify the signature, respond fast, process asynchronously, dedupe by event id. rate limits with 429 and retry-after . correlation ids ( traceparent ) passed through every hop.

integration styles (oldest to newest) file transfer: one system writes files, another reads them. simple and still common for bulk data. shared database: several systems read and write the same tables. avoid: no system owns the schema. remote procedure call: one system calls another's api (rest, grpc). simple; couples availability. messaging: systems exchange messages through a broker. decoupled in time; more moving parts. from enterprise integration patterns (hohpe and woolf), still the best catalogue of messaging patterns.

the idea in one paragraph a graphql server publishes a schema : the types, their fields and how they connect. clients send a query to a single endpoint (usually post /graphql ) describing the shape of data they want, and get back json in exactly that shape. reads are queries , writes are mutations , live updates are subscriptions . each field is filled by a resolver function on the server, which can read from a database, another service or a cache. rest graphql endpoints many, one per resource one response shape fixed by the server chosen by the client nested data several round trips or custom endpoints one request contract openapi (optional) the schema (built in, introspectable) http caching natural for get harder: needs persisted queries or client caches errors http status codes usually 200 with an errors array; partial data possible versioning /v1, /v2 evolve one schema; deprecate fields best for public apis, simple resources, caching uis combining many related entities; many client types

schema (sdl) type query { order(id: id!): order searchorders(q: string!, store: string, first: int = 20, after: string): orderconnection! } type mutation { addtolist(listid: id!, orderid: id!): savedlist! } type subscription { orderadded(store: string!): order! } type order { id: id! orderref: string! orderdate: date # custom scalar store: store! items: [string!]! similar(first: int = 10): [order!]! } type store { code: id! name: string! state: string } scalar date ! means non-null. [string!]! is a non-null list of non-null strings.

queries, variables, fragments query search($q: string!, $store: string, $after: string) { searchorders(q: $q, store: $store, first: 10, after: $after) { edges { node { ...ordercard } } pageinfo { hasnextpage endcursor } } } fragment ordercard on order { id orderref orderdate store { name } } # variables (sent separately as json): # { "q": "umbrella", "store": "1_05" } curl -s https://api.example.com/graphql \ -h "authorization: bearer $token" -h "content-type: application/json" \ -d '{"query":"query($id:id!){order(id:$id){orderref store{name}}}","variables":{"id":"123"}}' always use variables, never string interpolation into the query: it enables caching of the parsed query and avoids injection.

resolvers and the n+1 problem asking for 20 orders, each with its store , naively runs 1 query for the list and 20 more for stores: n+1 queries. batch loading (dataloader pattern): collect all the store ids requested in one execution step, fetch them in one query, and hand each order its store. per-request cache: the same store requested twice in one query is loaded once. spring: @batchmapping . quarkus: a resolver taking @source list<…> . python strawberry: dataloader . measure: log query counts per graphql request in tests.

spring for graphql // schema files: src/main/resources/graphql/*.graphqls @controller class ordergraphql { private final orderservice orders; private final storeservice stores; ordergraphql(orderservice o, storeservice s) { orders = o; stores = s; } @querymapping order order(@argument string id) { return orders.find(id).orelse(null); // null → field is null, no error } @mutationmapping savedlist addtolist(@argument string listid, @argument string orderid) { return orders.addtolist(listid, orderid); // check ownership inside } @batchmapping // one query for all stores map<order, store> store(list<order> list) { map<string, store> bycode = stores.bycodes( list.stream().map(order::storeid).collect(collectors.toset())); return list.stream().collect(collectors.tomap(o -> o, o -> bycode.get(o.storeid()))); } } // scalar date needs an implementation, here from graphql-java-extended-scalars @configuration class graphqlconfig { @bean runtimewiringconfigurer scalars() { return w -> w.scalar(extendedscalars.date); } } // test @graphqltest(ordergraphql.class) class ordergraphqltest { @autowired graphqltester tester; @mockitobean orderservice orders; @mockitobean storeservice stores; @test void returnsnullforunknownid() { tester.document("{ order(id: \"x\") { orderref } }") .execute().path("order").valueisnull(); } }

quarkus (smallrye graphql) // quarkus ext add smallrye-graphql → schema generated from code @graphqlapi public class orderapi { @inject orderservice orders; @inject storeservice stores; @query public order order(@nonnull string id) { return orders.find(id).orelse(null); } @mutation public savedlist addtolist(@nonnull string listid, @nonnull string orderid) { return orders.addtolist(listid, orderid); } // batched field resolver: adds order.store, one call for all orders public list<store> store(@source list<order> list) { return stores.inorderfor(list); } } // graphql ui in dev mode: http://localhost:8080/q/graphql-ui spring for graphql is schema-first (you write sdl); smallrye graphql is code-first (the schema comes from your classes).

python (strawberry) import strawberry from strawberry.dataloader import dataloader async def load_stores(codes: list[str]) -> list["store"]: rows = await db.stores_by_codes(codes) # one query by = {r.code: r for r in rows} return [by.get(c) for c in codes] # same order as input @strawberry.type class store: code: strawberry.id name: str @strawberry.type class order: id: strawberry.id order_ref: str store_id: strawberry.private[str] @strawberry.field async def store(self, info: strawberry.info) -> store: return await info.context["store_loader"].load(self.store_id) @strawberry.type class query: @strawberry.field async def order(self, id: strawberry.id) -> order | none: return await db.order(id) schema = strawberry.schema(query=query) # context per request: {"store_loader": dataloader(load_fn=load_stores)}

pagination: connections type orderconnection { edges: [orderedge!]! pageinfo: pageinfo! totalcount: int # optional; can be expensive } type orderedge { cursor: string! node: order! } type pageinfo { hasnextpage: boolean! endcursor: string } cursor-based (the relay connection convention): stable under inserts, works with keyset queries in the database. cap first on the server (e.g. max 100). make cursors opaque (base64 of the sort key and id).

errors { "data": { "order": null }, "errors": [{ "message": "not authorised to view this order", "path": ["order"], "extensions": { "code": "forbidden" } }] } a response can hold partial data plus errors; clients must check errors even on http 200. put a stable machine-readable extensions.code on every error. expected business outcomes (validation failed, not found) can also be modelled in the schema as result types ( union saveresult = savedlist | validationerror ). never leak stack traces or sql in message .

security authorise per field and per object in resolvers or the service layer; one endpoint means url-based rules cannot protect anything. limit query depth and complexity so a client cannot request similar { similar { similar … } } a thousand levels deep. cap list sizes and set timeouts per request. persisted queries (allow-list of known query hashes) for first-party clients: blocks arbitrary queries and enables get caching. introspection: consider disabling it in production for private apis; it is not a security boundary, just less help to attackers. rate limit by cost, not by request count, since one request can be cheap or enormous. batching attacks: limit the number of operations or aliases per request (aliases can repeat a login mutation hundreds of times).

performance and caching batch loaders everywhere a field fetches by key. select only needed columns: look at the requested fields (selection set) before querying. client caches (apollo client, relay, urql) normalise results by type and id; give every object a stable id . http caching needs get with persisted queries; otherwise cache in resolvers or the data layer. trace per resolver (opentelemetry) to find slow fields.

schema evolution and scale add freely: new types, new fields, new optional arguments. deprecate before removing: oldfield: string @deprecated(reason: "use newfield") , then watch usage and remove. never change a field's type or meaning in place. schema checks in ci compare against the published schema and fail on breaking changes. federation: several teams own subgraphs (orders, users, billing) composed by a router into one supergraph (apollo federation, graphql mesh). behind a gateway: apigee or another gateway can still handle authentication and rate limits in front of /graphql .

the model concept meaning topic a named stream of records, e.g. order.placed partition an ordered, append-only log; a topic has many. ordering is guaranteed only within a partition. record key, value, headers, timestamp. the key decides the partition (same key → same partition → ordered). offset a record's position in its partition. consumers track how far they have read. broker a server storing partitions. a cluster has several. replication factor copies of each partition on different brokers (3 is typical). leader / isr one replica takes reads and writes; in-sync replicas are caught-up followers. consumer group consumers sharing the work: each partition is read by one consumer in the group. max parallelism = partition count. retention records kept for a time or size, then deleted, regardless of whether they were read. compaction keep only the latest record per key; a table-like topic. kraft kafka's built-in metadata quorum, replacing zookeeper (removed in kafka 4.0). unlike a queue, reading does not remove a record. many groups can read the same topic independently, and a group can rewind to replay.

durability and delivery settings producer acks=all with topic min.insync.replicas=2 and replication factor 3: a write survives one broker failure. enable.idempotence=true (the default in modern clients): retries do not create duplicates within a partition. at-least-once consuming: process, then commit the offset. a crash between the two replays the record, so consumers must be idempotent. at-most-once: commit before processing. rarely what you want. exactly-once inside kafka (read-process-write between topics) with transactions and isolation.level=read_committed . side effects outside kafka still need idempotency. ordering: choose the key for the entity whose events must stay in order (order id, account id).

cli essentials b=localhost:9092 kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server $b --create --topic order.placed \ --partitions 6 --replication-factor 3 --config retention.ms=604800000 kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server $b --describe --topic order.placed kafka-console-producer.sh --bootstrap-server $b --topic order.placed \ --property parse.key=true --property key.separator=: # type: ord123:{"store":"1_05"} kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server $b --topic order.placed \ --group debug --from-beginning --property print.key=true kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server $b --describe --group indexer # lag per partition kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server $b --group indexer \ --reset-offsets --to-datetime 2026-11-01t00:00:00.000 --topic order.placed --execute consumer lag (latest offset minus committed offset) is the key health metric: growing lag means consumers cannot keep up.

spring for apache kafka # application.yml spring: kafka: bootstrap-servers: ${kafka_bootstrap} producer: acks: all key-serializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.stringserializer value-serializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.jsonserializer consumer: group-id: indexer auto-offset-reset: earliest key-deserializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.stringdeserializer value-deserializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.jsondeserializer # the default is string properties: spring.json.trusted.packages: "com.example.events" # spring kafka 4 (boot 4) deprecates jsonserializer/jsondeserializer for jacksonjsonserializer/jacksonjsondeserializer @service class publisher { private final kafkatemplate<string, orderplaced> kafka; publisher(kafkatemplate<string, orderplaced> kafka) { this.kafka = kafka; } void publish(orderplaced e) { kafka.send("order.placed", e.orderref(), e); } // key = order ref } @component class indexer { @kafkalistener(topics = "order.placed", groupid = "indexer") void on(orderplaced e) { index.upsert(e); // idempotent: same event twice is harmless } } // retries and a dead-letter topic for poison messages @bean defaulterrorhandler errorhandler(kafkatemplate<object, object> t) { return new defaulterrorhandler(new deadletterpublishingrecoverer(t), new fixedbackoff(1000l, 3)); }

quarkus with kafka # application.properties (quarkus-messaging-kafka) kafka.bootstrap.servers=${kafka_bootstrap} mp.messaging.incoming.placed.connector=smallrye-kafka mp.messaging.incoming.placed.topic=order.placed mp.messaging.incoming.placed.group.id=indexer mp.messaging.outgoing.indexed.connector=smallrye-kafka mp.messaging.outgoing.indexed.topic=order.indexed # the emitter below needs its own channel: a channel has one producer unless you merge mp.messaging.outgoing.reindexed.connector=smallrye-kafka mp.messaging.outgoing.reindexed.topic=order.indexed @applicationscoped public class indexer { @incoming("placed") @outgoing("indexed") public orderindexed process(orderplaced e) { return index.upsert(e); } } @applicationscoped public class publisher { @inject @channel("reindexed") emitter<orderindexed> out; // not "indexed": the method above feeds that void send(orderindexed e) { out.send(e); } } in dev and test, dev services starts a kafka-compatible broker for you.

python (confluent-kafka) from confluent_kafka import producer, consumer p = producer({"bootstrap.servers": bootstrap, "acks": "all", "enable.idempotence": true}) p.produce("order.placed", key=order_ref, value=json.dumps(evt), callback=lambda err, msg: err and log.error("send failed: %s", err)) p.flush() c = consumer({"bootstrap.servers": bootstrap, "group.id": "indexer", "auto.offset.reset": "earliest", "enable.auto.commit": false}) c.subscribe(["order.placed"]) while true: msg = c.poll(1.0) if msg is none: continue if msg.error(): log.error(msg.error()); continue handle(json.loads(msg.value())) # idempotent c.commit(message=msg, asynchronous=false) # commit after processing

the ecosystem schema registry with avro, protobuf or json schema: producers and consumers agree on schemas; compatibility rules block breaking changes. kafka connect: ready-made source and sink connectors (databases, gcs, bigquery) without custom code. debezium: change data capture from databases into kafka topics. kafka streams: a java library for stateful stream processing (joins, windows, aggregates) inside your service. flink: a separate engine for large-scale stream processing. on gcp: managed service for apache kafka runs clusters for you; dataflow and bigquery have kafka connectors.

kafka vs pub/sub kafka pub/sub model partitioned log; consumers track offsets topics and subscriptions; per-message ack ordering per partition (by key) per ordering key, when enabled replay rewind offsets within retention seek to a time or snapshot within retention capacity you size brokers and partitions (managed or self-run) serverless, scales automatically ecosystem connect, streams, schema registry, debezium native gcp integrations (bigquery, gcs, dataflow, eventarc) choose when kafka skills or tools exist; log semantics, compaction, very high throughput gcp-native, simple operations, global delivery

designing topics name by event, past tense: order.placed , order.paid . partitions: enough for peak consumer parallelism with headroom; adding later changes key-to-partition mapping. keys: the entity that needs ordering; avoid hot keys. payload: include an event id, type, version and timestamp; keep events self-describing. retention: long enough to recover from a consumer outage and replay. dead-letter topic for records that keep failing, with alerting on it.

who is involved party role customer pays with a card, upi, net banking or wallet merchant you: the business being paid payment gateway / aggregator collects payment details securely, routes the transaction, gives you apis, checkout and webhooks (razorpay, stripe, payu, cashfree) acquirer the merchant's bank, which receives the funds card network visa, mastercard, rupay: routes card transactions between banks issuer the customer's bank, which approves or declines upi (npci) india's real-time account-to-account network; apps such as phonepe, google pay, paytm act as front ends regulator in india the rbi: rules on recurring payments, tokenisation, data storage and aggregators

card payment lifecycle authorise: the issuer checks funds and fraud and places a hold. with 3-d secure (otp or app approval) the customer authenticates. capture: the merchant confirms the charge (automatically or later, e.g. after shipping). an uncaptured authorisation expires. settle: funds move to the gateway, then to your bank account, usually t+1 or t+2, minus fees. refund: full or partial, returned through the same route; takes days to reach the customer. chargeback / dispute: the customer disputes with their bank; you submit evidence or lose the funds plus a fee.

upi in brief intent / qr flow: your checkout opens the customer's upi app (or shows a qr); they approve with their upi pin. collect flow: you send a payment request to a upi id; the customer approves in their app. (being phased down for many use cases; check current npci rules.) real-time and irrevocable from the customer's side; refunds are separate transactions. upi autopay: recurring mandates the customer approves once, for subscriptions. pending is normal: a payment can sit in a pending state for minutes; your system must wait for the final status rather than assume failure.

standard integration flow (server-verified) create an order on your server with the amount in the smallest unit (paise) and your own receipt id. store it as created . open the gateway's checkout in the browser or app with that order id. card and upi details go to the gateway, never to your servers. checkout returns payment id, order id and a signature to your client, which sends them to your server. verify the signature on the server and fetch the payment from the gateway api to confirm amount, currency and status. webhooks ( payment.captured , payment.failed , refunds, disputes) arrive at your endpoint; verify their signature and update state idempotently. treat webhooks and api fetches as the source of truth, never the browser. fulfil only when your order is paid according to the server. reconcile daily against the gateway's settlement reports.

razorpay: order and verification # create an order (amount in paise: 50000 = ₹500.00) curl -u "$rzp_key_id:$rzp_key_secret" \ -x post https://api.razorpay.com/v1/orders \ -h "content-type: application/json" \ -d '{"amount":50000,"currency":"inr","receipt":"order_8421"}' // verify checkout signature: hmac-sha256(order_id + "|" + payment_id, key_secret) static boolean validcheckout(string orderid, string paymentid, string signature, string keysecret) throws exception { mac mac = mac.getinstance("hmacsha256"); mac.init(new secretkeyspec(keysecret.getbytes(utf_8), "hmacsha256")); string expected = hexformat.of().formathex( mac.dofinal((orderid + "|" + paymentid).getbytes(utf_8))); return messagedigest.isequal(expected.getbytes(utf_8), signature.getbytes(utf_8)); // constant time } // webhook: hmac-sha256 of the raw request body with the webhook secret, // compared with the x-razorpay-signature header. never re-serialise the json first. // the same event can arrive more than once: dedupe on the x-razorpay-event-id header.

stripe: paymentintent and webhook import stripe stripe.api_key = stripe_secret_key intent = stripe.paymentintent.create( amount=50000, currency="inr", metadata={"order_id": "order_8421"}, idempotency_key="order_8421-create", # safe to retry ) # return intent.client_secret to the front end, which confirms the payment # webhook endpoint def stripe_webhook(request): payload = request.body # raw bytes sig = request.headers["stripe-signature"] try: event = stripe.webhook.construct_event(payload, sig, webhook_secret) except (valueerror, stripe.signatureverificationerror): # older sdks: stripe.error.signatureverificationerror return 400 if not seen_before(event["id"]): # dedupe: webhooks repeat handle(event) return 200

payment state machine created ──checkout──▶ pending ──captured──▶ paid ──refund──▶ partially_refunded / refunded │ │ │ │ ├──failed──▶ failed └──dispute──▶ disputed ──▶ won / lost └──expired──▶ expired └──timeout──▶ (stay pending; poll the gateway; never assume) allow only valid transitions; reject or log anything else. events can arrive late or out of order (a webhook before the browser callback, a failure after a success for a different attempt). decide by the gateway's fetched status. keep every transition as an append-only event with its source (webhook, api fetch, user).

money-handling rules integers in the smallest unit (paise, cents) or decimal types; never floats. store the currency with every amount. compute prices and totals on the server. never trust an amount sent by the client. idempotency keys on every create, capture and refund call, derived from your own ids, so a retry cannot charge twice. webhook handlers are idempotent : dedupe by event id; applying the same event twice changes nothing. unknown is not failed: a timeout means "we do not know yet". poll the gateway before telling the customer it failed or retrying the charge. round once, at a defined step, with a documented rule (taxes, discounts, splits).

double-entry ledger create table ledger_entry ( id bigint generated always as identity primary key, txn_id uuid not null, -- groups the entries of one transaction account text not null, -- 'customer_receivable', 'gateway_clearing', 'revenue', 'gst_payable' amount_paise bigint not null, -- positive = debit, negative = credit currency char(3) not null, created_at timestamptz not null default now() ); -- every txn_id must sum to zero select txn_id from ledger_entry group by txn_id having sum(amount_paise) <> 0; -- must return nothing append only: corrections are new entries, never edits. balances are sums. this makes every rupee traceable and reconciliation possible.

subscriptions and recurring payments gateways model plans (price, interval) and subscriptions (a customer on a plan) with a mandate or saved token for charging. india: rbi e-mandate rules govern recurring card and upi payments: customer registration with authentication, pre-debit notifications, and extra authentication above a limit. check the current limits and rules; they have changed over time. handle the lifecycle via webhooks: activated, charged, payment failed, halted, cancelled, completed. dunning: retries on failed renewals, customer notices, grace periods, then downgrade or cancel. entitlements (what the user may use) are derived from subscription state in your system, updated only from verified events. proration rules for upgrades and downgrades mid-period, decided and written down.

security and compliance pci dss: use hosted checkout or the gateway's elements so card data never reaches your servers; your compliance scope stays small. card tokenisation (india): merchants may not store card numbers; saved cards use network or issuer tokens through the gateway. data localisation: rbi requires payment system data to be stored in india; confirm your gateway and your own storage comply. secrets: api keys and webhook secrets in a secret manager; separate test and live keys; rotate on staff changes. webhook endpoint: verify signatures on the raw body, reject old timestamps where provided, respond quickly, process asynchronously. fraud: use the gateway's risk tools, 3-d secure, velocity limits, and watch for card testing (many small failed attempts). tax and invoices: gst-compliant invoices with the correct rates and place of supply.

reconciliation download settlement and transaction reports from the gateway daily (api or dashboard). match each gateway transaction to your order by order id and amount. match settlements to bank credits, accounting for fees and taxes. flag mismatches: paid at gateway but not in your system (missed webhook), paid in your system but not settled, amount differences, unexpected refunds or disputes. resolve each one and record why. a rising mismatch count is an incident. run reconciliation as a scheduled job with run records, like any pipeline.

testing payments use the gateway's test mode keys, test cards and test upi ids for success, failure, 3-d secure and pending cases. replay recorded webhook payloads in automated tests; build fixtures from real test-mode events, not guesses. test duplicates, out-of-order events, timeouts and partial refunds explicitly. keep a test-mode end-to-end checkout in your release checks. never test with live keys or real cards in non-production environments.

operating payments metrics: payment success rate by method and bank, latency, webhook delay, pending count and age, refund rate, dispute rate. alerts: success rate drops, webhooks stop arriving, pending payments older than a threshold, reconciliation mismatches. support tools: look up an order's full event history; never let support edit payment state by hand. multiple gateways: routing or failover between gateways improves success rates, at the cost of more reconciliation.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain authorisation, capture, settlement, refunds and chargebacks explain the order → checkout → verify → webhook flow know why card data must never touch your servers 2 practitioner integrate a gateway with server-side verification and signed webhooks make payment calls and webhook handling idempotent model payments as a state machine; test with test-mode fixtures 3 senior design subscriptions, dunning and entitlements build a double-entry ledger and daily reconciliation own payment security, pci scope and regulatory rules (rbi) 4 expert design multi-gateway routing and payment platforms lead payments compliance and audits set money-handling standards across the organisation each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

data access // jdbcclient (3.2): plain sql, records out @repository class orderdao { private final jdbcclient jdbc; orderdao(jdbcclient jdbc) { this.jdbc = jdbc; } optional<orderdto> find(string orderref) { return jdbc.sql("select order_ref, order_date from orders where order_ref = :order_ref") .param("order_ref", orderref) .query(orderdto.class) .optional(); } int upsert(orderdto o) { return jdbc.sql(""" insert into orders (order_ref, order_date) values (:order_ref, :d) on conflict (order_ref) do update set order_date = excluded.order_date""") .param("order_ref", o.orderref()).param("d", o.orderdate()).update(); } } // spring data jpa interface orderrepo extends jparepository<order, long> { list<order> findbystoreidandorderdateafter(string store, localdate d); @query("select o from order o where o.orderref in :refs") list<order> byorderrefs(collection<string> refs); } @transactional // on a public method of a spring bean, called from outside it public void reload() { ... } @transactional(readonly = true) public list<orderdto> list() { ... } @transactional works through a proxy: a call from another method in the same class skips it.

event-driven systems services communicate by publishing events (facts about something that happened: orderplaced , orderpaid ) to a broker. other services subscribe and react. the producer does not know or wait for its consumers. term meaning event something that happened, past tense, immutable. many consumers. command a request to do something ( loadpartition ). one handler, may be refused. broker pub/sub, kafka, eventarc: stores and delivers messages. topic / subscription where events are published / one consumer group's view of them. at-least-once the usual guarantee: a message may arrive twice. consumers must be idempotent. ordering usually not global. use an ordering key (per order, per entity) when sequence matters. dead-letter queue where messages go after repeated failures, so one bad message does not block the rest. gains: loose coupling, independent scaling, new consumers added without touching producers. costs: eventual consistency, harder debugging (no single call stack), duplicates and reordering to handle, schema changes that ripple to unknown consumers.

choreography vs orchestration choreography orchestration how each service reacts to events and emits its own. no one is in charge. a central orchestrator tells each service what to do next and tracks state. analogy dancers who each know their cue a conductor with the score good for few steps, independent teams, fan-out reactions ("on landing, also index and notify") many steps, strict order, retries, compensation, a need to answer "where is this run?" risk the overall flow exists only in people's heads; cycles and lost steps are hard to see the orchestrator is a central dependency and can grow into a god service tools pub/sub, kafka, eventarc airflow, cloud workflows, temporal, step functions, a custom orchestrator with a ledger many systems mix them: orchestration inside a bounded process (a data pipeline's stages), choreography between domains (the pipeline publishes "ready"; the search team reacts).

saga: transactions across services a distributed transaction across several databases cannot use one acid commit. a saga splits it into local transactions, each with a compensating action that undoes it if a later step fails. book a paid subscription: 1. billing: create pending invoice ↺ compensate: void invoice 2. payments: charge card ↺ compensate: refund charge 3. accounts: activate plan ↺ compensate: deactivate plan 4. email: send welcome (no compensation: an email cannot be undone, so it runs last) step 3 fails → run compensations in reverse: refund (2), void invoice (1). orchestrated saga: a coordinator runs the steps and the compensations, and stores the saga's state. easier to follow and test. choreographed saga: each service listens for the previous step's event and emits its own, including failure events that trigger compensation. compensation is a new action, not a rollback: a refund is not "un-charging". some steps (an email sent) cannot be undone, so put them last. every step and compensation must be idempotent, because messages repeat. expose intermediate states ( pending , active , cancelled ): other readers will see them.

transactional outbox problem: you update your database and publish an event. if one succeeds and the other fails, they disagree. begin; update orders set status = 'paid' where id = 42; insert into outbox (id, topic, payload, created_at) values (gen_random_uuid(), 'order.paid', '{"order_id":42}', now()); commit; -- relay process (or cdc on the outbox table) select * from outbox where published_at is null order by created_at limit 100 for update skip locked; -- publish each, then update outbox set published_at = now() where id = any($1); one local transaction makes the state change and the intent to publish atomic. the relay may publish twice; consumers dedupe by event id.

idempotent consumers -- remember what you processed, in the same transaction as the effect create table processed_events (event_id uuid primary key, processed_at timestamptz); begin; insert into processed_events values ($event_id, now()) on conflict do nothing; -- if 0 rows inserted: duplicate, skip the effect update accounts set plan = 'pro' where id = $account; commit; prefer naturally idempotent operations: set status = 'paid' rather than balance = balance + 10 . apis take an idempotency key header so a retried post does not charge twice. batch jobs overwrite a partition or merge on a key.

cqrs & event sourcing cqrs (command query responsibility segregation): writes go to a model shaped for updates; reads come from separate models shaped for queries (a search index, a denormalised table). reads are eventually consistent. event sourcing: store the sequence of events as the source of truth; current state is derived by replaying them. full audit history and time travel, at the cost of complexity, schema versioning of old events, and snapshots for speed. append-only ledger is the lightweight version many data platforms use: one row per state change, current state from a "latest event" view. never update, never delete. use them where history and audit are the product. most crud services do not need either.

common architectural patterns pattern what it is use when / watch out layered (n-tier) controller → service → repository → database default for a service. keep controllers thin and rules in services. hexagonal (ports & adapters) domain logic in the centre; databases, apis and queues are adapters behind interfaces logic you want to test without infrastructure, or swap providers. modular monolith one deployable with enforced module boundaries most teams' best starting point. split later along boundaries that proved real. microservices independently deployed services owning their data many teams, different scaling needs. costs: network failures, distributed data, ops overhead. api gateway single entry point: routing, auth, rate limits many backends behind one public surface. backend for frontend (bff) a thin api per client type (web, mobile) clients with very different data needs. strangler fig route features one by one from the old system to the new replacing a legacy system without a big-bang rewrite. cache-aside read the cache; on a miss read the db and fill the cache read-heavy data that tolerates brief staleness. decide invalidation up front. circuit breaker stop calling a failing dependency for a while; fail fast prevents one slow service taking down its callers. retry with backoff + jitter retry transient failures with growing, randomised waits only for idempotent calls. cap attempts; never retry 4xx validation errors. bulkhead separate pools for separate dependencies one slow dependency cannot exhaust all threads or connections. queue-based load levelling put work on a queue; workers drain it at their pace spiky load in front of a resource with fixed capacity. sidecar a helper container next to the app (proxy, log shipper) cross-cutting concerns in kubernetes and service meshes.

consistency & trade-offs cap: during a network partition a distributed store chooses consistency (refuse some requests) or availability (answer, possibly stale). pacelc: and when there is no partition, it trades latency against consistency. strong consistency: every read sees the latest write. eventual: replicas converge, reads may lag. read-your-writes: a user always sees their own changes. exactly-once delivery is rarely real end to end; build at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing. fallacies of distributed computing: the network is not reliable, latency is not zero, bandwidth is not infinite, and the topology changes.

design review checklist who owns each piece of data, and who may write it? what happens when each dependency is slow, down, or returns garbage? which operations must be atomic, and how is that achieved across boundaries? what is retried, and is it idempotent? how do we see a request or run end to end (ids, traces, ledger)? what is the expected load, and what breaks first at 10×? how do we deploy, migrate and roll back without downtime? what is the simplest design that meets today's need?

choosing a style list the quality attributes that matter most, in order: e.g. correctness and auditability, then cost, then latency. note the constraints: team size and skills, budget, regulations, existing systems. pick the simplest style that satisfies the top attributes; resist adding patterns "for later". identify the riskiest assumption and test it with a spike or prototype. record the decision and its trade-offs in an adr.

architecture decision record # adr 0042: serve order search from postgres, not a search engine status: accepted (2026-11-12) context: 20 m orders, ~60 searches/s peak, p95 < 500 ms; team already runs postgres; no search-engine skills. decision: postgres full-text (gin) + b-tree filters on a read replica; revisit if p95 > 500 ms or relevance complaints exceed x/month. alternatives: elasticsearch (more ops, better relevance); bigquery (latency too high for interactive search). consequences: + one database to run − relevance tuning limited links: load test results, issue #… one decision per record, numbered, never edited after acceptance; supersede it with a new one. keep them in the repo.
