monolith, modular monolith, microservices monolith modular monolith microservices deployables one one, with enforced internal modules many, deployed independently data one shared database one database, schema per module each service owns its data calls between parts in-process in-process through module apis over the network scaling whole app whole app per service team fit one small team one to a few teams many teams owning services end to end main cost tangling as it grows discipline to keep boundaries distributed-systems complexity and operations most systems should start as a modular monolith and extract a service only when a boundary has proved stable and there is a concrete reason: independent scaling, a different release cadence, a separate team, or different technology or security needs.

what microservices buy, and cost gains teams deploy their service without coordinating a big release. scale and tune each service for its own load. a failure can be contained to one service. different services can use different technologies where it helps. costs network calls fail, time out and add latency. no cross-service transactions: sagas and eventual consistency instead. debugging needs distributed tracing; testing needs contracts. many pipelines, deployments, dashboards and on-call rotations.

how to split services by business capability or bounded context (domain-driven design): search, carts, billing, identity. not by technical layer (a "database service" is an anti-pattern). each service owns its data and is the only one that writes it. others ask through its api or react to its events. high cohesion inside, loose coupling between: a typical change should touch one service. align with teams (conway's law): one team owns a service end to end. size by responsibility, not lines of code. too many tiny services ("nano-services") multiply network calls and operations for no gain. test the split: if two services must always deploy together, they are one service.

communication style use for watch out for synchronous rest / grpc queries that need an answer now chains of calls: latency adds up and availability multiplies down asynchronous events (kafka, pub/sub) telling others something happened eventual consistency, duplicates, ordering asynchronous commands (queues) work another service should do retries, dead letters, idempotency prefer events between domains; keep synchronous calls shallow (ideally one hop). cache or replicate the data you need from other services (from their events) rather than calling them on every request. see apis & integration , kafka and graphql .

infrastructure around services service discovery: kubernetes dns names, cloud run urls, or a registry. never hard-code instance ips. api gateway at the edge for authentication, rate limits and routing ( apigee ); a backend for frontend per client type when needs differ. service mesh (istio / cloud service mesh) for mtls, retries and traffic splitting between services, without code in each one. configuration and secrets injected at runtime per environment. platform blueprint: a service template with logging, tracing, health checks, security and ci already wired, so each new service starts correct.

resilience in code (spring + resilience4j) @service class mirrorclient { private final restclient http; mirrorclient(restclient http) { this.http = http; } @circuitbreaker(name = "mirror", fallbackmethod = "unavailable") @retry(name = "mirror") listing list(string prefix) { return http.get().uri("/objects?prefix={p}", prefix).retrieve().body(listing.class); } // honest degradation: "cannot see", never "nothing there" listing unavailable(string prefix, throwable t) { return listing.unknown("mirror unavailable: " + t.getmessage()); } } resilience4j: circuitbreaker: instances: mirror: slidingwindowsize: 20 failureratethreshold: 50 waitdurationinopenstate: 30s retry: instances: mirror: maxattempts: 3 waitduration: 200ms enableexponentialbackoff: true quarkus offers the same through microprofile fault tolerance ( @retry , @circuitbreaker , @timeout , @fallback ). always set a client timeout too.

data across services database per service: separate schemas or instances; no other service reads its tables. cross-service transactions become sagas with compensating steps. reliable events with the transactional outbox , so a state change and its event never disagree. queries across services: api composition (call and combine) for small cases; a read model built from events (cqrs) for heavy ones. reporting goes to the warehouse via events or cdc, not by joining services' databases. details on architecture and event sourcing .

observability is not optional distributed tracing (opentelemetry): one trace id follows a request through every service, queue and database call. structured logs with trace id, service, version and request id on every line. metrics per service: rate, errors, duration (red) and saturation; slos on user-facing ones. health endpoints: liveness (restart me) separate from readiness (send me traffic). dependency maps from traces show who calls whom, and where latency comes from.

testing microservices unit and component tests inside each service, with its own database in a container. contract tests (pact, spring cloud contract) between consumers and providers, run in both pipelines, so a provider cannot break a consumer unnoticed. a few end-to-end tests of critical journeys in a shared environment. event schema checks with a schema registry and compatibility rules. resilience tests: kill or slow a dependency and check the caller degrades as designed.

security between services zero trust: authenticate every call, even inside the network. service identity: mtls from a mesh, or google-signed id tokens between cloud run services. user context: propagate the user's token or a signed internal token; each service still checks its own permissions. least privilege per service: its own service account, database user and secrets.

anti-patterns distributed monolith: services that must be deployed together or share a database. shared database written by several services. chatty synchronous chains: a calls b calls c calls d for one request. nano-services too small to justify their operational cost. shared libraries with business logic that force lock-step upgrades (shared infrastructure blueprints are fine). no ownership: services nobody is on call for. splitting before understanding the domain: boundaries drawn too early are expensive to move.

migrating from a monolith make the monolith modular first: enforce module boundaries and separate each module's data. pick one capability with a clear boundary and a real reason to move. put a routing layer (gateway or proxy) in front, and route that capability's traffic to the new service ( strangler fig ). move its data, with a period of syncing or dual reads, and make the new service the only writer. remove the old code. repeat only if the first extraction paid off.

readiness checklist can you deploy a service with one automated pipeline, in minutes? do you have centralised logs, metrics and tracing? can you create a new service from a template in under an hour? do teams own services end to end, including on-call? are the domain boundaries understood and stable? if several answers are no, a modular monolith will serve you better for now.

the idea most systems store current state and overwrite it: a subscription row says plan = 'pro' . event sourcing stores the sequence of facts instead: subscriptionstarted(basic) , planupgraded(pro) , paymentfailed , paymentsucceeded . current state is computed by replaying (folding) those events. the events are the source of truth; every other view is derived from them and can be rebuilt. term meaning event an immutable fact in the past tense, with data and metadata (who, when, causation) stream the ordered events of one entity, e.g. subscription-42 aggregate the entity that enforces business rules; rebuilt from its stream; decides which new events a command produces command a request to change something ( upgradeplan ); may be rejected event store append-only storage of streams with per-stream versions projection / read model a view built from events for querying (a table, a search index, a cache) snapshot saved aggregate state at a version, to avoid replaying long streams cqrs separate models for writes (commands) and reads (queries); event sourcing usually comes with it

when it is worth it good fits history is the product: audit trails, finance, legal records, compliance. you need to answer "what was the state on date x, and why?" several different read models from the same changes. complex domains where business events are first-class (orders, claims, subscriptions). poor fits simple crud with no interest in history. teams new to the pattern on a deadline. data that must be truly deleted on request with no workaround. apply it to the one part of the system that needs it, not the whole system.

the flow a command arrives: upgradeplan(subscription-42, pro) . load the aggregate's events (from the latest snapshot) and fold them into current state. the aggregate checks business rules and decides zero or more new events. append them with the expected version (optimistic concurrency). if someone else appended first, reload and retry. projections consume new events and update read models. queries read from the read models, which may lag slightly behind.

an aggregate in java sealed interface subevent permits started, planupgraded, cancelled {} record started(string id, string plan, instant at) implements subevent {} record planupgraded(string id, string plan, instant at) implements subevent {} record cancelled(string id, string reason, instant at) implements subevent {} enum status { active, cancelled } record subscription(string id, string plan, status status, int version) { static subscription replay(list<subevent> events) { subscription s = null; for (subevent e : events) s = apply(s, e); return s; } static subscription apply(subscription s, subevent e) { // pure: no side effects return switch (e) { case started st -> new subscription(st.id(), st.plan(), status.active, 1); case planupgraded u -> new subscription(s.id(), u.plan(), s.status(), s.version() + 1); case cancelled c -> new subscription(s.id(), s.plan(), status.cancelled, s.version() + 1); }; } list<subevent> upgrade(string newplan, instant now) { // decide if (status != status.active) throw new illegalstateexception("subscription not active"); if (plan.equals(newplan)) return list.of(); // idempotent: nothing to do return list.of(new planupgraded(id, newplan, now)); } } separate decide (rules, may reject) from apply (pure state change). apply must never fail for a stored event: it already happened.

an event store in postgres create table events ( global_position bigint generated always as identity primary key, stream_id text not null, version int not null, type text not null, data jsonb not null, metadata jsonb not null default '{}', -- user, causation_id, correlation_id recorded_at timestamptz not null default now(), unique (stream_id, version) -- optimistic concurrency ); -- load a stream select type, data, version from events where stream_id = 'subscription-42' order by version; -- append, expecting the stream to be at version 3 insert into events (stream_id, version, type, data) values ('subscription-42', 4, 'planupgraded', '{"plan":"pro"}'); -- unique violation → another writer got version 4 first → reload, re-decide, retry caution: identity values are assigned at insert, not commit, so with concurrent writers a projection reading by global_position can miss a row committed late. dedicated event stores (kurrentdb, formerly eventstoredb) or a transactional outbox with careful checkpointing handle this.

projections and read models // a projection keeps a checkpoint and is idempotent void handle(storedevent e) { tx.run(() -> { switch (e.payload()) { case started s -> db.upsert("subscription_view", s.id(), map.of("plan", s.plan(), "status", "active")); case planupgraded u -> db.update("subscription_view", u.id(), map.of("plan", u.plan())); case cancelled c -> db.update("subscription_view", c.id(), map.of("status", "cancelled")); } db.savecheckpoint("subscription_view", e.globalposition()); // same transaction }); } store the checkpoint in the same transaction as the update, so a crash never applies an event twice or skips one. to change a read model, build a new one by replaying all events, then switch reads to it. read models are eventually consistent. show users "updating…" or read their own writes from the aggregate when it matters.

evolving events events are immutable and permanent. you cannot fix old ones in place; plan their shape carefully. additive changes (new optional fields with defaults) are safe. version the event type ( planupgraded.v2 ) when the meaning changes. upcasting: convert old event versions to the current shape when reading, so the code handles one version. never rename or reuse an event type for a different meaning. name events in business language ( paymentfailed ), not technical ( rowupdated ).

snapshots, size and deletion snapshots every n events (or when replay gets slow) store state plus version; load the snapshot, then only later events. keep streams short-lived where the domain allows (one stream per billing period, not per customer forever). personal data and deletion: keep personal data out of events where possible (reference an id), or encrypt it per person and destroy the key to "forget" them (crypto-shredding). archiving: move closed streams to cold storage after their retention period.

testing: given, when, then @test void upgradeemitseventwhenactive() { var given = list.<subevent>of(new started("s1", "basic", t0)); var events = subscription.replay(given).upgrade("pro", t1); // when assertthat(events).containsexactly(new planupgraded("s1", "pro", t1)); // then } @test void cannotupgradecancelled() { var given = list.<subevent>of(new started("s1", "basic", t0), new cancelled("s1", "user", t1)); assertthatthrownby(() -> subscription.replay(given).upgrade("pro", t2)) .hasmessagecontaining("not active"); } aggregates tested this way need no database or mocks: given past events, when a command, then expected events or a rejection.

c.h: The lightweight version: an append-only ledger
c.x: the lightweight version: an append-only ledger many systems get most of the benefit without full event sourcing: an append-only table with one row per state change, and current state from a "latest event" view. never update, never delete. -- bigquery: current state of each pipeline stage from its event log create or replace view `p.ops.v_job_run_latest` as select * from `p.ops.job_run_events` where true qualify row_number() over (partition by run_date, stage order by event_ts desc) = 1; you get history, auditability and "what happened on date x" with ordinary sql. add aggregates, projections and replay only if the domain needs them.

tools kurrentdb (formerly eventstoredb): a database built for event streams, subscriptions and projections. axon framework / axon server (java): aggregates, sagas, projections and an event store. postgres with an events table: simple and often enough, with the caveats above. kafka is a good event log for distribution, but a weak event store : no efficient per-entity stream reads and no per-stream optimistic concurrency. many systems store events in a database and publish them to kafka through an outbox.

common mistakes event sourcing the whole system instead of the part that needs history. events that mirror table changes ( customerupdated with every field) instead of business facts. side effects (emails, payments) inside apply , so a replay sends them again. querying the event store for lists and searches instead of building read models. no plan for event versioning, personal data or replay time. treating eventual consistency of read models as a bug rather than designing for it.

the method, in order clarify requirements. functional: what users can do. non-functional: scale, latency, availability, consistency, durability, cost, security, compliance. write down what is out of scope. estimate. users, requests per second (average and peak), read/write ratio, data size per item, storage per year, bandwidth. numbers decide the design. define the api. the few endpoints or events that deliver the functional requirements, with their inputs and outputs. model the data. entities, keys, access patterns ("fetch by x, list by y sorted by z"), and which store fits each pattern. draw the high-level design. clients, load balancer, services, stores, caches, queues. one request path end to end. deep-dive the hard parts. the component that is hottest, biggest or most consistency-sensitive. show how it scales and fails. find bottlenecks and failure modes. what breaks first at 10×? what happens when each dependency is down? state trade-offs. what you chose, what you gave up, and what would make you change it. the same steps make a good design document. start simple, and add a component only when a requirement or a number demands it.

scaling playbook, cheapest first measure. find the actual bottleneck: cpu, memory, db queries, a slow dependency. fix the query. indexes, fewer round trips, no n+1. often 10–100× for free. scale up the instance. boring and effective. make services stateless and scale out behind a load balancer. cache hot reads; add a cdn for public content. read replicas for read-heavy databases. move work off the request path to queues and workers. partition big tables; archive cold data. shard or move to a distributed database only when one primary cannot take the writes.

caching strategies cache-aside: app reads cache, on a miss reads the db and fills the cache. most common. read-through: the cache library loads from the db itself on a miss. write-through: write to cache and db together; reads always warm, writes slower. write-behind: write to cache, flush to db later; fast, but data can be lost. ttl bounds staleness; explicit invalidation on write keeps it fresher but is easy to miss. stampede: a popular key expires and thousands of requests hit the db. use request coalescing, a lock, or early random refresh. what to key on: include everything that changes the answer (user, locale, version). a missing part of the key serves one user's data to another.

rate limiting token bucket: tokens refill at a steady rate up to a burst size; each request takes one. allows short bursts. the usual choice. leaky bucket: requests drain at a fixed rate; smooths traffic, no bursts. fixed window: n per minute; simple, but allows 2n across a window boundary. sliding window: counts over the last 60 s; fairer, slightly more state. where: at the gateway per api key or user; inside services to protect a fragile dependency. response: http 429 with retry-after , so well-behaved clients back off. distributed: keep counters in redis with atomic increments, or accept per-instance limits.

distributing data replication copies data for availability and read scale. leader-follower is the common model; multi-leader and leaderless trade consistency for write availability. partitioning / sharding splits data for write scale and size. choose a key that spreads load and matches the main access pattern. consistent hashing places keys and nodes on a ring, so adding or removing a node moves only about 1/n of the keys. used by caches and distributed stores. hot keys (one celebrity, one big tenant, today's date) defeat even spreading. split them, cache them, or add a random suffix. quorums: with n replicas, reading r and writing w where r + w > n means every read set overlaps every write set, so a read sees the latest acknowledged write.

designing for failure timeouts on every network call , shorter than the caller's own timeout. retries only for idempotent operations, with backoff and jitter, and a cap. circuit breakers and bulkheads so one sick dependency cannot take down the rest. graceful degradation: serve cached or partial results, and say so. never present "could not check" as "nothing found". redundancy: multiple instances across zones; regional failover only if the requirement justifies the cost. backpressure: queues with limits; shed load early (429/503) instead of collapsing. backups you have restored, with a known recovery point (rpo: how much data you can lose) and recovery time (rto: how long you can be down).

worked example: a url shortener requirements: create a short link; redirect fast; links never change; 100 m new links/year; reads 100× writes; 99.9% available. estimates: writes ≈ 3/s average; reads ≈ 300/s, peak ~1,500/s. 100 m × 500 b ≈ 50 gb/year. api: post /links {url} → {code} ; get /{code} → 301/302 redirect. data: link(code pk, url, created_at, owner) . access pattern is lookup by code only: any key-value store or postgres works. code generation: base62 of a unique id (7 chars ≈ 3.5 trillion codes). use a sequence or id service to avoid collisions; random codes need a uniqueness check. high level: load balancer → stateless service → cache (hot codes) → database. cdn can cache redirects for popular links. deep dive: reads are the load: cache-aside with long ttl works because links are immutable. writes are tiny. trade-offs: 301 is cached by browsers (fewer hits, no click counting); 302 keeps analytics. click analytics go to a queue and a warehouse, not the redirect path.

c.h: Worked example: search over 20 M orders
c.x: worked example: search over 20 m orders requirements: keyword and filter search (store, date, product), open an order, look up its refunds. results within 500 ms at p95. data refreshed daily. a customer's erasure request must apply everywhere immediately. estimates: ~60 searches/s at peak; 20 m records, ~40 gb metadata, ~140 gb line items and notes. data flow: order-system exports → landing bucket → warehouse layers (raw → foundation → consumable) → serving postgres. the warehouse is the record; postgres is a read-optimised copy. see data engineering . serving: stateless api on cloud run; postgres with full-text (gin) and b-tree indexes on filter columns; read replica for search; cache for hot queries and order pages. stable identity: ids never renumber, because urls, invoices and refunds refer to them. loads upsert on a stable key. erasure requests: checked on every read path (search, page, api, exports) from the application database, not baked into the copy, so a new request takes effect without a reload. freshness and honesty: each result carries its source and date; when a source is stale or unreachable, the api says so rather than returning a confident empty result. scaling later: move search to a dedicated index (or add semantic search with embeddings) when relevance or load outgrows postgres; keep postgres for lookups.

more practice problems rate limiter for a public api notification service (email, push, sms) with retries and user preferences news feed or timeline chat with presence and message history file upload and processing pipeline job scheduler that runs millions of tasks reliably metrics and logging pipeline rag question-answering over company documents payment flow with a saga and idempotency keys for each: run the method above, and write the trade-offs down. the written reasoning is the skill.

the method set a goal in numbers: "p95 search latency under 500 ms at 60 requests/s", "nightly load finishes in 40 minutes", "cost under ₹x per 1,000 requests". no goal, no finish line. measure the current state in a production-like environment with realistic data and traffic. find the bottleneck: the one resource or step limiting everything (cpu, memory, i/o, a lock, a query, a dependency). use traces and profiles, not intuition. change one thing that addresses it. measure again the same way. keep the change only if the numbers improved and nothing else got worse. repeat until the goal is met, then stop. then guard it with a performance test in ci. most of the gain usually comes from one or two fixes: a missing index, an n+1 query, a synchronous chain, an oversized payload. find those before tuning anything clever.

laws worth knowing little's law: items in the system = arrival rate × time in system (l = λw). 100 requests/s × 0.2 s = 20 requests in flight, so you need about 20 concurrent workers or connections. amdahl's law: speeding up a part only helps by that part's share. making a step that takes 10% of the time infinitely fast saves 10%. queueing: as utilisation approaches 100%, waiting time grows sharply, not linearly. plan for 60–70% utilisation at peak. tail amplification: if one call is slow 1% of the time, a request that fans out to 100 such calls is slow 1 − 0.99 100 ≈ 63% of the time. latency vs throughput: batching raises throughput and usually raises latency; tune for whichever the goal names.

percentiles, not averages an average hides the users having a bad time. report p50 (typical), p95 and p99 (the tail), and max. you cannot average percentiles across instances; compute them from histograms. measure at the edge the user sees (load balancer, client), and also per dependency. watch for coordinated omission in load tests: a tool that waits for slow responses before sending the next request under-reports latency. use open-model (arrival-rate) tests.

kinds of performance test test question load do we meet the goal at expected peak? stress where does it break, and how does it fail? spike what happens on a sudden 10× burst? does autoscaling keep up? soak does it degrade over hours (leaks, growing queues)? capacity how much traffic per instance, and what will growth cost? micro-benchmark is this function faster than that one? (jmh, pytest-benchmark) load-test example with k6 is on the testing tab. test against production-sized data; a query fast on 10,000 rows can be slow on 20 million.

profiling the jvm # java flight recorder: low overhead, safe in production jcmd <pid> jfr.start duration=60s filename=/tmp/rec.jfr # or at startup java -xx:startflightrecording=duration=60s,filename=rec.jfr -jar app.jar # open rec.jfr in jdk mission control: hot methods, allocations, locks, gc # async-profiler: flame graphs of cpu, allocation or wall-clock time asprof -d 30 -e cpu -f cpu.html <pid> asprof -d 30 -e alloc -f alloc.html <pid> jcmd <pid> gc.heap_info jcmd <pid> thread.print # thread dump: what is everyone waiting on? flame graph: width = time spent; look for wide plateaus near the top. containers: set -xx:maxrampercentage ; watch gc pause time and allocation rate. startup: cds/aot caches, lazy initialisation, or native images for scale-to-zero. blocking i/o: virtual threads (21+) raise concurrency cheaply; cpu-bound work still needs cores.

micro-benchmarks done right (jmh) @state(scope.benchmark) @benchmarkmode(mode.averagetime) @outputtimeunit(timeunit.microseconds) @warmup(iterations = 3) @measurement(iterations = 5) @fork(1) public class parsebench { string raw = "05-05-1959"; @benchmark public localdate parse() { return orderdateparser.parse(raw); // return the result so it is not optimised away } } hand-written timing loops on the jvm lie: no warm-up, dead-code elimination, jit effects. use jmh, and only after a profile shows the code matters.

profiling python # sampling profiler, attach to a running process, no code changes py-spy top --pid 1234 py-spy record -o profile.svg --pid 1234 # flame graph # deterministic profiler for a script python -m cprofile -o out.prof -m loader python -c "import pstats; pstats.stats('out.prof').sort_stats('cumtime').print_stats(20)" # memory python -x importtime -m loader 2> imports.txt # slow imports pip install memray && memray run -m loader # allocations replace python loops over rows with vectorised work: sql in the warehouse, polars, pyarrow, numpy. threads or asyncio for i/o-bound work; processes for cpu-bound work. stream large files instead of reading them whole into memory.

where time usually goes area common cause fix database missing index, n+1 queries, fetching unused columns, lock waits explain analyze, indexes, joins or batch loads, select only needed columns ( database design ) connection pools pool too small (queueing) or too large (database overload) size from little's law; watch pool wait time service calls sequential calls, no timeouts, new connection per call parallelise independent calls, keep-alive, http/2, timeouts payloads huge json responses, no compression, no pagination paginate, compress, return only needed fields serialisation reflection-heavy mapping in hot paths profile; precompiled serialisers; smaller objects memory and gc high allocation rate, heap too small, large object churn profile allocations; reuse buffers; tune heap and collector cold starts large images, eager initialisation, jvm warm-up smaller images, cpu boost, min instances, aot/native ( cloud run ) warehouse queries full scans, skewed joins, repeated subqueries partition filters, clustering, pre-aggregation ( sql skills ) pipelines one object at a time through one container; small files parallel tasks, bulk loads, purpose-built engines (dataflow), compact files llm calls long prompts, sequential calls, large models for simple tasks prompt caching, parallel calls, streaming, smaller models where evals allow

concurrency and backpressure bound every queue and pool; an unbounded queue turns overload into an out-of-memory crash. shed load early (429/503) when saturated rather than accepting work you cannot finish in time. set timeouts shorter than the caller's, so work is not done for a caller that has given up. cloud run concurrency and max instances, and database pool size, must agree: instances × pool size ≤ database connection limit. locks and synchronised blocks serialise work; look for them in thread dumps under load.

performance as a habit performance budgets in ci: fail the build if a key benchmark or bundle size regresses beyond a threshold. track p95/p99 per endpoint after every deploy, with deploy markers on dashboards. cost per unit of work (per request, per row loaded) next to latency: faster that costs 5× may be the wrong trade. capacity reviews before expected growth or launches. write down the numbers of each investigation, so the next one starts from evidence.

where caches live layer example good for watch out for browser http cache static assets, per-user responses wrong cache-control serving stale pages cdn cloud cdn public content near users caching personalised responses by mistake gateway apigee responsecache identical api responses keys that ignore the caller's identity in-process caffeine, functools.lru_cache hot reference data, nanosecond reads each instance has its own copy; memory per instance distributed redis / memorystore shared across instances, sessions, rate limits network hop; one more system to run database buffer cache, materialised views repeated queries and aggregates refresh schedules warehouse bigquery cached results, bi engine repeated dashboard queries cache is skipped for some queries (non-deterministic functions, changed tables) model api prompt caching long, repeated prompt prefixes any change in the prefix invalidates it a cache is a copy, so every cache is a consistency decision. add one when measurements show the need, and decide up front how stale its data may be.

read and write patterns cache-aside (lazy loading): read the cache; on a miss, read the source and fill the cache. simple and the most common. read-through: the cache library loads from the source itself on a miss (caffeine loadingcache ). write-through: writes go to the cache and the source together; reads are always warm; writes are slower. write-behind: write to the cache, persist later. fast, but a crash loses writes. rarely worth it. refresh-ahead: refresh popular entries before they expire so users never wait for a miss.

invalidation ttl: entries expire after a set time. bounds staleness; simplest and most robust. every cache entry should have one. delete on write: after updating the source, delete the cache key (not update it), so the next read reloads fresh data. versioned keys: include a version in the key ( order:v3:123 , or a data version number); bump it to invalidate everything at once. event-driven: consume change events (cdc, domain events) and evict affected keys. immutable data (an issued invoice, a fingerprinted file) can be cached forever. the race to know: reader a misses and reads the old value; writer b updates the source and deletes the key; a then writes the old value into the cache. a ttl bounds the damage; versioned keys avoid it.

stampedes (thundering herd) a popular key expires and thousands of requests miss at once and hit the database together. single flight / request coalescing: only one caller loads; the others wait for its result (caffeine does this per key in-process). distributed lock: set lock:key 1 nx ex 10 in redis; the winner loads, others briefly serve stale or wait. stale-while-revalidate: serve the expired value while one background refresh runs. jittered ttls: add randomness so many keys do not expire at the same moment. probabilistic early refresh: refresh slightly before expiry with rising probability.

key design include every input that changes the answer: ids, filters, page, locale, user or tenant, and the api or data version. normalise inputs (sort filters, lower-case where meaning allows) so equal requests share a key. namespace keys: service:entity:version:id . never share a cache entry across users when the response depends on permissions; include the permission scope in the key, or cache only the permission-independent part. keep values small ; large values make the cache slow and evict everything else.

c.h: What not to cache, or not that way
c.x: what not to cache, or not that way errors and outages as "not found": caching an empty result because the source was down turns "cannot see" into a confident "nothing there" for the whole ttl. negative results (genuinely not found) only briefly, if at all. secrets and tokens in shared caches. personalised data in public caches (cdn, gateway) without per-user keys. data with legal effect (an erasure request, a deletion) behind a long ttl: it must take effect immediately, so check it outside the cache or evict on change. cheap queries: if the source answers in 1 ms, a cache adds complexity for little gain.

c.h: Spring Cache with Caffeine or Redis
c.x: spring cache with caffeine or redis @configuration @enablecaching class cacheconfig { @bean cachemanager cachemanager() { var m = new caffeinecachemanager("orders", "stores"); m.setcaffeine(caffeine.newbuilder() .maximumsize(10_000) .expireafterwrite(duration.ofminutes(10)) .recordstats()); // hit ratio for metrics return m; } } @service class orderservice { @cacheable(cachenames = "orders", key = "#id", unless = "#result == null") public order get(string id) { return repo.find(id).orelse(null); } @cacheevict(cachenames = "orders", key = "#o.id()") public void update(order o) { repo.save(o); } } # switch to redis shared across instances spring: cache: type: redis redis: time-to-live: 10m key-prefix: "shop:v3:" data: redis: host: ${redis_host} port: 6379 @cacheable works through a proxy, like @transactional : calling the method from inside the same class skips the cache.

python: in-process and redis from functools import lru_cache from cachetools import ttlcache, cached @lru_cache(maxsize=1024) # immutable inputs, never expires def store_name(code: str) -> str: ... @cached(ttlcache(maxsize=10_000, ttl=600)) # expires after 10 minutes def order_summary(order_id: str) -> dict: ... import json, random, redis r = redis.redis(host=redis_host, port=6379, decode_responses=true) def get_order(order_id: str) -> dict | none: key = f"shop:order:v3:{order_id}" if (hit := r.get(key)) is not none: return json.loads(hit) o = db.load_order(order_id) # raises if the db is down: do not cache that if o is not none: r.set(key, json.dumps(o), ex=600 + random.randint(0, 60)) # jittered ttl return o def update_order(o: dict) -> none: db.save(o) r.delete(f"shop:order:v3:{o['id']}") # delete after write

redis essentials set order:v3:123 '{"order_ref":"…"}' ex 600 # with ttl set lock:order:123 1 nx ex 10 # only if absent: a simple lock get order:v3:123 del order:v3:123 ttl order:v3:123 incr ratelimit:app42:202611121015 # counters, rate limits expire ratelimit:app42:202611121015 60 info stats # keyspace_hits, keyspace_misses, evicted_keys set maxmemory and an eviction policy ( allkeys-lru or allkeys-lfu for a pure cache). avoid keys * in production; use scan . design so the system still works (slower) if redis is down; a cache should not be a single point of failure. on gcp: memorystore for redis or valkey, private ip, auth and in-transit encryption on.

http and cdn caching # fingerprinted static assets cache-control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable # public api response, shared caches allowed, short freshness cache-control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=30 etag: "v3-123-a1b2" # per-user data cache-control: private, max-age=30 # sensitive cache-control: no-store more on headers on web fundamentals . configure the cdn to vary on, or bypass for, the authorization header and cookies.

caching in the data stack bigquery cached results: identical queries reuse results for free for about 24 hours, unless tables changed or the query is non-deterministic. materialised views: bigquery keeps aggregates up to date incrementally and can rewrite queries to use them. bi engine: in-memory acceleration for dashboards. serving tables: a consumable table in postgres is itself a cache of the warehouse; it needs a refresh rule and freshness monitoring like any other cache. pipeline-level: skip work whose inputs have not changed (compare etags or content hashes) instead of recomputing.

measuring a cache hit ratio (hits ÷ requests): low ratios mean wrong keys, short ttls or data that is not reused. latency on hit and on miss. evictions and memory: constant evictions mean the cache is too small for the working set. staleness: how old served data is, against the agreed maximum. source load with and without the cache, to prove it earns its keep.

c.h: The layers, from the ground up
c.x: the layers, from the ground up layer what it really is why it matters to you buildings data centres: power, cooling, physical security, fibre. a zone is one or more of them that fail together; a region is a group of zones close enough to talk fast spread work across zones to survive a building failing; pick a region for latency and data residency servers racks of ordinary machines: cpus, memory, local disks, network cards. they fail every day at this scale design as if any one machine can disappear, because it will virtualisation a hypervisor splits one physical server into many virtual machines, each believing it has its own hardware your "server" shares a machine with strangers; isolation is the provider's hardest job network software-defined networking: your private network, firewall rules and load balancers are configuration on shared switches and fibre moving data costs money and time, especially between regions and out to the internet storage block disks attached over the network, object stores that spread copies of your files across machines and zones, managed file systems durability comes from copies in different places; every copy and every read has a price control plane the apis, identity and permissions, scheduling, quotas and billing that turn all of the above into "click to create" every console click and every terraform line is an api call; iam decides who can make it managed services databases, queues, serverless and ai services: software the provider runs for you, built from the same layers you trade control for convenience; the parts underneath still fail and still cost money

virtual machines, containers and sandboxes a virtual machine has its own operating system kernel on virtual hardware. strong isolation, slower to start. a container shares the host's kernel and isolates processes with kernel features. fast and light, but sharing a kernel means weaker isolation. providers close the gap with sandboxes. firecracker, developed at amazon web services for services such as aws lambda and now open source, uses linux kvm to run lightweight "microvms" that start fast but keep virtual-machine isolation. gvisor, open-sourced by google, is an "application kernel" that sits between a container and the host, because, in its own words, containers are not a sandbox. serverless is this underneath: someone else's servers, packed densely, started on demand, and billed by the request or the second.

scheduling: who runs where a scheduler decides which machine runs each piece of work, packing jobs tightly to use the hardware well and moving them when machines fail. kubernetes brings this idea to everyone. its own readme says it builds on google's experience running production workloads at scale with an internal system called borg. why you care: requests and limits, bin packing and preemption decide both your bill and whether your work gets evicted. see kubernetes .

what "managed" really means a managed database is still a database server on virtual machines with disks, replicas and backups. the provider patches and fails it over for you. object storage is many machines holding copies or encoded fragments of your files, with an api in front. that is why it is durable, cheap and slower than a local disk. a serverless function runs in a sandbox on a shared machine; a "cold start" is that sandbox being created for you. knowing the parts helps you ask the right questions: where are the copies, what happens when a zone fails, what is billed, and what can i take elsewhere.

shared responsibility the provider secures the cloud: buildings, hardware, hypervisors, their network and their services. you secure what you put in it: identities and permissions, your data, your network rules, your code and its dependencies, and the settings you choose. the more managed the service, the more the provider takes on, but your identities, data and settings are always yours. most cloud breaches are a setting someone left open, not a broken data centre. see security .

c.h: Follow one request through the layers
c.x: follow one request through the layers you open a web page served from the cloud. your request reaches the provider's edge and a load balancer (software on shared hardware), which picks a healthy instance in one zone. that instance is a container or virtual machine, placed by a scheduler on a physical server in a data centre. it reads from a managed database (more virtual machines, with a replica in another zone) and from object storage (copies spread across machines), writes logs and metrics (yet more storage), and every step is checked against permissions and metered for the bill. when one machine, or one building, fails, the layers above route around it, if you designed for it. try it yourself: run a small app on cloud run , then find each layer in the console: the region and zone, the revision and its instances, the logs, the iam roles, and the bill.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain zones, regions and why work is spread across them tell a virtual machine from a container and a serverless function name what the provider secures and what you secure 2 practitioner choose zones and regions for a service's availability, latency and data residency read a bill and trace each line to a layer: compute, storage, network explain what a managed service still leaves to you 3 senior design for a machine, a zone or a region failing, and test it choose isolation (vm, container, sandbox) for untrusted or multi-tenant work estimate cost from first principles, including egress and copies 4 expert set organisation standards for failure domains, tenancy and shared responsibility lead decisions on regions, providers and lock-in with the layers in view teach how the cloud works underneath, not only which button to press each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

c.h: Where each tends to stand out
c.x: where each tends to stand out google cloud: data and analytics (bigquery is serverless with nothing to size), global networking with a global vpc and single-ip global load balancing, kubernetes (gke), developer-friendly serverless (cloud run), and ai with vertex ai. projects make isolation simple. aws: the broadest and deepest service catalogue, the largest ecosystem and talent pool, many regions, and mature options for almost every niche. more configuration choices, and more to learn. azure: enterprises standardised on microsoft (entra id, microsoft 365, windows, sql server, .net), hybrid setups (azure arc), and the microsoft data and ai stack (fabric, power bi, azure openai). all three are capable for almost any workload. the deciding factors are usually existing skills and contracts, specific services you depend on, data location, and price after discounts.

differences that bite iam thinking: gcp binds roles to principals on resources; aws writes json policies with explicit allow/deny and resource arns; azure assigns roles at a scope in a strict hierarchy. networking: a gcp vpc spans regions; aws and azure networks are regional and are joined with peering or transit gateways/hubs. isolation unit: gcp teams often use many projects; aws uses many accounts; azure uses subscriptions plus resource groups. warehouses: bigquery bills by bytes scanned or by slots with no cluster to run; redshift has provisioned clusters or serverless capacity units; fabric uses capacity units shared across workloads. discounts: gcp committed and sustained use discounts; aws savings plans and reserved instances; azure reservations and savings plans. spot or preemptible capacity everywhere for interruptible work. egress: data leaving a cloud costs money on all three; cross-region and cross-cloud traffic adds up. design data placement before choosing multi-cloud.

regions in india (data residency) provider regions google cloud mumbai ( asia-south1 ), delhi ( asia-south2 ) aws mumbai ( ap-south-1 ), hyderabad ( ap-south-2 ) azure central india (pune), south india (chennai), west india (mumbai), plus newer regions not every service or model is available in every region. check availability per service, and for ai models check which regions actually process the data.

staying portable (where it matters) containers and kubernetes run the same on gke, eks and aks; cloud run-style serverless is less portable but simpler. terraform for all infrastructure, with provider-specific modules behind your own interfaces. open data formats (parquet, iceberg, delta) in object storage keep data readable by any engine. open protocols: postgres, kafka, opentelemetry, oidc, s3-compatible apis. dbt and sql transfer between warehouses with dialect adjustments. accept lock-in deliberately where a managed service saves real effort (bigquery, spanner, dynamodb); write down the exit cost. multi-cloud for its own sake doubles skills, tooling and egress. use it for a concrete reason: a customer requirement, a unique service, resilience against a provider-wide failure, or negotiation.

reference architectures pattern flow fits batch elt source → storage transfer / cloud run job → gcs (raw) → bigquery load → dbt layers → marts → looker / api daily or hourly data, files and exports, most analytics streaming apps → pub/sub → dataflow (parse, enrich, window) → bigquery (+ gcs archive) seconds-level freshness, clickstreams, iot, fraud signals simple streaming apps → pub/sub → bigquery subscription events that need no transformation before landing cdc replication postgres/mysql → datastream → bigquery (merged or append) → dbt analytics on an operational database without load on it lakehouse gcs (parquet/iceberg) ← dataproc spark / dataflow; biglake tables → bigquery sql open formats shared by several engines reverse etl / serving bigquery mart → export or loader → cloud sql / alloydb → api serving curated data to an application with low latency rag over documents gcs docs → parse (dataflow / cloud run) → chunks + embeddings (bigquery ml / vertex ai) → vector search → model ai question answering over your corpus

choosing between similar services sql in bigquery vs dataflow: if it can be expressed in sql over data already in bigquery, use sql (dbt). use dataflow for streaming, non-sql parsing, or work before data reaches bigquery. dataflow vs dataproc: dataflow for new pipelines (serverless, beam, streaming). dataproc for existing spark code or spark libraries. cloud run job vs dataflow: a job for simple, bounded work (copy files, call an api). dataflow when data volume needs many workers and autoscaling. composer vs workflows: composer for many pipelines with dependencies, backfills and sensors. workflows plus scheduler for a handful of steps; much cheaper to run. dbt vs dataform: both do sql elt with tests. dataform is built into bigquery; dbt has the larger ecosystem and runs on any warehouse. pub/sub vs kafka: pub/sub is serverless and global with nothing to size. kafka gives log semantics, replay by offset, compaction and the kafka ecosystem. cloud sql vs alloydb vs spanner: cloud sql for most postgres needs; alloydb for heavier postgres workloads and analytics; spanner for global scale with strong consistency.

handy commands # pub/sub straight into bigquery gcloud pubsub topics create order-events gcloud pubsub subscriptions create order-to-bq \ --topic=order-events \ --bigquery-table=my-proj:raw.order_events \ --use-table-schema # storage transfer: one-off copy between buckets gcloud transfer jobs create gs://source-bucket gs://my-landing # serverless for apache spark (dataproc batches): run a pyspark job gcloud dataproc batches submit pyspark job.py \ --region=asia-south1 --deps-bucket=gs://my-deps # dataflow: list and inspect jobs gcloud dataflow jobs list --region=asia-south1 --status=active gcloud dataflow jobs describe job_id --region=asia-south1 # datastream streams gcloud datastream streams list --location=asia-south1

iam for data, in practice one service account per pipeline component (landing, load, transform, serve), each with only its roles. dataset-level grants rather than project-wide: bigquery.dataeditor on the datasets it writes, dataviewer on those it reads. bigquery.jobuser on the project that pays for queries; this is separate from data access. bucket-level roles with uniform bucket-level access; objectviewer for readers, objectadmin only for the writer. policy tags for sensitive columns; authorised views to share a subset. serving databases get a read-only user for the api.

cost controls partition and cluster; require partition filters on large tables. set per-user and per-project custom query quotas, and maximum_bytes_billed on jobs. export billing to bigquery and build a cost dashboard by label. label every resource with team, component and environment. gcs lifecycle rules to move old raw data to nearline/coldline/archive. stop or scale down non-production cloud sql, dataproc and composer when unused. dataflow: right-size workers, use streaming engine, and set max workers. keep development windows small: a few partitions, not the full history.

c.h: Data quality and governance on GCP
c.x: data quality and governance on gcp dbt tests in the transformation layer for keys, relationships and accepted values. dataplex data quality scans for rules on tables, scheduled, with results in bigquery. dataplex data profiling to see distributions, nulls and distinct counts. lineage from bigquery jobs and dataflow appears automatically in dataplex. run records of your own: every pipeline run writes what it read, wrote and rejected. sensitive data protection scans to find personal data you did not know you had.

partitioned, clustered table create table if not exists `proj.analytics.orders` ( order_id string not null, order_ref string, store_id string, order_date date, lines array<struct<sku string, qty int64>>, _landed_at timestamp ) partition by date_trunc(order_date, month) cluster by store_id, order_ref options ( require_partition_filter = true, description = 'orders, one row per order_id', labels = [('layer', 'analytics')] ); -- integer range partition partition by range_bucket(order_year, generate_array(1995, 2031, 1)) -- ingestion-time partition partition by _partitiondate limit: 10,000 partitions per table. daily partitions over 30 years (about 11,000 days) overflow it; use month or year.

deduplicate with qualify -- latest version of each key select * from `proj.raw.orders` where order_year = 2024 qualify row_number() over ( partition by store_id, order_ref order by _landed_at desc ) = 1; -- latest event per entity (append-only ledger → current state) select * except(rn) from ( select *, row_number() over (partition by run_id, stage order by event_ts desc) rn from `proj.ops.job_run_events`) where rn = 1; -- whole row of the max, no window select array_agg(t order by order_date desc limit 1)[offset(0)].* from `proj.analytics.orders` t group by store_id;

merge (upsert) merge `proj.mart.serving` t using ( select * from `proj.analytics.orders` where order_date >= date_sub(current_date(), interval 7 day) ) s on t.order_id = s.order_id and t.order_date >= date_sub(current_date(), interval 7 day) -- prune t when matched and t.row_hash != s.row_hash then update set order_ref = s.order_ref, order_date = s.order_date, row_hash = s.row_hash when not matched by target then insert row when not matched by source and t.order_date >= date_sub(current_date(), interval 7 day) then delete; -- change detection hash to_hex(sha256(to_json_string(struct(order_ref, store_id, order_date)))) as row_hash farm_fingerprint(concat(store_id, '|', order_ref)) -- int64 key

dates & safe parsing parse_date('%d-%m-%y', '05-05-1959') -- errors on bad input safe.parse_date('%d-%m-%y', raw) -- null on bad input safe_cast(order_seq as int64) -- never let a parse failure hide as a null: count it select countif(raw is not null and safe.parse_date('%d-%m-%y', raw) is null) as unparsed from t; date_trunc(d, month) date_add(d, interval 1 day) date_diff(a, b, day) last_day(d, month) extract(year from d) format_date('%y%m%d', d) timestamp_trunc(ts, hour) datetime(ts, 'asia/kolkata') current_date('asia/kolkata') unix_millis(ts) timestamp_micros(n) -- calendar spine for gap finding select d from unnest(generate_date_array('2025-01-01', current_date())) d left join facts f on f.dt = d where f.dt is null;

array, struct, unnest, json -- explode select o.order_ref, i.sku, i.qty from `proj.analytics.orders` o, unnest(o.lines) i; -- comma = cross join -- keep rows with empty arrays left join unnest(o.lines) i -- build select order_ref, array_agg(struct(sku, qty) order by sku) lines from order_lines group by order_ref; array_length(a) a[safe_offset(0)] array_to_string(a, ',') 'x' in unnest(a) exists(select 1 from unnest(a) v where v > 3) -- json json_value(payload, '$.store.code') -- scalar as string json_query(payload, '$.lines') -- json fragment json_query_array(payload, '$.lines') -- array<json> on a json column, array<string> on a string lax_int64(payload.count) -- on a json column to_json_string(struct(a, b)) parse_json(s)

window functions select store, order_date, n, sum(n) over (partition by store order by order_date) as running, avg(n) over (partition by store order by order_date rows between 6 preceding and current row) as avg_7d, lag(n) over (partition by store order by order_date) as prev, n / sum(n) over (partition by store) as share, rank() over (partition by store order by n desc) as rnk, ntile(4) over (order by n) as quartile from daily; -- named window select sum(n) over w, max(n) over w from daily window w as (partition by store order by order_date); approx_count_distinct(order_ref) approx_quantiles(n, 100)[offset(50)]

load, export, external load data into `proj.raw.orders` from files (format = 'parquet', uris = ['gs://landing/data/year=2024/*.parquet']); export data options ( uri = 'gs://exports/serving/2025-01-31/*.parquet', -- one * required format = 'parquet', overwrite = true, compression = 'snappy' ) as select * from `proj.mart.serving` where _run_date = '2025-01-31'; create or replace external table `proj.raw.orders_ext` with partition columns options (format = 'parquet', uris = ['gs://landing/data/*'], hive_partition_uri_prefix = 'gs://landing/data');

scripting & procedures declare run_date date default current_date(); declare n int64; set n = (select count(*) from `proj.analytics.orders` where _run_date = run_date); if n = 0 then raise using message = format('no rows for %t', run_date); end if; begin transaction; delete from `proj.mart.serving` where _run_date = run_date; insert into `proj.mart.serving` select * from staging; commit transaction; execute immediate format('select count(*) from `proj.%s.t`', ds); create or replace procedure `proj.ops.rebuild`(d date) begin ... end; call `proj.ops.rebuild`(date '2025-01-31');

pipe syntax from `proj.analytics.orders` |> where order_date >= '2024-01-01' |> aggregate count(*) as n group by store_id |> order by n desc |> limit 10; -- other operators: select, extend (add columns), set, drop, rename, -- join, as (alias), pivot, unpivot, tablesample, call reads top to bottom in execution order. mixes freely with standard sql in the same project.

metadata & cost queries -- most expensive queries in the last day select user_email, job_id, round(total_bytes_billed / pow(1024, 4), 3) as tib_billed, total_slot_ms, left(query, 120) as q from `region-asia-south1`.information_schema.jobs where creation_time > timestamp_sub(current_timestamp(), interval 1 day) and job_type = 'query' order by total_bytes_billed desc limit 20; -- partitions and their row counts select partition_id, total_rows, total_logical_bytes from `proj.analytics.information_schema.partitions` where table_name = 'orders' order by partition_id; -- columns of a table select column_name, data_type, is_nullable from `proj.analytics.information_schema.columns` where table_name = 'orders'; -- table sizes select table_id, row_count, size_bytes / 1e9 as gb from `proj.analytics.__tables__` order by size_bytes desc;

time travel, snapshots, wildcards -- read the table as it was (up to 7 days back by default) select * from `proj.analytics.orders` for system_time as of timestamp_sub(current_timestamp(), interval 1 hour); -- undo a bad write create or replace table `proj.analytics.orders_restore` as select * from `proj.analytics.orders` for system_time as of '2025-01-31 06:00:00+00'; -- zero-copy snapshot / clone create snapshot table `proj.backup.orders_20250131` clone `proj.analytics.orders`; create table `proj.dev.orders` clone `proj.analytics.orders`; -- sharded tables select * from `proj.logs.events_*` where _table_suffix between '20250101' and '20250131';

cost & performance rules name columns. storage is columnar; select * bills every column. select * except(raw_html) drops wide ones. filter on the partition column with a constant or parameter. a filter through a function of another table's subquery may not prune. limit does not reduce bytes on a regular table. use table preview or tablesample system (1 percent) . dry-run first and set maximum_bytes_billed on jobs that could run away. cluster on high-cardinality filter/join columns; order matters, first column filters best. join big to small after filtering; pre-aggregate before joining. avoid row-by-row dml. batch into one merge; dml quotas and costs are per statement. materialised views for repeated aggregates; bi engine for dashboards. execution graph in the console shows skew, spills and which stage costs the slots.

bq cli bq query --use_legacy_sql=false --dry_run 'select ...' bq query --use_legacy_sql=false --format=prettyjson --max_rows=20 \ --parameter=from_d:date:2024-01-01 \ 'select count(*) from `proj.analytics.orders` where order_date >= @from_d' bq query --nouse_legacy_sql --maximum_bytes_billed=10000000000 < q.sql bq ls proj:analytics bq show --schema --format=prettyjson proj:analytics.orders bq head -n 10 proj:analytics.orders bq load --source_format=parquet --replace \ 'proj:raw.events$20250131' 'gs://landing/events/dt=2025-01-31/*.parquet' # one partition bq extract --destination_format=parquet proj:mart.serving 'gs://exp/serving-*.parquet' bq cp proj:analytics.orders proj:backup.orders_20250131 bq mk --table --time_partitioning_field=order_date --clustering_fields=store_id \ proj:analytics.t schema.json bq ls -j -a -n 20 # recent jobs bq show -j <job_id>

services, jobs, worker pools kind runs when use it for service a request arrives (http, grpc, websocket, pub/sub push, eventarc) apis, web apps, webhooks. scales on traffic, down to zero. job someone executes it (cli, api, cloud scheduler, workflows) batch loads, migrations, nightly exports. runs n tasks in parallel, then exits. worker pool always, with no http endpoint pull-based consumers (kafka, pub/sub pull). newer resource: check it is available in your region.

container contract listen on $port (default 8080) on 0.0.0.0 , not 127.0.0.1 . jobs do not listen at all. stateless. any instance can serve any request; instances come and go. the filesystem is in memory and counts against the memory limit. write big files to gcs or a mounted volume. shutdown: the container gets sigterm , then about 10 seconds before sigkill . flush and close there. logs: anything written to stdout/stderr goes to cloud logging. jobs: exit code 0 means the task succeeded; anything else fails it (and retries it if max-retries > 0). platform: build images for linux/amd64 . an arm64 image from a mac will not start.

deploy a service gcloud run deploy api \ --image=asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/apps/api:3f2a9c1 \ --region=asia-south1 \ --service-account=api@my-proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com \ --no-allow-unauthenticated \ --cpu=1 --memory=1gi \ --concurrency=80 --min-instances=0 --max-instances=10 \ --timeout=300 \ --cpu-boost \ --set-env-vars=app_profile=prod,dataset=analytics \ --set-secrets=db_password=db-password:3 \ --labels=env=prod,team=data # build from source with cloud build + buildpacks / dockerfile gcloud run deploy api --source . --region=asia-south1 gcloud run services describe api --region=asia-south1 --format='value(status.url)' gcloud run services list --set-env-vars replaces all env vars; --update-env-vars adds or changes only the ones named.

revisions & traffic # deploy without sending traffic; reach it at a tagged url gcloud run deploy api --image=…:4b1c2d0 --no-traffic --tag=canary # → https://canary---api-xxxxx.a.run.app # shift 10% to the new revision gcloud run services update-traffic api \ --to-revisions=api-00042-xyz=10,api-00041-abc=90 gcloud run services update-traffic api --to-latest # 100% to newest gcloud run services update-traffic api --to-tags=canary=100 # roll back = send traffic to the previous revision gcloud run revisions list --service=api --region=asia-south1 gcloud run services update-traffic api --to-revisions=api-00041-abc=100 every deploy or config change creates a new immutable revision. settings live on the revision, so rolling back traffic also rolls back env vars and secrets.

jobs gcloud run jobs deploy loader \ --image=asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/apps/loader:3f2a9c1 \ --region=asia-south1 \ --service-account=loader@my-proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com \ --tasks=10 --parallelism=5 \ --task-timeout=3600s --max-retries=0 \ --cpu=2 --memory=4gi \ --args=--year=2024 gcloud run jobs execute loader --region=asia-south1 --wait gcloud run jobs execute loader --wait \ --args=--year=2023 --update-env-vars=dry_run=true # overrides for this run only gcloud run jobs executions list --job=loader --region=asia-south1 gcloud run jobs executions describe loader-abc12 --region=asia-south1 gcloud run jobs executions cancel loader-abc12 --region=asia-south1 an execution's status is cloud run's word on whether the container exited 0. whether it did the right work is your job to record, e.g. a summary row or log line per run.

shard work across job tasks every task gets these environment variables: cloud_run_task_index : 0 … tasks − 1 cloud_run_task_count : the --tasks value cloud_run_task_attempt : 0 on the first try cloud_run_execution , cloud_run_job : names for logs and run records # python import os i = int(os.environ.get("cloud_run_task_index", 0)) n = int(os.environ.get("cloud_run_task_count", 1)) mine = [u for k, u in enumerate(sorted(all_uris)) if k % n == i] // java int i = integer.parseint(system.getenv().getordefault("cloud_run_task_index", "0")); int n = integer.parseint(system.getenv().getordefault("cloud_run_task_count", "1")); list<string> mine = intstream.range(0, uris.size()) .filter(k -> k % n == i).maptoobj(uris::get).tolist(); sort the input first so every task sees the same order. make each task idempotent: a retry repeats the whole shard.

scaling & cost concurrency (default 80, max 1000): requests one instance handles at once. set 1 only for code that is not thread-safe. min instances keep warm instances to avoid cold starts; they bill while idle. max instances cap spend and protect downstream databases (connections = instances × pool size). cpu allocation: by default cpu is only allocated during requests, so background threads stall after the response. --no-cpu-throttling keeps cpu on (instance-based billing). startup cpu boost ( --cpu-boost ) gives extra cpu while the container starts: helps jvm cold starts. cold start cuts: smaller images, lazy initialisation, cds/aot for java, quarkus or spring native images. jobs bill for the time each task runs, at the cpu and memory you asked for.

calling private services # grant the caller the invoker role gcloud run services add-iam-policy-binding api --region=asia-south1 \ --member=serviceaccount:caller@my-proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com \ --role=roles/run.invoker # from your terminal curl -h "authorization: bearer $(gcloud auth print-identity-token)" https://api-xxxxx.a.run.app/health gcloud run services proxy api --region=asia-south1 --port=8080 # local tunnel # python: id token whose audience is the service url import google.auth.transport.requests, google.oauth2.id_token, requests aud = "https://api-xxxxx.a.run.app" tok = google.oauth2.id_token.fetch_id_token(google.auth.transport.requests.request(), aud) requests.get(f"{aud}/health", headers={"authorization": f"bearer {tok}"}) // java (google-auth-library) idtokencredentials creds = idtokencredentials.newbuilder() .setidtokenprovider((idtokenprovider) googlecredentials.getapplicationdefault()) .settargetaudience(aud).build(); creds.refresh(); string token = creds.getidtoken().gettokenvalue(); services need an id token (audience = url). google apis, including the cloud run admin api that executes a job, need an access token.

networking # who may reach the service --ingress=all # internet (still iam-checked) --ingress=internal # vpc and some google sources only --ingress=internal-and-cloud-load-balancing # put a load balancer / cloud armor in front # reach private ips (memorystore, internal services) with direct vpc egress --network=main --subnet=run-egress --vpc-egress=private-ranges-only --vpc-egress=all-traffic # everything via vpc → cloud nat gives a static egress ip # cloud sql via the built-in connector: unix socket in the container --add-cloudsql-instances=my-proj:asia-south1:shop # jdbc: jdbc:postgresql:///shop?cloudsqlinstance=my-proj:asia-south1:shop&socketfactory=com.google.cloud.sql.postgres.socketfactory # psycopg: host=/cloudsql/my-proj:asia-south1:shop a third party that allowlists ips needs all-traffic egress through cloud nat with a reserved address. without it, egress comes from shared google ranges.

secrets, config, volumes # secret as env var: read once, when the instance starts --set-secrets=db_password=db-password:3 # secret as a file: read when your code opens it --set-secrets=/secrets/sa.json=sa-key:latest # the runtime service account needs to read it gcloud secrets add-iam-policy-binding db-password \ --member=serviceaccount:api@my-proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com \ --role=roles/secretmanager.secretaccessor # gcs bucket or in-memory volume --add-volume=name=data,type=cloud-storage,bucket=my-landing \ --add-volume-mount=volume=data,mount-path=/data --add-volume=name=scratch,type=in-memory,size-limit=1gi pin secret versions ( :3 ) in prod so a rotation is a deliberate deploy. with :latest in an env var, running instances keep the old value until they restart.

triggers cloud scheduler → job: post to https://run.googleapis.com/v2/projects/p/locations/r/jobs/j:run with an oauth token (see the terraform tab). cloud scheduler → service: http target with an oidc token whose audience is the service url. pub/sub push: subscription pushes to the service url with an oidc token; return 2xx to ack, anything else retries. eventarc: route events (gcs object finalised, bigquery job done, audit log entries) to a service. cloud tasks: queued http calls with rate limits and retries. workflows: run jobs in sequence, wait for each, branch on results. gcloud eventarc triggers create on-landing --location=asia-south1 \ --destination-run-service=ingest --destination-run-region=asia-south1 \ --event-filters=type=google.cloud.storage.object.v1.finalized \ --event-filters=bucket=my-landing \ --service-account=eventarc@my-proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com

dockerfiles that start fast # java (spring boot / quarkus jar) from eclipse-temurin:21-jdk as build workdir /src copy . . run ./gradlew bootjar -x test from eclipse-temurin:21-jre run useradd -u 1001 app user 1001 copy --from=build /src/build/libs/app.jar /app.jar env java_tool_options="-xx:maxrampercentage=75 -xx:+useserialgc" entrypoint ["java", "-jar", "/app.jar"] # python from python:3.12-slim env pythonunbuffered=1 pip_no_cache_dir=1 workdir /app copy requirements.txt . run pip install -r requirements.txt copy . . user 1001 cmd exec gunicorn --bind :$port --workers 1 --threads 8 --timeout 0 app:app docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64 -t asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/apps/api:$(git rev-parse --short=12 head) --push . use the exec form ( ["java", …] or exec ) so your process is pid 1 and receives sigterm .

logging & health # one json object per line on stdout → structured log entry {"severity":"error","message":"load failed","uri":"gs://…","run_id":"r-42", "logging.googleapis.com/trace":"projects/my-proj/traces/abc123"} gcloud logging read 'resource.type="cloud_run_revision" and resource.labels.service_name="api" and severity>=error' --freshness=1h --limit=50 gcloud logging read 'resource.type="cloud_run_job" and resource.labels.job_name="loader" and severity>=error' --freshness=1d --limit=20 # service.yaml fragment: probes spec: template: spec: containers: - image: … startupprobe: httpget: { path: /health/started, port: 8080 } failurethreshold: 30 periodseconds: 2 livenessprobe: httpget: { path: /health/live, port: 8080 } without severity , every line is logged at default, and severity-based alerts never fire.

declarative yaml gcloud run services describe api --region=asia-south1 --format=export > service.yaml # edit, then: gcloud run services replace service.yaml --region=asia-south1 gcloud run jobs describe loader --region=asia-south1 --format=export > job.yaml gcloud run jobs replace job.yaml --region=asia-south1 the yaml follows the knative serving schema. in a team, keep the definition in terraform ( google_cloud_run_v2_service / _job ) and use the cli for reading and one-off executions.

c.h: Errors and what they usually mean
c.x: errors and what they usually mean symptom usually means "container failed to start and listen on the port defined by port" app listens on the wrong port or on 127.0.0.1, crashes on boot (missing env var or secret), or the image is arm64. read the revision's logs. 403 calling a service caller lacks roles/run.invoker , sent an access token instead of an id token, or the token's audience is not the service url. 404 calling a service wrong url or region, or ingress is internal and you called from outside the vpc. 429 / "no available instance" max-instances reached with all instances at full concurrency. 503 with "memory limit exceeded" in logs oom: raise --memory , or stop writing large files to the in-memory filesystem. 504 / request cancelled request ran past --timeout . permission denied on secret runtime service account lacks secretmanager.secretaccessor on that secret. image pull denied the cloud run service agent cannot read the artifact registry repo (common across projects). job execution failed, logs empty task timed out, was oom-killed, or crashed before logging. executions describe shows the reason per task. background work never finishes cpu is throttled after the response. finish before responding, use --no-cpu-throttling , or hand the work to a job or cloud tasks.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation deploy a service and read its logs execute a job and check its result roll traffic back to a previous revision 2 practitioner set scaling, cpu, memory, concurrency and timeouts deliberately secure services with iam, secrets and service accounts connect to private resources with vpc egress 3 senior design job sharding, retries and run records tune cold starts and cost design service-to-service auth and traffic management 4 expert set the serverless platform blueprint for the organisation decide cloud run vs gke vs other compute design multi-region serverless architectures each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

core concepts concept meaning organisation top-level apigee container, tied to a gcp project environment a runtime context where proxies are deployed (dev, test, prod) environment group hostnames that route to one or more environments api proxy the façade clients call; it applies policies and forwards to the backend proxy endpoint client-facing side: base path, request and response flows target endpoint backend-facing side: the service url, its auth and timeouts flow ordered steps: preflow, conditional flows, postflow, on request and response policy a reusable step: verify a key, check a token, rate-limit, transform, cache shared flow a reusable sequence of policies used by many proxies (security, logging) api product a bundle of proxies and operations with quotas and scopes, offered to consumers developer / app a consumer and their registered app, which gets keys for products apigee x is the google cloud-hosted version; apigee hybrid runs the runtime in your own kubernetes clusters. apigee edge is the older generation.

proxy endpoint <!-- apiproxy/proxies/default.xml --> <proxyendpoint name="default"> <preflow name="preflow"> <request> <step><name>vk-verifykey</name></step> <step><name>sa-spikearrest</name></step> <step><name>q-perapp</name></step> </request> </preflow> <flows> <flow name="search"> <condition>proxy.pathsuffix matchespath "/search" and request.verb = "get"</condition> </flow> </flows> <httpproxyconnection> <basepath>/shop/v1</basepath> </httpproxyconnection> <routerule name="default"> <targetendpoint>default</targetendpoint> </routerule> </proxyendpoint>

target endpoint to cloud run <!-- apiproxy/targets/default.xml --> <targetendpoint name="default"> <httptargetconnection> <authentication> <googleidtoken> <audience>https://shop-api-xxxxx.a.run.app</audience> </googleidtoken> </authentication> <url>https://shop-api-xxxxx.a.run.app</url> </httptargetconnection> </targetendpoint> apigee calls the private cloud run service with a google id token from the proxy's service account, which needs roles/run.invoker . clients never reach cloud run directly; set its ingress accordingly.

common policies <verifyapikey name="vk-verifykey"> <apikey ref="request.header.x-api-key"/> </verifyapikey> <oauthv2 name="oa-verifytoken"> <operation>verifyaccesstoken</operation> </oauthv2> <spikearrest name="sa-spikearrest"> <rate>30ps</rate> <!-- smooths bursts --> </spikearrest> <quota name="q-perapp"> <interval>1</interval> <timeunit>day</timeunit> <allow count="10000"/> <identifier ref="client_id"/> </quota> <assignmessage name="am-removekey"> <remove><headers><header name="x-api-key"/></headers></remove> </assignmessage> category policies security verifyapikey, oauthv2, verifyjwt, basicauthentication, accesscontrol, cors traffic spikearrest, quota, responsecache mediation assignmessage, extractvariables, jsontoxml, xmltojson, raisefault extension javascript, servicecallout, messagelogging, flowcallout (shared flows) spikearrest protects the backend from bursts; quota enforces each consumer's allowance. use both.

products, apps and keys build a proxy and deploy it to an environment. create an api product listing the proxy (and operations), environments, quota and scopes, e.g. "shop api – standard: 10,000 calls/day". a developer registers an app and subscribes it to the product. the app gets a consumer key (and secret for oauth). the proxy's verifyapikey or oauthv2 policy checks it and loads the product's quota. analytics then report traffic, latency and errors per product, app and developer. products are how you package the same api differently: free and paid tiers, internal and partner access.

apigee vs api gateway apigee api gateway scope full api management lightweight managed gateway features products, developer portal, monetisation, rich policies, analytics, hybrid openapi-defined routes, api keys, jwt auth, quotas backends anything reachable cloud run, cloud functions, app engine and others cost significant; subscription or pay-as-you-go low, per call choose when many apis, external consumers, governance, analytics a few apis, mostly internal or simple cloud endpoints is the older google option; new designs generally pick api gateway or apigee.

delivering proxies like code keep the apiproxy/ bundle and shared flows in git; review policy changes like code. deploy from ci with the apigee api, apigeecli or the apigee maven plugin, to dev → test → prod environments. manage organisations, environments and environment groups with terraform ( google_apigee_* resources). lint bundles with apigeelint before deploying. use shared flows as your blueprint: one security and logging flow every proxy calls, instead of copied policies. test with the trace/debug tool, and with automated api tests against each environment.

security and operations validate oauth tokens or jwts at the edge; the backend still checks object-level permissions. strip credentials before forwarding; add a trusted identity header only from apigee. use advanced api security to detect abuse and misconfigured proxies. put cloud armor in front of the external load balancer for waf and ddos protection. log to cloud logging with messagelogging; never log keys or tokens. watch latency split: total vs target response time tells you if the gateway or the backend is slow.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain proxies, policies, products and apps call an api through apigee with a key read apigee analytics for an api 2 practitioner build a proxy with key/token verification, spike arrest and quota use shared flows; deploy through environments from ci connect securely to cloud run backends 3 senior design api products, tiers and the developer portal run apigee across environments with terraform and ci secure apis at the edge with oauth and advanced api security 4 expert own the organisation's api management platform and governance design hybrid or multi-region apigee deployments lead api monetisation and partner programmes each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.
