git you will use daily git switch -c feat/123-short-name origin/main git add -p # stage hunk by hunk git commit -m "fix: reject unparseable order dates" git fetch origin && git rebase origin/main git push -u origin feat/123-short-name git push --force-with-lease # after a rebase; never plain --force git log --oneline --graph -20 git log -s "parse_date" --oneline # commits that added/removed a string git blame -l 40,60 file.py git diff origin/main...head # what my branch changes git show <sha>:path/file # a file at a revision git stash push -m wip; git stash pop git restore file # discard local edits git revert <sha> # undo a merged commit safely git bisect start bad good # binary-search a regression git worktree add ../wt2 -b other origin/main # second checkout git reflog # find "lost" commits

branching & pr habits trunk-based: short-lived branches off main , merged within a day, behind feature flags if unfinished. one concern per pr. if the title needs "and", split it. protect main : pr required, checks required, no force pushes. commit messages say why, not only what. conventional prefixes ( feat: , fix: , chore: ) help changelogs. review for behaviour: tests that would fail without the change, error paths, what happens when a dependency is down. promote artefacts, not branches: build once, tag the image with the commit sha, deploy that same image to each environment.

github actions → gcp (no keys) name: deploy on: push: { branches: [main] } permissions: contents: read id-token: write # needed for workload identity federation concurrency: { group: deploy-${{ github.ref }}, cancel-in-progress: false } jobs: test: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v7 - uses: actions/setup-java@v6 with: { distribution: temurin, java-version: 21, cache: gradle } - run: ./gradlew test deploy: needs: test runs-on: ubuntu-latest environment: prod # environment secrets, protection rules steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v7 - uses: google-github-actions/auth@v3 with: workload_identity_provider: ${{ vars.wif_provider }} service_account: ${{ vars.deploy_sa }} - uses: google-github-actions/setup-gcloud@v3 - run: | img=asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/${{ vars.gcp_project }}/apps/api:${github_sha::12} gcloud auth configure-docker asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev --quiet docker build -t "$img" . && docker push "$img" echo "img=$img" >> "$github_env" - uses: google-github-actions/deploy-cloudrun@v3 with: { service: api, region: asia-south1, image: "${{ env.img }}" } the major versions shown were current in november 2026; check each action's latest release. for security, pin third-party actions to a full commit sha rather than a tag. a workflow-level paths: filter on a required check can leave a pr waiting forever; skip inside the job instead.

release strategies strategy how when rolling replace instances a few at a time default for stateless services blue/green run old and new side by side, switch traffic at once fast rollback, needs double capacity canary send a small % to the new version, watch metrics, increase risky changes with good metrics feature flag ship code dark, turn it on per user or percentage separating deploy from release expand / contract add the new schema, migrate, remove the old in a later release database changes with zero downtime every release needs a rollback you have practised. a database migration that cannot be rolled back makes the whole release one-way.

blue-green, in plain words think of a theatre with two stages. the audience watches the blue stage while the crew builds the next show on the green one. when green is ready and rehearsed, you swing the audience over in one move. if something goes wrong, you swing them straight back: blue is still standing. before the switch: green gets the same checks real users would give it, through a private url or a test route. the switch is all at once, so a fault reaches every user, but only until you switch back, which takes seconds. keep blue running until you trust green. pulling it down early leaves you with no way back. # kubernetes: a deployment per colour, # labelled version: blue / version: green. # the service's selector picks the live one. kubectl patch service shop-api \ -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"version":"green"}}}' # roll back: patch it back to "blue". # cloud run: deploy green with no traffic gcloud run deploy api --image=…:4b1c2d0 \ --no-traffic --tag=green # test https://green---api-xxxxx.a.run.app gcloud run services update-traffic api \ --to-tags=green=100 the price: for a while you run two full copies, so you pay for twice the capacity. read martin fowler's bluegreendeployment .

canary, in plain words miners once took a canary underground: if the air turned bad, the bird showed it first. a canary release works the same way. a small share of real users gets the new version, you watch closely, and only when it looks healthy do you send more. go in steps: for example 1%, then 5%, 25%, 50%, 100%, pausing at each step long enough to learn something. compare the canary with the old version running at the same time, not with yesterday: error rate, p95 and p99 latency, saturation, and one number the business cares about. decide the stop rule before you start. "roll back if errors rise above 1% for five minutes" is a rule; "keep an eye on it" is not. # kubernetes gateway api: # weights on an httproute apiversion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: httproute metadata: name: shop-api spec: parentrefs: - name: public-gw rules: - backendrefs: - name: shop-api-stable port: 8080 weight: 95 - name: shop-api-canary port: 8080 weight: 5 # cloud run: move traffic by revision gcloud run services update-traffic api \ --to-revisions=api-00042-xyz=5,api-00041-abc=95 with istio, the same weights live on a virtualservice (see service mesh ). read the gateway api guide to http traffic splitting and fowler's canaryrelease .

c.h: Choosing between them, and the hard parts
c.x: choosing between them, and the hard parts pick blue-green when you need an instant, whole switch and an instant way back, and you can afford two copies for a while. it suits releases you can test fully before users arrive. pick canary when you have enough traffic and good metrics to learn from a small slice. at 1% of 100 requests an hour you learn almost nothing, so a quiet service is better served by blue-green and a thorough test. the database is the hard part of both. old and new versions run at the same time against the same data, so every schema change has to work for both: add first, move the data, remove the old shape in a later release (expand and contract). sessions and caches: a user who bounces between versions may see two behaviours, so keep a user on one version where that matters, and make sure caches and queues can be read by both. feature flags are a separate tool. a deploy puts code on servers; a flag decides who sees the feature. used together, a canary checks the code is healthy and a flag controls the release to users. automate it once you understand it. argo rollouts and flagger run blue-green and canary steps on kubernetes with automatic analysis, and harness has both built in. do it by hand a few times first, so you know what the tool is deciding for you. whichever you pick, rehearse the rollback before you need it. the way back is the part of a release that matters most when things go wrong, and it is usually the part nobody practised.

observability logs say what happened (structured json, with a request or run id). metrics say how much and how often. traces say where the time went across services. golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation. red for services (rate, errors, duration); use for resources (utilisation, saturation, errors). sli: a measured ratio, e.g. requests under 500 ms ÷ all requests. slo: the target, e.g. 99.5% over 30 days. error budget: the 0.5% you may spend on releases and incidents. alert on symptoms users feel (slo burn rate), not on every cpu spike. every alert needs an owner and a runbook. know "nothing there" from "cannot see": a check whose data source is down must report unknown, not zero or green.

incident response declare it early and name an incident lead. one channel, one timeline. mitigate before you diagnose: roll back, fail over, scale up, turn the flag off. communicate status on a schedule, even "no change". write down what you saw and did, with timestamps, as you go. review blamelessly afterwards: what happened, why the system allowed it, which guard would have caught it. track the follow-ups to done.

supply-chain & secrets no long-lived keys: workload identity federation for ci, service accounts for workloads. secrets in a secret manager, injected at runtime. never in git, images, logs or ci output. least privilege: one service account per workload, with only the roles it uses. dependency updates automated (dependabot or renovate), with tests gating them. scan code (sast), dependencies (sca), images (trivy) and committed secrets (gitleaks, github secret scanning). know what you ship: sboms and signed images (cosign) make "are we affected by cve-x?" a query, not a hunt.

measuring delivery dora metric question deployment frequency how often do we ship to production? lead time for changes commit to production: how long? change failure rate what share of deploys cause a failure? failed deployment recovery time (formerly time to restore) how fast do we recover from a failed deploy? deployment rework rate what share of deploys are unplanned fixes for a production incident? speed and stability rise together when changes are small, tested and easy to roll back.

twelve-factor, short version one codebase, many deploys; config in the environment, not the code. dependencies declared and pinned; backing services (db, queue) attached by url. build, release and run are separate steps; the same build goes to every environment. processes are stateless and disposable: fast start, graceful shutdown on sigterm . logs are an event stream to stdout; the platform collects them. admin tasks (migrations, backfills) run as one-off processes from the same release. dev and prod as similar as possible: same images, same database engine.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation use git daily: branch, commit, rebase, pr read a ci run and find why it failed roll back a deploy 2 practitioner write ci/cd workflows with caching and keyless cloud auth add structured logs, metrics and alerts take part in incident response 3 senior design release strategies (canary, blue/green, flags) define slos and alerting on symptoms improve dora metrics; lead post-incident reviews 4 expert build an internal developer platform and golden paths set delivery and reliability standards for the organisation lead culture change toward small, safe, frequent releases each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

signals and what each answers signal is answers cost driver logs timestamped records of events, ideally structured json what exactly happened in this request or run? volume and retention metrics numbers aggregated over time (counts, gauges, histograms) how much, how often, how fast, trending where? number of time series (label cardinality) traces a request's path across services as a tree of timed spans where did the time go? which dependency failed? sampling rate profiles where cpu and memory go inside the code which function is slow or allocating? usually low (continuous sampling) events / run records business or pipeline facts (deploys, run outcomes) what changed, and did the job do its work? low monitoring tells you that something is wrong from questions you planned. observability lets you find out why , including for failures nobody predicted. you need both.

structured logging {"timestamp":"2026-11-12t06:15:04.120z", "severity":"error", "message":"load failed", "service":"orders-load", "version":"3f2a9c1", "env":"prod", "run_id":"r-2026-11-12", "stage":"raw_load", "object":"gs://landing/data/year=2024/part-3.parquet", "error":"400 bad request", "error_body":"invalidargument: …", "logging.googleapis.com/trace":"projects/p/traces/4bf92f…"} one json object per line; a severity field so levels work. always include service, version, environment, and a request or run id. log the evidence: the upstream error body, the input that failed, counts. a log that says only "failed" helps no one. never log secrets, tokens or unnecessary personal data. levels: error needs attention; warn is unusual but handled; info is a business event; debug is off in production.

metrics that matter counter: only goes up (requests, errors, rows loaded). graph its rate. gauge: current value (queue depth, connections, lag). histogram: distribution of values (latency); gives percentiles. red for services: rate, errors, duration. use for resources: utilisation, saturation, errors. golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation. cardinality: each unique label combination is a separate series. never use user ids, request ids or urls with ids as labels. percentiles, not averages: p50 for typical, p95/p99 for the users having a bad time.

distributed tracing a trace is one request end to end; a span is one operation in it (an http call, a query), with start, duration, attributes and status. context propagation: the trace id travels in the w3c traceparent header and in message attributes across queues. sampling: keep a percentage of traces (head sampling), or keep all errors and slow ones (tail sampling in a collector). link logs to traces by writing the trace id into every log line. batch jobs: one trace per run, a span per stage or partition.

opentelemetry the vendor-neutral standard for producing logs, metrics and traces: one api in your code, an sdk that processes and exports, the otlp protocol, and an optional collector that receives, filters, samples and forwards to any backend. # java: zero-code instrumentation with the agent (http, jdbc, kafka, grpc …) java -javaagent:/otel/opentelemetry-javaagent.jar -jar app.jar # otel_service_name=shop-api # otel_exporter_otlp_endpoint=http://otel-collector:4318 # otel_traces_sampler=parentbased_traceidratio otel_traces_sampler_arg=0.1 # python: auto-instrumentation pip install opentelemetry-distro opentelemetry-exporter-otlp opentelemetry-bootstrap -a install otel_service_name=orders-load opentelemetry-instrument python -m loader # manual span around meaningful work (python) from opentelemetry import trace tracer = trace.get_tracer("orders-load") with tracer.start_as_current_span("load_object") as span: span.set_attribute("object.uri", uri) rows = load(uri) span.set_attribute("rows.loaded", rows) # collector: receive otlp, batch, send to google cloud receivers: otlp: protocols: grpc: http: processors: batch: exporters: googlecloud: googlemanagedprometheus: service: pipelines: traces: { receivers: [otlp], processors: [batch], exporters: [googlecloud] } logs: { receivers: [otlp], processors: [batch], exporters: [googlecloud] } metrics: { receivers: [otlp], processors: [batch], exporters: [googlemanagedprometheus] }

spring boot and micrometer # application.yml management: endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,prometheus tracing.sampling.probability: 0.1 otlp.tracing.endpoint: http://otel-collector:4318/v1/traces # boot 4: opentelemetry.tracing.export.otlp.endpoint observations.annotations.enabled: true # makes @observed work (needs aspectj on the classpath) logging.structured.format.console: ecs # 3.4+ @component class loadmetrics { private final counter loaded, failed; private final timer duration; loadmetrics(meterregistry r) { loaded = counter.builder("orders.objects").tag("outcome", "loaded").register(r); failed = counter.builder("orders.objects").tag("outcome", "failed").register(r); duration = timer.builder("orders.load.duration").publishpercentilehistogram().register(r); } } @observed(name = "order.search") // timer + span in one annotation public list<order> search(string q) { … }

google cloud observability tool use it for cloud logging all logs from cloud run, gke, bigquery jobs and audit logs; logs explorer; log sinks to bigquery or gcs; log-based metrics cloud monitoring metrics, dashboards, uptime checks, alerting policies, slos; queries in promql managed service for prometheus prometheus metrics at scale without running prometheus cloud trace distributed traces and latency analysis cloud profiler continuous cpu and heap profiling in production error reporting groups exceptions from logs, shows new and recurring errors audit logs who did what: admin activity always on; enable data access logs for sensitive services # logs explorer query resource.type="cloud_run_revision" resource.labels.service_name="shop-api" severity>=error jsonpayload.run_id="r-2026-11-12" timestamp>="2026-11-12t00:00:00z" # log-based metric from a marker in the text gcloud logging metrics create pipeline_incidents \ --description="pipeline incidents" \ --log-filter='textpayload:"pipeline_incident"' # promql in cloud monitoring: 5xx ratio and p95 latency sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count[5m])) histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_bucket[5m])))

dashboards that get used one overview per service: traffic, errors, latency percentiles, saturation, last deploy marker. top-down: user-facing slos first, then dependencies, then resources. same layout for every service (a dashboard template is a blueprint). show the denominator: "12 errors" means nothing without "of 1.2 million requests". annotate deploys and incidents so changes line up with effects. delete dashboards nobody opens.

alerting page on symptoms users feel (slo burn rate, failed runs, stale data), not on causes (cpu at 80%). every page is actionable and links to a runbook. if nobody needs to act, it is a ticket or a dashboard, not a page. alert when the signal is missing: a job that did not run, a metric that stopped reporting. silence is not health. match on fields you control (a marker in the message, a structured field), not on a severity that may not be set. prove each alert fires once in a test environment before trusting it. review noisy alerts monthly: tune, fix the cause, or delete.

observing data pipelines dimension check run outcome every scheduled run recorded succeeded, failed or unknown; missing runs alert freshness newest data per source within its expected age volume row and object counts within expected ranges; reconciliation in = out + rejected schema unexpected new, missing or retyped columns detected quality test results (nulls, keys, parse failures) tracked over time cost and duration bytes, slot time and runtime per run, trended the most important rule: a check whose source is unreachable reports unknown, never zero and never green.

observing ai features log model id, input and output tokens, latency, stop reason and cost per call. trace each tool call and retrieval step as a span. track refusals, empty retrievals, citation failures and "not found" rates. sample real conversations for quality review and feed them into evals (with privacy controls).

keeping observability affordable exclude noisy, low-value logs at the router (exclusion filters) or lower their level. sample traces; keep 100% of errors and slow requests with tail sampling. watch metric cardinality; drop unused labels. route long-term logs to bigquery or gcs with retention rules instead of keeping everything hot. label resources so observability cost can be attributed to teams.

following a journey across services give every request an id, and pass it on to every service the request touches. log it with every line. give every user journey an id too, when several requests belong together, such as a multi-step form or a checkout. then you can follow the whole journey, not just one request. use the standard for tracing: the w3c trace context traceparent header carries a trace id and the caller's span id between services, so tools from different vendors can join the pieces up. opentelemetry propagates it for you. an audit trail makes rollback safe. if a journey fails halfway, you can only undo the steps you know were taken. record each step and why, then compensate in reverse order (see architecture on sagas). # a w3c trace context header: version, trace id, parent span id, flags traceparent: 00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01

levels: what to expect 1 foundation find a request's or run's logs and errors in cloud logging read a service dashboard: traffic, errors, latency write structured logs with ids and evidence 2 practitioner instrument a service with opentelemetry and custom metrics write log queries, log-based metrics and promql build dashboards and actionable alerts with runbooks 3 senior design observability for a system: signals, sampling, cardinality, cost trace problems across services, queues and pipelines set dashboard and alert templates for teams 4 expert own the observability platform and its standards lead cost and data-governance strategy for telemetry drive observability-led reliability across the organisation each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

how they fit together tool category does gcp-native alternative prometheus metrics scrapes and stores time-series metrics; promql; alert rules managed service for prometheus, cloud monitoring alertmanager alert routing groups, silences and routes prometheus alerts to people and tools cloud monitoring notification channels grafana visualisation dashboards and alerting over many data sources; loki (logs), tempo (traces), mimir (metrics) in the same family cloud monitoring dashboards fluentd / fluent bit log shipping collect, parse, enrich and forward logs to any backend the built-in logging agents on gke and cloud run dynatrace full-stack apm / observability platform auto-instrumentation, topology, traces, logs, metrics, ai root-cause analysis cloud trace, profiler, logging, monitoring together servicenow it service management incidents, problems, changes, requests, cmdb, approvals and workflow none: itsm sits above monitoring typical flow: apps emit telemetry → fluent bit ships logs, prometheus scrapes metrics (or dynatrace's agent collects all) → grafana or dynatrace shows it → alerts route through alertmanager → servicenow opens an incident, pages on-call, and tracks the change that fixes it.

prometheus: model pull model: prometheus scrapes /metrics endpoints on an interval (spring: /actuator/prometheus ). exporters expose metrics for systems that do not: node_exporter (hosts), postgres_exporter, blackbox_exporter (probes). time series = metric name + labels. keep label values bounded. service discovery finds targets in kubernetes, gce and others. short-term storage locally; long-term in thanos, mimir or google's managed service. recording rules precompute expensive queries; alerting rules fire when an expression holds for a duration.

prometheus: configuration # prometheus.yml global: scrape_interval: 30s scrape_configs: - job_name: shop-api metrics_path: /actuator/prometheus static_configs: - targets: ["shop-api:8080"] rule_files: ["rules/*.yml"] alerting: alertmanagers: - static_configs: - targets: ["alertmanager:9093"] # rules/shop-api.yml groups: - name: shop-api rules: - record: job:http_5xx_ratio:rate5m expr: | sum by (job) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{status=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum by (job) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count[5m])) - alert: shopapihigherrorrate expr: job:http_5xx_ratio:rate5m{job="shop-api"} > 0.02 for: 10m labels: { severity: page } annotations: summary: "shop-api 5xx above 2% for 10 minutes" runbook_url: "https://runbooks.example.com/shop-api/high-errors" - alert: ordersloadmissing expr: time() - orders_load_last_success_timestamp_seconds > 26 * 3600 labels: { severity: page } annotations: { summary: "no successful orders load for 26 hours" }

promql you will use rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count[5m]) # per-second rate of a counter sum by (status) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count[5m])) # grouped histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_bucket[5m]))) # p95 latency increase(orders_objects_total{outcome="failed"}[1h]) # count over a window up == 0 # targets not scraped absent(orders_load_last_success_timestamp_seconds) # metric missing entirely topk(5, sum by (pod) (container_memory_working_set_bytes)) # top memory users always rate() a counter before summing; never sum raw counters. alert on absent() or up == 0 so a dead exporter is not mistaken for health.

alertmanager routing route: receiver: team-ticket group_by: [alertname, job] group_wait: 30s repeat_interval: 4h routes: - matchers: [ 'severity="page"' ] receiver: oncall-page receivers: - name: oncall-page pagerduty_configs: - routing_key_file: /etc/alertmanager/secrets/pagerduty_key - name: team-ticket webhook_configs: - url: https://integration.example.com/servicenow/alerts # creates a servicenow incident group related alerts, silence during planned work, and inhibit child alerts when the parent (a whole cluster down) is firing.

grafana data sources: prometheus, loki, tempo, cloud monitoring, bigquery, postgres and many more, in one dashboard. dashboards as code: provision from files or the grafana terraform provider; keep json in git and review changes. variables ( $service , $env ) make one dashboard serve every service: a dashboard template is a blueprint. grafana alerting can evaluate rules across data sources; pick one alerting system per signal to avoid duplicates. explore view for ad-hoc queries, and jumping from a metric spike to logs and traces of the same time window. # provisioning/datasources/prometheus.yaml apiversion: 1 datasources: - name: prometheus type: prometheus access: proxy url: http://prometheus:9090 isdefault: true

fluentd and fluent bit fluent bit: lightweight (c), the usual choice as a node agent or sidecar in kubernetes. fluentd: heavier (ruby), huge plugin ecosystem, often used as a central aggregator. pipeline: input → parser → filter (enrich, drop, mask) → buffer → output. on gke and cloud run logs are collected for you; add fluent bit when you need other destinations or self-managed clusters. mask secrets and personal data in filters before logs leave the node. # fluent bit (kubernetes node agent) [input] name tail path /var/log/containers/*.log multiline.parser cri tag kube.* [filter] name kubernetes match kube.* [filter] name grep match kube.* exclude log healthcheck [output] name stackdriver match * # fluentd <source> @type tail path /var/log/app/*.log pos_file /var/log/fluentd/app.pos tag app <parse> @type json </parse> </source> <filter app> @type record_transformer <record> env prod </record> </filter> <match app> @type stdout </match>

dynatrace oneagent: installed on hosts or via the kubernetes operator; instruments jvm, python, node, databases and more without code changes. smartscape: a live topology of hosts, processes, services and their dependencies. purepath: end-to-end distributed traces, down to code-level timing. davis ai: detects anomalies and groups related events into one "problem" with a probable root cause. grail and dql: stores logs, metrics, traces and events together and queries them with dynatrace query language. slos, synthetic monitoring, real-user monitoring and opentelemetry ingestion. // dql example: error logs per namespace in the last hour fetch logs, from:now()-1h | filter loglevel == "error" | summarize errors = count(), by:{k8s.namespace.name} | sort errors desc commercial platforms trade cost for breadth and automation. instrument with opentelemetry where you can, so changing vendor later does not mean re-instrumenting.

servicenow: the itsm side record is incident something is broken now; restore service problem the underlying cause of one or more incidents; fix it for good change request a planned change to production: standard (pre-approved), normal (assessed and approved), emergency request a user asking for something (access, a new environment) cmdb ci a configuration item: a service, app, database or host and its relationships event management turns monitoring alerts into correlated alerts and incidents, linked to the affected ci. change automation: ci/cd pipelines (harness, github actions, jenkins) open and update change requests automatically, so low-risk deploys are approved by policy rather than a weekly board. keep the cmdb generated from real sources (cloud apis, terraform state, service catalogues); hand-maintained cmdbs drift.

servicenow table api # open p1 incidents curl -s -u "$sn_user:$sn_pass" -h "accept: application/json" \ "https://$instance.service-now.com/api/now/table/incident?sysparm_query=active=true^priority=1&sysparm_limit=10&sysparm_fields=number,short_description,state" # create an incident from an automated check curl -s -u "$sn_user:$sn_pass" -x post \ -h "content-type: application/json" -h "accept: application/json" \ "https://$instance.service-now.com/api/now/table/incident" \ -d '{"short_description":"orders load missing for 26h", "urgency":"2","impact":"2", "assignment_group":"<sys_id of the data platform group>", "description":"ledger shows no succeeded land since 2026-11-11 06:15 utc. runbook: …"}' use an integration user with only the roles it needs, oauth rather than basic auth where available, and dedupe on a correlation id so a flapping alert does not open fifty incidents.

choosing and combining all on gcp, small team: cloud logging, monitoring and trace with opentelemetry; little to run. kubernetes-heavy, open source: prometheus + grafana + loki + tempo + fluent bit; you operate them (or use managed versions). large enterprise, many stacks: dynatrace (or similar) for automatic coverage and root cause, servicenow for process. whatever you choose: one alerting path per signal, runbooks on every alert, telemetry defined as code, and opentelemetry at the source.

principles 100% is the wrong target. users cannot tell 99.99% from 100%, and chasing it stops all change. pick the reliability users actually need. service level objectives make that target explicit and measurable. error budgets turn it into a decision rule: budget left, ship faster; budget spent, slow down and fix reliability. toil is reduced by engineering: automate repetitive manual work rather than staffing it. blameless postmortems: incidents are system failures to learn from, not people to blame. simplicity: every component you do not have cannot fail. no person or laptop is the mechanism: if something only works while a human watches it, it is not built yet.

sli, slo, sla, error budget term is example sli a measured ratio of good events to valid events search requests answered successfully in under 500 ms ÷ all search requests slo the target for an sli over a window 99.5% over 28 days error budget 1 − slo: the failure you may spend 0.5% of requests ≈ 3.4 hours of full outage in 28 days sla a contract with consequences, looser than the slo 99% monthly, or credits measure slis as close to the user as possible (load balancer or client), not from inside the server, which cannot see its own outages.

choosing slis system typical slis request/response api availability (non-5xx), latency (fraction under a threshold) data pipeline freshness (data newer than x), completeness (rows reconciled), correctness (tests passing) batch job runs completed on time; runs succeeded storage durability, read/write availability and latency ai feature successful responses, latency, grounded-answer rate from evals pipeline freshness slo example sli: minutes in which the newest order_date served is < 26 h old ÷ minutes in the window slo: 99% over 28 days budget: ≈ 6.7 hours of staleness per 28 days

error budget policy budget healthy: ship at normal speed; take calculated risks. budget at risk (e.g. 50% spent early): extra review on risky changes; reliability work moves up the backlog. budget exhausted: freeze non-urgent feature releases for the service until reliability fixes land and the budget recovers. one incident ate over 20% of the budget: a postmortem with tracked actions is mandatory. agree the policy with product owners before it is needed.

alerting on slos: burn rates burn rate = how fast you are spending the budget, relative to spending exactly all of it over the window. burn rate 1 uses the budget in exactly 28–30 days; burn rate 14.4 uses 2% of a 30-day budget in one hour. alert burn rate long window short window budget consumed action fast burn 14.4 1 hour 5 minutes 2% page medium burn 6 6 hours 30 minutes 5% page slow burn 1 3 days 6 hours 10% ticket both windows must exceed the threshold: the long one shows it matters, the short one shows it is still happening, so the alert stops soon after recovery. these are the starting values from google's sre workbook; tune to your traffic.

on-call sustainable load: few enough pages that each one gets real attention; track pages per shift. every page has a runbook: what it means, how to check, how to mitigate, who to escalate to. primary and secondary on rotation, with handover notes. access ready in advance: break-glass roles, dashboards, tooling; never "i need permissions" at 3 a.m. reduce pages continuously: every page should lead to a fix, a tuned alert, or an automated response.

incident response role does incident commander owns the incident, coordinates, decides; does not debug operations lead investigates and applies mitigations communications lead updates stakeholders and users on a schedule scribe keeps the timeline: what was seen, decided, done, when declare early; set severity; open one channel. mitigate first: roll back, fail over, disable the feature, shed load. communicate status regularly, including "no change". resolve, confirm with the slis, then hand over to the postmortem.

severity levels sev example response 1 product down or data loss or leak for many users page now, all hands, exec updates 2 major feature broken or badly degraded page now, incident roles 3 minor feature or few users affected; workaround exists business hours 4 cosmetic or internal only ticket

blameless postmortem template # incident: <title> sev: 2 date: 2026-11-12 ## summary what happened, impact, duration (2–3 sentences) ## impact users affected, slo budget spent, data affected ## timeline (utc) detection, escalation, mitigation, resolution ## root cause(s) the conditions that allowed it, not a person ## detection how we found out; how we should have ## what went well ## what went badly ## where we got lucky ## action items owner · due date · ticket — prevent, detect, mitigate ## lessons what we now know about the system ask "what made this possible?" five times, not "who did it?". turn each lesson into a guard: a test, an alert, a policy, an automation.

toil toil is manual, repetitive, automatable, reactive work that grows with the service and leaves no lasting value: restarting jobs by hand, re-running loads, copying credentials. cap it (google aims for under 50% of an sre's time) and spend the rest on engineering that removes it. measure it: log toil tasks and their time; automate the biggest first. automation must be durable: a scheduler and a job in the platform, not a script on someone's laptop or a session polling in a loop.

production readiness review slos defined, measured and on a dashboard. alerts on slo burn and on missing runs, each with a runbook; proven to fire. logs structured, traces flowing, dashboards from the template. capacity tested at expected peak plus headroom. deploys automated, with canary or rollback tested. backups exist and a restore has been tested ; rpo and rto written down. dependencies listed with their failure behaviour. security review done; secrets in a manager; least-privilege iam. on-call rotation and escalation path in place.

reliability practices progressive delivery: canaries, feature flags and automatic rollback. capacity planning: forecast from growth, load-test to find limits, keep headroom. graceful degradation: serve partial or cached results and say so. disaster recovery: multi-zone by default; multi-region when the slo needs it; rehearsed restores. game days and chaos tests: break things on purpose in a controlled way to test detection and response. dependency slos: your slo cannot exceed what your critical dependencies provide unless you add redundancy.

slos on google cloud cloud monitoring service monitoring defines services and slos (request-based or window-based) and charts budget. alert policies can use the slo burn rate directly. declare slos and alerts in terraform ( google_monitoring_slo , google_monitoring_alert_policy ) so they are reviewed and versioned. for pipelines, compute freshness and completeness slis from run records in bigquery and export them as custom or log-based metrics.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain sli, slo, error budget and sla follow a runbook and escalate during an incident contribute to a blameless postmortem 2 practitioner define slis and slos for a service or pipeline set up burn-rate alerts and runbooks take on-call shifts and lead mitigation 3 senior act as incident commander; run postmortems and track actions write and enforce an error budget policy with product owners run production readiness reviews and capacity plans 4 expert set reliability strategy and sre practice for the organisation design multi-region resilience and dr programmes build a culture of blameless learning and toil reduction each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

modules module does continuous integration builds and tests, with caching and test intelligence (runs only tests affected by a change) continuous delivery & gitops deploys services to kubernetes, serverless, vms and more, with strategies, approvals, verification and rollback; argo cd-based gitops feature flags turn features on per user or percentage, separating deploy from release security testing orchestration runs scanners in pipelines and gathers their results cloud cost management cost visibility, budgets and recommendations chaos engineering inject failures to test resilience infrastructure as code management run and govern terraform/opentofu workspaces internal developer portal backstage-based service catalogue and templates modules and their names change over time; check the current harness docs for what your account includes.

building blocks account → organisation → project: the hierarchy for access control and shared resources. pipeline: stages run in order or parallel; each stage has steps. stage types: build (ci), deploy (cd), approval, custom. service: what you deploy (manifests, artefact). environment and infrastructure definition: where you deploy (dev, prod; a cluster or project). connector: a stored, permissioned link to github, gcp, a registry or a cluster. delegate: an agent running in your infrastructure that executes tasks, so harness never needs inbound access. secrets: stored in harness or referenced from google secret manager or vault. templates: versioned step, stage and pipeline templates teams reuse. triggers: start pipelines on git events, artefact pushes or schedules.

pipeline as code (shape) pipeline: name: shop-api identifier: shop_api orgidentifier: default projectidentifier: shop stages: - stage: name: build identifier: build type: ci spec: clonecodebase: true execution: steps: - step: type: run name: test identifier: test spec: shell: sh command: ./gradlew test - stage: name: approve prod identifier: approve type: approval spec: execution: steps: - step: type: harnessapproval name: founder approval identifier: founder timeout: 1d spec: approvers: usergroups: [prod_approvers] minimumcount: 1 - stage: name: deploy prod identifier: deploy_prod type: deployment spec: # service, environment, infrastructure and strategy # (rolling / canary / blue-green) go here ... this shows the structure only. build pipelines in the harness editor first and copy its yaml into git, since exact step specs vary by module and version.

expressions <+pipeline.sequenceid> run number <+pipeline.executionid> unique run id <+codebase.commitsha> the commit being built <+codebase.branch> <+artifact.tag> deployed image tag <+env.name> target environment <+service.name> <+secrets.getvalue("db_password")> resolved at runtime, masked in logs <+pipeline.variables.region>

deploying safely strategies: rolling, canary and blue-green built in, with automatic rollback steps. continuous verification: compares metrics and logs (from prometheus, datadog, cloud monitoring and others) of the new version against the old, and fails the stage when they degrade. approvals: harness user groups, or jira/servicenow tickets. freeze windows: block deployments during set periods. policy as code: opa policies on pipelines (e.g. "prod deploys must have an approval stage and a verification step"). audit trail: who ran what, with which inputs, when.

harness vs github actions github actions harness strength ci next to the code; huge action marketplace cd: strategies, verification, approvals, governance at scale deployment model you script it in workflow steps first-class services, environments and strategies governance environments, rulesets, required reviewers opa policies, templates, rbac, freeze windows, audit fits small and medium teams; code-centric workflows many teams and services needing a standard, governed path to production a common split: github actions builds and tests on every pr; harness promotes the built artefact through environments.

c.h: End to end: commit to production on Google Cloud
c.x: end to end: commit to production on google cloud trigger: a push or merged pull request on github starts the pipeline (webhook trigger on main ; pr trigger runs ci only). ci stage: clone, restore cache, compile and run tests (with test intelligence), run scanners, then build the image once and push it to artifact registry tagged with the commit sha. deploy to dev: a cd stage deploys that exact image to the dev environment (gke or cloud run) with a rolling strategy. verify dev: smoke tests and continuous verification against dev metrics and logs. approval: a named group approves prod (or a policy auto-approves outside freeze windows). deploy to prod: canary or blue-green with the same artefact; verification watches error rate and latency; automatic rollback on degradation. notify and record: slack/email notification, deployment recorded with who, what, which commit, and the verification result. build once, promote the same artefact. rebuilding per environment means prod runs something that was never tested.

harness ci in depth build infrastructure: harness cloud (hosted machines), your kubernetes cluster (pods per build), your own vms, or a local runner. choose by network access, cost and isolation. codebase: the repo connector and clone settings for the pipeline; each ci stage can clone automatically. run step: any shell command in a container image you choose ( eclipse-temurin:21 , python:3.12 ). test step with test intelligence: selects only tests affected by the change, and reports results in the ui (junit xml). background step: a service the build needs, such as postgres or a kafka broker, running beside the steps. build and push steps: build an image and push it to artifact registry, docker hub or another registry. caching: cache intelligence for common build tools, or explicit save/restore cache steps to gcs or s3. plugins: drone plugins and many github actions can run as steps. outputs: steps export variables for later steps and stages, e.g. the image tag.

a ci stage (shape) - stage: name: build identifier: build type: ci spec: clonecodebase: true platform: { os: linux, arch: amd64 } runtime: { type: cloud, spec: {} } # harness cloud machines execution: steps: - step: type: run name: unit tests identifier: unit_tests spec: image: eclipse-temurin:21 shell: sh command: ./gradlew test reports: type: junit spec: paths: ["**/build/test-results/test/*.xml"] - step: type: buildandpushgar name: image identifier: image spec: connectorref: gcp_bld host: asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev projectid: my-proj imagename: apps/shop-api tags: [<+codebase.shortcommitsha>] field names follow harness's yaml at the time of writing; generate the stage in the editor and compare before committing.

harness cd in depth service: what you deploy: the artefact source (artifact registry image), manifests (kubernetes yaml, helm chart, kustomize) and variables. environment: dev or prod, marked pre-production or production, with environment-level overrides (replicas, urls, secrets). infrastructure definition: the exact target: a gke cluster and namespace, or a gcp project and region for serverless. deployment types: kubernetes, native helm, serverless targets, vms over ssh/winrm, tanzu, ecs, and custom deployments for anything else. check harness's current list for google cloud targets such as cloud run and cloud functions. execution: generated from the chosen strategy, editable step by step; failure strategies say what to do on each kind of error (retry, rollback, manual intervention). rollback: a rollback section per stage, run automatically on failure or on a failed verification. input sets and overlays: saved sets of runtime inputs (which service, which tag) so one pipeline serves many services. multi-service and multi-environment deployments from a single stage.

deployment strategies in harness strategy how harness runs it use when rolling replaces pods or instances gradually; rollback restores the previous release default for stateless services canary deploys a small canary set, verifies, then rolls out fully and deletes the canary risky changes with good metrics blue-green deploys the new version as a stage set, tests it, then swaps traffic instant switch and rollback; capacity for two copies basic / custom your own steps (shell, http, terraform, approvals) targets without a built-in type

connecting harness to google cloud gcp connector with oidc (workload identity federation) where your plan supports it, so no service account key is stored. otherwise inherit credentials from a delegate running in gke with workload identity. one service account per environment with only the roles deploys need (artifact registry reader/writer, gke developer or cloud run developer, and service account user on the runtime account). delegates run inside your network (for example a gke namespace), so private clusters and services are reachable without opening inbound access. run at least two for availability. secrets referenced from google secret manager through a secret manager connector. github connector with a github app for cloning, pr status checks and webhooks.

github actions → harness mapping github actions harness workflow pipeline job stage step / action step / plugin on: push, pull_request triggers runner build infrastructure / delegate secrets and variables secrets, variables, connectors environments + required reviewers environments + approval stages + opa policies reusable workflows templates services: containers background steps matrix looping strategies (matrix, repeat, parallelism)

troubleshooting symptom check step queued, never starts no healthy delegate or build infrastructure matching the selector connector test fails delegate network egress, credentials, or the account's iam roles image pull error in deploy cluster or runtime identity lacks artifact registry read; wrong tag expression deployment times out readiness probes failing; check pod events and logs in the step output verification fails unexpectedly baseline too short, wrong metric query, or too few data points; read the analysis detail expression resolves to null wrong scope or step identifier; use the expression picker in the editor pipeline in git differs from ui remote pipeline branch selection; check which branch the run used

good practice keep pipelines, templates and input sets in git, reviewed like code. one pipeline template per deployment shape; services pass only inputs. run unit and integration tests in ci on every pr; deploy only from main . promote by artefact tag or digest; never rebuild per environment. every prod stage has verification and an automatic rollback. enforce with opa: prod needs approval, verification, and an artefact from the trusted registry. watch delegate health and versions; alert when none are connected. track dora metrics from harness deployment data.

harness as a blueprint publish account-level templates for "build a jvm service", "deploy to cloud run", "deploy to gke". teams reference the template version; a fix to the template reaches every pipeline that uses it. enforce the template with opa policies rather than reviews. keep pipelines in git (remote pipelines) so changes are reviewed like code. this is the same idea as the ai tab's blueprints card: decide once, reuse everywhere.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation run a pipeline and read its logs understand stages, steps, services and environments approve or roll back a deployment 2 practitioner build ci and cd pipelines with connectors, secrets and triggers use canary or blue-green with verification keep pipelines in git and use templates 3 senior design org-wide templates and opa policies set up delegates, rbac and environments securely integrate verification with monitoring and feature flags 4 expert own the delivery platform strategy and its governance lead migrations from other ci/cd tools measure and improve delivery (dora) across teams each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

cli workflow terraform init # providers + backend terraform init -upgrade # newer providers within constraints terraform fmt -recursive terraform validate terraform plan -var-file=env/dev.tfvars -out=plan.tfplan terraform show plan.tfplan # read it before applying terraform apply plan.tfplan # applies exactly what you read terraform plan -destroy terraform plan -target=module.landing # emergency only terraform apply -replace=google_cloud_run_v2_job.loader terraform output -json terraform console # try expressions terraform providers lock -platform=linux_amd64 -platform=darwin_arm64 validate checks syntax and types only. a missing optional module argument or a wrong iam wiring shows up in a plan, not before.

providers & backend terraform { required_version = ">= 1.7" required_providers { google = { source = "hashicorp/google", version = "~> 8.0" } # pin the major version you have tested } backend "gcs" { bucket = "my-proj-tfstate" # versioning on! prefix = "dataplatform" } } provider "google" { project = var.project_id region = var.region default_labels = { managed_by = "terraform", env = var.env } } # backend values cannot use variables; pass them at init: # terraform init -backend-config="bucket=my-proj-dev-tfstate"

variables, locals, outputs variable "env" { type = string validation { condition = contains(["dev", "prod"], var.env) error_message = "env must be dev or prod." } } variable "stages" { type = map(object({ enabled = bool args = optional(list(string), []) })) } variable "db_password" { type = string sensitive = true } locals { name_prefix = "dp-${var.env}" enabled = { for k, v in var.stages : k => v if v.enabled } } output "bucket_url" { value = google_storage_bucket.landing.url } # env/dev.tfvars env = "dev" stages = { land = { enabled = true, args = ["--max-objects=50"] } }

count, for_each, dynamic # for_each over a set or map: stable addresses by key (prefer over count) resource "google_bigquery_dataset" "layer" { for_each = toset(["raw", "analytics", "mart"]) dataset_id = each.key location = var.region } # reference: google_bigquery_dataset.layer["analytics"].dataset_id # count for on/off resource "google_cloud_scheduler_job" "tick" { count = var.clock_enabled ? 1 : 0 ... } # reference: one(google_cloud_scheduler_job.tick[*].id) # dynamic nested blocks dynamic "env" { for_each = var.env_vars content { name = env.key value = env.value } } # list of objects → map for for_each for_each = { for t in var.tables : t.name => t } with count , removing an item in the middle renumbers everything after it and terraform destroys and recreates those resources.

bigquery dataset & table resource "google_bigquery_dataset" "analytics" { dataset_id = "analytics" location = "asia-south1" delete_contents_on_destroy = false labels = { layer = "analytics" } } resource "google_bigquery_table" "orders" { dataset_id = google_bigquery_dataset.analytics.dataset_id table_id = "orders" deletion_protection = true require_partition_filter = true time_partitioning { type = "month" field = "order_date" } clustering = ["store_id", "order_ref"] schema = jsonencode([ { name = "order_id", type = "string", mode = "required" }, { name = "store_id", type = "string" }, { name = "order_ref", type = "string" }, { name = "order_date", type = "date" }, ]) } resource "google_bigquery_dataset_iam_member" "api_reader" { dataset_id = google_bigquery_dataset.analytics.dataset_id role = "roles/bigquery.dataviewer" member = "serviceaccount:${google_service_account.api.email}" } tables that dbt builds should not also be declared here; two owners fight over the schema. declare datasets and iam, let dbt own its tables.

gcs bucket resource "google_storage_bucket" "landing" { name = "${var.project_id}-landing" location = "asia-south1" storage_class = "standard" uniform_bucket_level_access = true public_access_prevention = "enforced" force_destroy = false versioning { enabled = true } lifecycle_rule { condition { age = 90 matches_prefix = ["tmp/"] } action { type = "delete" } } lifecycle_rule { condition { age = 365 } action { type = "setstorageclass" storage_class = "coldline" } } }

cloud run job + cloud scheduler resource "google_cloud_run_v2_job" "loader" { name = "${local.name_prefix}-loader" location = var.region deletion_protection = false template { task_count = 1 template { service_account = google_service_account.loader.email timeout = "3600s" max_retries = 0 containers { image = var.loader_image # pass a tag or digest, never :latest args = ["--year=2024"] resources { limits = { cpu = "1", memory = "2gi" } } env { name = "db_password" value_source { secret_key_ref { secret = google_secret_manager_secret.db.secret_id version = "latest" } } } } } } } resource "google_cloud_scheduler_job" "daily" { name = "${local.name_prefix}-daily" region = var.region schedule = "15 6 * * *" time_zone = "etc/utc" paused = var.clock_paused http_target { http_method = "post" uri = "https://run.googleapis.com/v2/projects/${var.project_id}/locations/${var.region}/jobs/${google_cloud_run_v2_job.loader.name}:run" oauth_token { service_account_email = google_service_account.scheduler.email scope = "https://www.googleapis.com/auth/cloud-platform" } } } the scheduler's service account needs roles/run.invoker (or run.developer for overrides) on the job.

iam: member, binding, policy # _member: adds one principal to one role. safe, composable. use this. resource "google_project_iam_member" "loader_bq" { project = var.project_id role = "roles/bigquery.jobuser" member = "serviceaccount:${google_service_account.loader.email}" } # _binding: owns the member list for one role (removes anyone else) # _policy: owns the whole policy (removes everything else, can lock you out) resource "google_service_account" "loader" { account_id = "dp-loader" display_name = "orders loader job" } # workload identity federation for github actions: no json keys resource "google_service_account_iam_member" "gh_deploy" { service_account_id = google_service_account.deploy.name role = "roles/iam.workloadidentityuser" member = "principalset://iam.googleapis.com/${google_iam_workload_identity_pool.gh.name}/attribute.repository/org/repo" } never mix _policy or _binding with _member for the same role: they overwrite each other on every apply.

modules modules/pipeline-job/ main.tf variables.tf outputs.tf versions.tf module "orchestrator" { source = "./modules/pipeline-job" name = "orchestrator" image = var.orchestrator_image service_account_email = google_service_account.orch.email args = ["--tick"] } module "jobs" { # for_each on modules (0.13+) source = "./modules/pipeline-job" for_each = local.enabled name = each.key args = each.value.args } output "job_names" { value = { for k, m in module.jobs : k => m.name } } # registry / git sources: pin a version source = "terraform-google-modules/cloud-storage/google" version = "~> 12.0" source = "git::https://github.com/org/tf-modules.git//bq?ref= v1.4.0 "

refactor without destroying # bring an existing resource under management (1.5) import { to = google_storage_bucket.landing id = "my-proj-landing" } # terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf # rename / move into a module (1.1) moved { from = google_cloud_run_v2_job.loader to = module.jobs["land"].google_cloud_run_v2_job.this } # stop managing, keep the real resource (1.7) removed { from = google_bigquery_table.legacy lifecycle { destroy = false } } # cli equivalents (no review step: prefer the blocks above) terraform state list terraform state show google_storage_bucket.landing terraform state mv 'a.b' 'module.x.a.b' terraform state rm google_bigquery_table.legacy

lifecycle, checks, preconditions resource "google_sql_database_instance" "shop" { ... lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true # plan fails instead of destroying ignore_changes = [settings[0].disk_size] # autoresize owns it create_before_destroy = false precondition { condition = var.env != "prod" || var.tier != "db-f1-micro" error_message = "prod needs a real tier." } } } # replace when something else changes (1.2) lifecycle { replace_triggered_by = [terraform_data.image_rev] } # check block: warns on every plan, never blocks (1.5) check "landing_bucket_reachable" { data "google_storage_bucket" "l" { name = google_storage_bucket.landing.name } assert { condition = data.google_storage_bucket.l.versioning[0].enabled error_message = "landing bucket versioning is off." } }

functions & expressions "${var.env}-landing" format("dp-%s-%03d", var.env, 7) join(",", var.stores) split(",", "a,b,c") merge(local.base_labels, var.labels) concat(list_a, list_b) lookup(var.tiers, var.env, "small") try(var.cfg.timeout, "600s") coalesce(var.override, "default") one(resource.x[*].id) flatten([for d in var.datasets : [for t in d.tables : "${d.name}.${t}"]]) toset(list) keys(map) values(map) zipmap(keys, vals) setproduct(var.envs, var.regions) contains(list, "x") can(regex("^[a-z]+$", var.name)) jsonencode(obj) yamldecode(file("${path.module}/rows.yaml")) templatefile("${path.module}/startup.sh.tftpl", { bucket = local.bucket }) var.enabled ? "a" : "b" [for s in var.stages : upper(s) if s != "skip"] { for k, v in var.stages : k => v.args } timestamp() # changes every plan: avoid in resource arguments

terraform test (1.6) # tests/stages.tftest.hcl variables { env = "dev" stages = { land = { enabled = true } } } run "bld_window_is_small" { command = plan assert { condition = length(local.enabled) <= 4 error_message = "dev enables too many stages." } } run "rejects_unknown_env" { command = plan variables { env = "staging" } expect_failures = [var.env] } # terraform test (mock_provider "google" {} keeps it offline, 1.7+)

safety checklist read every plan line that says destroy or -/+ (replace). a replaced database or bucket loses its data. state bucket: versioning on, uniform access, only the deploy identity can write. state holds secrets in plain text. one state per environment (separate prefix or project). workspaces suit identical copies, not dev vs prod with different shapes. pin providers with ~> and commit .terraform.lock.hcl . images by tag or digest from a variable, never :latest , so a plan shows when the image moves. no secrets in tfvars. reference secret manager; mark variables sensitive . apply from ci with workload identity federation, from a saved plan file. config is not state: after an apply, read the live resource to confirm it.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation run init, plan and apply; read a plan change a resource's arguments safely use variables and outputs 2 practitioner write reusable modules with validation manage state in a remote backend; use moved and import blocks run terraform from ci with keyless auth 3 senior design module and state layout for many environments refactor live infrastructure without destroying it write terraform tests and policy checks 4 expert own infrastructure-as-code standards for the organisation design org-wide landing zones and guardrails lead provider upgrades and large migrations each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

core objects kind use it for pod one or more containers sharing network and volumes. rarely created directly. deployment stateless apps: keeps n replicas, rolling updates, rollback. statefulset stable names and per-pod disks: databases, kafka, zookeeper. daemonset one pod per node: log shippers, node agents. job / cronjob run to completion, once or on a schedule: batch loads, migrations. service stable virtual ip and dns name in front of matching pods. ingress / gateway http routing from outside into services (gateway api is the newer model). configmap / secret configuration and credentials, as env vars or files. persistentvolumeclaim a request for durable storage. serviceaccount identity for pods (and, on gke, the link to a google service account). horizontalpodautoscaler scale replicas on cpu, memory or custom metrics. networkpolicy pod-level firewall rules. namespace a scope for names, quotas and rbac.

kubectl daily kubectl config get-contexts kubectl config use-context gke_my-proj_asia-south1_main kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=shop kubectl get pods -o wide kubectl get deploy,svc,ing kubectl get all -a # every namespace kubectl describe pod api-7d9f-abcde # events at the bottom kubectl logs deploy/api -f --since=10m kubectl logs api-7d9f-abcde -c sidecar --previous # crashed container kubectl exec -it deploy/api -- sh kubectl port-forward svc/api 8080:80 kubectl top pods # needs metrics-server kubectl apply -f k8s/ --dry-run=server # validate against the cluster kubectl diff -f k8s/ kubectl apply -f k8s/ kubectl rollout status deploy/api kubectl rollout undo deploy/api kubectl rollout restart deploy/api # new pods re-read env from secrets/configmaps (re-pull only with imagepullpolicy: always) kubectl scale deploy/api --replicas=3 kubectl get events --sort-by=.lasttimestamp kubectl explain deployment.spec.strategy # built-in field docs

deployment + service apiversion: apps/v1 kind: deployment metadata: { name: api, labels: { app: api } } spec: replicas: 2 selector: { matchlabels: { app: api } } strategy: { rollingupdate: { maxunavailable: 0, maxsurge: 1 } } template: metadata: { labels: { app: api } } spec: serviceaccountname: api containers: - name: api image: asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/apps/api:3f2a9c1 ports: [{ containerport: 8080 }] envfrom: [{ configmapref: { name: api-config } }] env: - name: db_password valuefrom: { secretkeyref: { name: db, key: password } } resources: requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 512mi } limits: { memory: 512mi } readinessprobe: httpget: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 } periodseconds: 5 livenessprobe: httpget: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 } initialdelayseconds: 20 startupprobe: httpget: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 } failurethreshold: 30 periodseconds: 2 --- apiversion: v1 kind: service metadata: { name: api } spec: selector: { app: api } ports: [{ port: 80, targetport: 8080 }]

job & cronjob apiversion: batch/v1 kind: cronjob metadata: { name: orders-load } spec: schedule: "15 6 * * *" timezone: "etc/utc" concurrencypolicy: forbid # never two runs at once startingdeadlineseconds: 600 successfuljobshistorylimit: 3 failedjobshistorylimit: 5 jobtemplate: spec: backofflimit: 0 # no automatic retries activedeadlineseconds: 3600 ttlsecondsafterfinished: 86400 template: spec: restartpolicy: never serviceaccountname: loader containers: - name: loader image: asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/apps/loader:3f2a9c1 args: ["--year=2024"] resources: { requests: { cpu: "1", memory: 2gi }, limits: { memory: 2gi } } kubectl create job --from=cronjob/orders-load manual-20250131 # run now kubectl get jobs; kubectl logs job/manual-20250131

services & traffic clusterip (default): reachable inside the cluster only. nodeport : a port on every node (30000–32767). mostly a building block. loadbalancer : provisions a cloud load balancer with an external (or internal, by annotation) ip. headless ( clusterip: none ): dns returns pod ips directly; used with statefulsets. dns name: <svc>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local ; within the same namespace just <svc> . a service with no endpoints means its selector matches no ready pod: check labels and readiness. apiversion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: ingress metadata: { name: api } spec: ingressclassname: nginx # gke's own controller uses the annotation kubernetes.io/ingress.class: gce instead # ingress nginx was retired in march 2026: prefer gateway api or a maintained controller rules: - host: api.example.com http: paths: - path: / pathtype: prefix backend: { service: { name: api, port: { number: 80 } } } kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=api

requests, limits, probes requests decide scheduling: the node must have that much free. limits cap use. over the memory limit → the container is killed ( oomkilled , exit 137). over the cpu limit → throttled, not killed. set memory request = limit for steady apps. many teams leave the cpu limit off to avoid throttling. jvm: size heap from the container with -xx:maxrampercentage=75 . readiness failing removes the pod from service traffic. liveness failing restarts it. startup holds the other two off until the app has booted. never make liveness depend on a database or another service: an outage then restarts every pod. qos: guaranteed (requests = limits for all), burstable, besteffort (none set; evicted first).

debug by status status usually means pending no node fits the requests, a pvc is unbound, or a node selector/taint excludes all nodes. describe pod → events. imagepullbackoff wrong image name or tag, or the node's identity cannot read the registry. crashloopbackoff the app starts and exits. logs --previous shows why: bad config, missing secret, failed probe. oomkilled memory limit too low, or a leak. check describe → last state. createcontainerconfigerror a referenced configmap or secret key does not exist. running, not ready readiness probe failing: wrong path or port, or a dependency is down. evicted node ran short of memory or disk. kubectl debug -it api-7d9f-abcde --image=busybox:1.36 --target=api # ephemeral debug container kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=nicolaka/netshoot -- bash # network toolbox pod

config, secrets, scaling, safety kubectl create configmap api-config --from-literal=dataset=analytics --from-file=app.yml kubectl create secret generic db --from-literal=password='...' # base64, not encrypted kubectl get secret db -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d # hpa kubectl autoscale deploy api --cpu-percent=70 --min=2 --max=10 # poddisruptionbudget: keep capacity during node upgrades apiversion: policy/v1 kind: poddisruptionbudget metadata: { name: api } spec: minavailable: 1 selector: { matchlabels: { app: api } } # networkpolicy: default deny ingress in the namespace apiversion: networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: networkpolicy metadata: { name: default-deny-ingress } spec: podselector: {} policytypes: [ingress] for real secrets use secret manager via the csi driver or external secrets, not values committed in yaml.

rbac & gke workload identity # pod's kubernetes sa → google service account (no json keys) apiversion: v1 kind: serviceaccount metadata: name: loader namespace: shop annotations: iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account: dp-loader@my-proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding \ dp-loader@my-proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com \ --role=roles/iam.workloadidentityuser \ --member="serviceaccount:my-proj.svc.id.goog[shop/loader]" # rbac: read-only on pods in one namespace kubectl create role pod-reader --verb=get,list,watch --resource=pods -n shop kubectl create rolebinding jo-reads --role=pod-reader --user=jo@example.com -n shop kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n shop --as=jo@example.com gke can also grant iam roles straight to the kubernetes principal ( principal://iam.googleapis.com/projects/<number>/locations/global/workloadidentitypools/<proj>.svc.id.goog/subject/ns/<ns>/sa/<ksa> ) without a google service account.

gke, helm, kustomize gcloud container clusters create-auto main --region=asia-south1 # autopilot gcloud container clusters get-credentials main --region=asia-south1 gcloud container clusters list # helm: packaged apps with values helm install redis oci://registry-1.docker.io/bitnamicharts/redis \ -n cache --create-namespace -f values.yaml # check the chart's readme for where its images come from helm upgrade --install api ./chart --set image.tag=3f2a9c1 helm template ./chart | kubectl diff -f - helm rollback api 1 # kustomize: one base, overlays per env (built into kubectl) k8s/base/kustomization.yaml resources: [deploy.yaml, svc.yaml] k8s/overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml resources: [../../base] images: [{ name: api, newtag: 3f2a9c1 }] patches: [{ path: replicas.yaml }] kubectl apply -k k8s/overlays/prod autopilot: google manages nodes and you pay per pod request. standard: you manage node pools. for one-shot batch work, cloud run jobs are often simpler than a cluster.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation use kubectl to get, describe, log and exec read a deployment and service manifest explain why a pod is pending or crashing 2 practitioner write manifests with probes, resources and config use helm or kustomize per environment set up workload identity and rbac 3 senior design namespaces, network policies and autoscaling run production clusters: upgrades, pdbs, capacity debug networking, dns and scheduling problems 4 expert design multi-cluster platforms and tenancy models build operators and platform abstractions set kubernetes strategy and security policy each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

concepts term meaning chart a package: templates, default values and metadata values inputs that fill the templates; defaults in values.yaml , overridden per environment release one installed instance of a chart in a namespace, with a name revision each install, upgrade or rollback of a release; the history helm can roll back to repository / registry where charts are published: an http chart repo or an oci registry (e.g. artifact registry) chart version vs app version version changes when the chart changes; appversion names the application it deploys

chart structure shop-api/ chart.yaml # name, versions, dependencies values.yaml # defaults values.schema.json # optional: validate values templates/ _helpers.tpl # named templates (labels, names) deployment.yaml service.yaml ingress.yaml configmap.yaml hpa.yaml notes.txt # printed after install tests/ test-connection.yaml charts/ # dependency charts (vendored) # chart.yaml apiversion: v2 name: shop-api description: shop api type: application # or "library" for shared templates only version: 0.3.0 # chart version (semver) appversion: "3f2a9c1" # image tag it deploys by default dependencies: - name: common version: "1.x.x" repository: oci://asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/charts

commands helm create shop-api # scaffold helm lint ./shop-api helm template shop ./shop-api -f values-prod.yaml # render locally, no cluster helm upgrade --install shop ./shop-api \ -n shop --create-namespace \ -f values-prod.yaml --set image.tag=3f2a9c1 \ --atomic --timeout 5m # roll back automatically on failure # helm 4 renamed --atomic to --rollback-on-failure; check `helm version` helm list -n shop helm history shop -n shop helm rollback shop 4 -n shop helm get values shop -n shop # what was applied helm get manifest shop -n shop helm uninstall shop -n shop helm dependency update ./shop-api helm package ./shop-api # → shop-api- 0.3.0 .tgz helm push shop-api- 0.3.0 .tgz oci://asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/charts helm install shop oci://asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/charts/shop-api --version 0.3.0

templates # templates/_helpers.tpl {{- define "shop-api.fullname" -}} {{- printf "%s-%s" .release.name .chart.name | trunc 63 | trimsuffix "-" -}} {{- end -}} {{- define "shop-api.selectorlabels" -}} app.kubernetes.io/name: {{ .chart.name }} app.kubernetes.io/instance: {{ .release.name }} {{- end -}} # templates/deployment.yaml apiversion: apps/v1 kind: deployment metadata: name: {{ include "shop-api.fullname" . }} labels: {{- include "shop-api.selectorlabels" . | nindent 4 }} app.kubernetes.io/version: {{ .values.image.tag | default .chart.appversion | quote }} spec: replicas: {{ .values.replicacount }} selector: matchlabels: {{- include "shop-api.selectorlabels" . | nindent 6 }} template: metadata: labels: {{- include "shop-api.selectorlabels" . | nindent 8 }} annotations: checksum/config: {{ include (print $.template.basepath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }} spec: containers: - name: app image: "{{ .values.image.repository }}:{{ .values.image.tag | default .chart.appversion }}" resources: {{- toyaml .values.resources | nindent 12 }} {{- with .values.env }} env: {{- toyaml . | nindent 12 }} {{- end }} envfrom: - secretref: name: {{ required "secretname is required" .values.secretname }} the checksum/config annotation restarts pods when the configmap changes. required fails the render with a clear message instead of deploying something broken.

values per environment # values.yaml (defaults: safe, small) replicacount: 1 image: repository: asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/apps/shop-api tag: "" # defaults to appversion resources: requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 512mi } limits: { memory: 512mi } env: [] secretname: "" # values-prod.yaml (only what differs) replicacount: 3 resources: requests: { cpu: "1", memory: 1gi } limits: { memory: 1gi } secretname: shop-api-secrets later -f files override earlier ones; --set overrides files. prefer files in git over --set . add values.schema.json so a typo in a value fails at install, not at runtime. never put secret values in values files; reference secrets created by external secrets or the secret manager csi driver.

hooks and tests # templates/migrate-job.yaml: run db migrations before an upgrade apiversion: batch/v1 kind: job metadata: name: {{ include "shop-api.fullname" . }}-migrate annotations: "helm.sh/hook": pre-install,pre-upgrade "helm.sh/hook-weight": "0" "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded spec: backofflimit: 0 template: spec: restartpolicy: never containers: - name: migrate image: "{{ .values.image.repository }}:{{ .values.image.tag | default .chart.appversion }}" args: ["migrate"] hook events: pre-install , post-install , pre-upgrade , post-upgrade , pre-rollback , pre-delete and more. migrations in a hook must be backward compatible: a rollback does not undo them. helm test shop runs pods annotated "helm.sh/hook": test to smoke-test a release. unit-test templates with the helm-unittest plugin; lint and install-test charts in ci with chart-testing ( ct ).

helm, kustomize and gitops helm kustomize approach templates + values plain yaml + patches per overlay packaging and versions yes: charts, releases, rollback no: just manifests best for distributing reusable apps; many similar services your own manifests with small per-environment differences risk template logic becomes hard to read many overlays become hard to follow gitops (argo cd, flux): the desired chart version and values live in git; a controller in the cluster applies them and reports drift. no one runs helm upgrade by hand in production. run helm diff upgrade (plugin) or the gitops diff before every production change.

chart best practices selector labels never change after the first release: kubernetes forbids changing a deployment's selector. standard labels ( app.kubernetes.io/name , instance , version , managed-by ). sensible defaults: resources, probes, security context (non-root, read-only root filesystem) on by default. keep templates boring: little logic; move complexity into values, not nested conditionals. a library chart of shared helpers is your blueprint: every service chart depends on it, so a fix reaches all of them. pin dependency versions ; publish charts to an oci registry with immutable versions. document values in values.yaml comments and the schema.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation install, upgrade, roll back and inspect a release read a chart's values and override them per environment render a chart locally with helm template 2 practitioner write charts with helpers, schema-validated values and sane defaults use hooks for migrations and helm test for smoke tests publish charts to an oci registry 3 senior design library charts as a shared blueprint for many services deliver charts with gitops (argo cd or flux) and diffs choose between helm and kustomize per case 4 expert own the organisation's deployment packaging standards run chart supply chain: signing, provenance, registries lead migrations between delivery models each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.
