the pattern a custom resource definition (crd) adds a new resource type to the kubernetes api, such as postgrescluster or pipelinerun . users create custom resources stating the desired state ( spec ): "three postgres replicas, version 16, nightly backups". a controller watches those resources and the objects it owns, and reconciles : observe the actual state, compare it with the spec, act to close the gap, and record what it saw in status . reconcile runs again on every change and periodically, so the system heals itself when reality drifts. controllers are level-triggered : they act on the current state, not on the event that woke them. that makes them robust to missed events and restarts, as long as every reconcile is idempotent.

operator or helm chart? helm chart operator does installs and upgrades a set of manifests continuously manages a system through its whole life day-2 operations none after apply backups, failover, scaling, upgrades, repair fits stateless services, most applications stateful systems (databases, kafka), complex platforms cost templates a program to build, test, secure and maintain most teams should use well-tested operators (often installed with helm), not write their own. write one only when you have real operational knowledge to automate and no existing operator does it.

operators worth knowing cert-manager: issues and renews tls certificates. prometheus operator: prometheus, alertmanager and scrape targets as resources ( servicemonitor , prometheusrule ). cloudnativepg: postgresql clusters with replication, failover and backups. strimzi: kafka clusters, topics and users. spark operator: spark applications as resources. argo cd / flux: gitops controllers. external secrets operator: syncs secrets from secret manager into kubernetes. config connector / crossplane: manage cloud resources (gcs buckets, cloud sql) as kubernetes objects.

a custom resource definition apiversion: apiextensions.k8s.io/v1 kind: customresourcedefinition metadata: name: pipelineruns.data.example.com spec: group: data.example.com scope: namespaced names: plural: pipelineruns singular: pipelinerun kind: pipelinerun shortnames: [plr] versions: - name: v1alpha1 served: true storage: true subresources: status: {} additionalprintercolumns: - { name: date, type: string, jsonpath: .spec.rundate } - { name: phase, type: string, jsonpath: .status.phase } schema: openapiv3schema: type: object properties: spec: type: object required: [rundate, stages] properties: rundate: { type: string, format: date } stages: type: array items: { type: string, enum: [land, raw_load, build] } status: type: object x-kubernetes-preserve-unknown-fields: true apiversion: data.example.com/v1alpha1 kind: pipelinerun metadata: { name: run-2026-11-12, namespace: data } spec: rundate: "2026-11-12" stages: [land, raw_load, build] # kubectl get plr -n data

go: kubebuilder and controller-runtime kubebuilder init --domain example.com --repo github.com/example/pipeline-operator kubebuilder create api --group data --version v1alpha1 --kind pipelinerun make manifests # generate crds and rbac from code markers make install run # install crds, run the controller locally func (r *pipelinerunreconciler) reconcile(ctx context.context, req ctrl.request) (ctrl.result, error) { var run datav1alpha1.pipelinerun if err := r.get(ctx, req.namespacedname, &run); err != nil { return ctrl.result{}, client.ignorenotfound(err) // deleted: nothing to do } // 1. observe: the jobs this run owns // 2. compare: which stage should run next, given spec and finished jobs? // 3. act: create that stage's job with a deterministic name // (creating it twice returns alreadyexists: idempotent) // and set an owner reference so it is garbage-collected with the run // 4. record: update status.phase and conditions via the status subresource return ctrl.result{requeueafter: time.minute}, nil }

java and python // java operator sdk @controllerconfiguration public class pipelinerunreconciler implements reconciler<pipelinerun> { @override public updatecontrol<pipelinerun> reconcile(pipelinerun run, context<pipelinerun> ctx) { // observe owned jobs, create the next stage's job if missing run.setstatus(computestatus(run, ctx)); return updatecontrol.patchstatus(run); } } // quarkus has an extension for the java operator sdk # python: kopf import kopf @kopf.on.create("data.example.com", "v1alpha1", "pipelineruns") @kopf.on.update("data.example.com", "v1alpha1", "pipelineruns") def reconcile(spec, name, namespace, status, logger, **_): next_stage = choose_next_stage(spec["stages"], status) if next_stage: ensure_job(name, namespace, next_stage) # idempotent create return {"phase": "running" if next_stage else "succeeded"} # kopf stores it under status.reconcile

rules for a good controller idempotent reconcile: running it ten times gives the same result as once. no in-memory state: everything needed is in the cluster (spec, status, owned objects), so restarts are safe. status and conditions: report ready , progressing , degraded with reasons and the observed generation. owner references so owned objects are cleaned up automatically; finalizers to clean up things outside the cluster (cloud resources) before deletion. requeue with backoff on errors; never tight-loop. leader election so only one replica acts at a time. least-privilege rbac , generated from the code. validate early: openapi schema and cel rules ( x-kubernetes-validations ) reject bad specs at the api. distinguish unknown from failed: if the controller cannot read a dependency, report that, rather than marking the resource failed or healthy.

testing and operating operators unit-test the decision logic (spec + observed state → actions) without a cluster. envtest (go) runs a real api server for integration tests; kind or k3d clusters for end-to-end tests. crd versioning: start at v1alpha1 ; add conversion webhooks when you introduce new versions; never break stored objects. metrics: reconcile counts, errors, duration and queue depth (controller-runtime exposes them). capability levels (operator framework): basic install → seamless upgrades → full lifecycle → deep insights → autopilot. aim for the level your users need. distribution: package the operator with a helm chart or olm bundle.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation explain crds, custom resources, controllers and reconcile use existing operators (cert-manager, cloudnativepg, strimzi) read a resource's status and conditions 2 practitioner write a crd with schema validation build a simple controller with kubebuilder, java operator sdk or kopf use owner references, finalizers and status correctly 3 senior design operators for stateful systems and day-2 operations test with envtest and real clusters; version crds with conversion decide operator vs helm vs managed service 4 expert build platform apis on kubernetes for the organisation maintain operators at high capability levels contribute to the operator ecosystem each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

what a mesh gives you capability what it means without a mesh mutual tls every call between services encrypted and authenticated with workload certificates, rotated automatically tls and certificates managed in each service workload identity and authorisation policies such as "only the frontend's service account may call get /api/*" network policies (ip-based) and code checks traffic management canary weights, header-based routing, mirroring, timeouts, retries load balancer rules or code resilience circuit breaking, outlier detection, connection limits libraries such as resilience4j in each service observability uniform request metrics, access logs and trace spans for every hop instrumentation in every service egress control only allow-listed external hosts reachable firewall and proxy rules north-south traffic (clients into the platform) is the gateway's job; east-west traffic (services to each other) is the mesh's. business logic belongs in neither.

when it is worth it good reasons many services on kubernetes, often in several languages. a requirement for encrypted, authenticated traffic between all services (zero trust, compliance). frequent canary or progressive releases. uniform telemetry without changing every service. reasons to wait a handful of services, or a modular monolith. serverless platforms such as cloud run, which already give service identity (iam) and tls. no one to own and upgrade the mesh: it is a critical system in every request path.

istio architecture control plane, istiod : turns your configuration into proxy configuration, issues workload certificates, and pushes both to the data plane. data plane, sidecar mode: an envoy proxy injected into every pod intercepts its inbound and outbound traffic. full l7 features per pod, at the cost of a proxy per pod. data plane, ambient mode: a per-node ztunnel provides l4 mtls and identity for all pods without sidecars; optional waypoint proxies add l7 features (routing, l7 authorisation) only where needed. lower overhead and no pod restarts to join. gateways: envoy deployments at the edge for ingress and egress, configured with the kubernetes gateway api or istio's own gateway resource. on google cloud, cloud service mesh offers a managed, istio-based mesh for gke and other environments.

install and enrol workloads # sidecar mode istioctl install --set profile=default -y kubectl label namespace shop istio-injection=enabled kubectl rollout restart deploy -n shop # pods get sidecars on restart # ambient mode istioctl install --set profile=ambient -y kubectl label namespace shop istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient # no restart needed istioctl waypoint apply -n shop --enroll-namespace # add l7 where needed istioctl analyze -n shop # check configuration for problems in production, install and upgrade istio through helm charts or your platform's managed offering, from git, with canary upgrades of the control plane (revisions).

the resources you will write resource purpose gateway + httproute (kubernetes gateway api) ingress and routing; the recommended api for new setups virtualservice istio routing rules: matches, weights, retries, timeouts, fault injection destinationrule policies for a destination: subsets (versions), load balancing, connection pools, outlier detection, tls peerauthentication mtls mode for workloads: strict or permissive authorizationpolicy who may call what: by service account, namespace, path, method, jwt claims requestauthentication validate end-user jwts at the proxy serviceentry register external services so they can be reached and controlled sidecar limit which services a sidecar knows about, to reduce memory and config size telemetry tune metrics, access logs and tracing

security: mtls and authorisation # mesh-wide strict mtls (after a permissive migration period) apiversion: security.istio.io/v1 kind: peerauthentication metadata: { name: default, namespace: istio-system } spec: mtls: { mode: strict } --- # only the frontend may call the api, and only get on /api/* apiversion: security.istio.io/v1 kind: authorizationpolicy metadata: { name: shop-api-allow, namespace: shop } spec: selector: { matchlabels: { app: shop-api } } action: allow rules: - from: - source: { principals: ["cluster.local/ns/web/sa/frontend"] } to: - operation: { methods: ["get"], paths: ["/api/*"] } --- # validate end-user jwts at the proxy apiversion: security.istio.io/v1 kind: requestauthentication metadata: { name: jwt, namespace: shop } spec: selector: { matchlabels: { app: shop-api } } jwtrules: - issuer: "https://auth.example.com/" jwksuri: "https://auth.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json" once any allow policy selects a workload, everything not allowed is denied. roll out in a test namespace first. the service still checks object-level permissions: the mesh knows which service is calling, not whether this user owns this case.

traffic: canary, retries, timeouts apiversion: networking.istio.io/v1 kind: destinationrule metadata: { name: shop-api, namespace: shop } spec: host: shop-api subsets: - { name: v1, labels: { version: v1 } } - { name: v2, labels: { version: v2 } } trafficpolicy: connectionpool: { http: { http1maxpendingrequests: 100 } } outlierdetection: # eject failing pods for a while consecutive5xxerrors: 5 interval: 10s baseejectiontime: 30s --- apiversion: networking.istio.io/v1 kind: virtualservice metadata: { name: shop-api, namespace: shop } spec: hosts: [shop-api] http: - timeout: 3s retries: { attempts: 2, pertrytimeout: 1s, retryon: "5xx,connect-failure" } route: - { destination: { host: shop-api, subset: v1 }, weight: 90 } - { destination: { host: shop-api, subset: v2 }, weight: 10 } # the same split with the gateway api apiversion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 kind: httproute metadata: { name: shop-api, namespace: shop } spec: parentrefs: [{ name: shop-gateway }] hostnames: ["api.example.com"] rules: - backendrefs: - { name: shop-api-v1, port: 8080, weight: 90 } - { name: shop-api-v2, port: 8080, weight: 10 } put retries in one place, mesh or application, not both: retries multiplied at every layer turn a slowdown into a retry storm. retry only idempotent requests.

egress control # with outbound traffic policy registry_only, only registered hosts are reachable apiversion: networking.istio.io/v1 kind: serviceentry metadata: { name: payment-gateway, namespace: shop } spec: hosts: ["api.example-payments.com"] ports: [{ number: 443, name: https, protocol: tls }] resolution: dns location: mesh_external route egress through an egress gateway when you need a fixed exit point, central logging, or to combine with cloud nat and firewall rules.

observability with a mesh metrics for every request, such as istio_requests_total and request duration histograms, labelled by source, destination and response code. kiali draws the live service graph with health and traffic. tracing: proxies create spans, but your application must forward the trace headers ( traceparent ) from incoming to outgoing requests, or traces break at every service. access logs per proxy, tunable with the telemetry resource. # 5xx rate per destination service sum by (destination_service) (rate(istio_requests_total{response_code=~"5.."}[5m])) / sum by (destination_service) (rate(istio_requests_total[5m]))

debugging istioctl analyze -a # config problems across namespaces istioctl proxy-status # is every proxy in sync with istiod? istioctl proxy-config routes deploy/shop-api -n shop istioctl proxy-config clusters deploy/shop-api -n shop istioctl x describe pod <pod> -n shop # which policies apply to this pod kubectl logs <pod> -c istio-proxy -n shop # sidecar access log symptom usually 503 with uf / urx flags upstream failing or refusing; check the app and outlier ejection 503 nr no route: virtualservice or httproute mismatch connection reset after enabling strict a client outside the mesh still sends plain text 403 rbac: access denied an authorizationpolicy denies it (or no allow rule matches) app fails at startup calling a dependency sidecar not ready yet; hold the app until the proxy starts jobs never complete sidecar keeps the pod alive; use native sidecars or ambient mode pod has no sidecar namespace not labelled, or pod created before the label

meshes compared mesh notes istio most features; sidecar or ambient; large community; more to learn and operate cloud service mesh google-managed, istio-based, integrated with gke and cloud monitoring linkerd simpler and lightweight, with its own rust proxy; fewer features cilium service mesh ebpf-based networking with mesh features, often without sidecars consul spans kubernetes and vms, with service discovery

adopting a mesh safely install in a non-production cluster; enrol one namespace. start with permissive mtls and observe traffic in kiali and metrics. move namespaces to strict once every client is in the mesh. add authorizationpolicies service by service, tested in ci against a cluster. move retries, timeouts and canaries into the mesh deliberately, removing duplicates from code. keep all mesh config in git, delivered by gitops, with istioctl analyze in ci. plan control-plane upgrades with revisions and canary them like any critical release.

how an llm works, briefly tokenise: text is split into tokens (word pieces). everything (price, limits, speed) is counted in tokens. embed: each token becomes a vector of numbers. transformer layers: attention lets every token look at every earlier token and mix in what is relevant; dozens of layers build up meaning. predict: the model outputs a probability for every possible next token; one is chosen, appended, and the process repeats. generation is one token at a time. stage what happens result pre-training predict the next token over a huge text and code corpus broad knowledge and language ability, up to a training cutoff post-training instruction tuning, reinforcement learning from human and ai feedback, safety training follows instructions, uses tools, refuses harmful requests inference your prompt in, tokens out, on gpus or tpus the responses you build on consequences you design around: no memory between calls; knowledge stops at a cutoff; outputs vary run to run; fluent text can be wrong; instructions inside data can be followed.

prompt, rag, tools or fine-tune? need reach for behaviour, format, tone clear instructions and examples in the prompt; structured outputs knowledge the model lacks (your documents, current data) rag : retrieve and include it live data or actions tools (function calling) or mcp servers a narrow task at high volume, cheaper or faster a smaller model, or fine-tuning one, after measuring consistent style the prompt cannot achieve fine-tuning (lora or full) try in that order. fine-tuning does not add reliable facts; it changes behaviour. facts belong in retrieval.

runtime options runtime what it is choose when hosted model api provider runs the model (anthropic api, others) best models, no gpus to run, pay per token cloud platform models through your cloud account (vertex ai, bedrock, foundry) billing, iam, region and data controls in your cloud managed open-model endpoints deploy open-weight models to a managed endpoint (vertex ai model garden) open models without running servers yourself self-hosted server vllm or llama.cpp server (hugging face tgi is now in maintenance mode) on your gpus (gke, cloud run with gpus, vms) data must stay on your infrastructure; steady high volume; custom models local ollama or llama.cpp on a laptop experiments, offline development, small models

self-hosting basics # vllm: openai-compatible server for an open-weight model vllm serve meta-llama/llama-3.1-8b-instruct --max-model-len 8192 # → http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions # ollama: local models with one command ollama run llama3.1 # → api on http://localhost:11434 # llama.cpp: quantised gguf models on cpu or gpu llama-server -m model-q4_k_m.gguf --port 8080 gpu memory ≈ parameters × bytes per parameter, plus the kv cache. an 8b model in 16-bit needs ~16 gb before the cache; 4-bit quantisation cuts that to ~5 gb at some quality cost. throughput comes from continuous batching (vllm) and caching the prompt prefix. measure time to first token, tokens per second, and cost per thousand requests against a hosted api before committing. licences of open-weight models differ; read them before commercial use.

c.h: Building on a runtime: four levels of harness
c.x: building on a runtime: four levels of harness a harness is the code around the model: the loop that sends messages, runs tools, feeds results back, manages context and stops. pick the least you need. level you write who runs the loop and tools fits 1. single call prompt and parsing no loop classify, extract, summarise 2. manual tool loop the while stop_reason == "tool_use" loop and the tools you, on your infrastructure full control over each step 3. sdk tool runner just the tool functions the sdk runs the loop; you host it most custom agents 4a. agent sdk a prompt and options claude code's harness as a library, with built-in file, shell and search tools; you host it coding and file-system agents on your own infrastructure 4b. managed agents agent configuration and your tool results the provider runs the loop and a sandbox per session long-running hosted agents without running infrastructure start at level 1 and move up only when the task needs model-driven, multi-step work. each level adds cost, latency and things to test.

level 2: a manual tool loop import anthropic, json client = anthropic.anthropic() tools = [{ "name": "pipeline_status", "description": "latest state of each pipeline stage for a date (yyyy-mm-dd).", "input_schema": {"type": "object", "properties": {"run_date": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["run_date"]}, }] def run_tool(name, args): if name == "pipeline_status": return json.dumps(read_ledger(args["run_date"])) # read-only return json.dumps({"error": f"unknown tool {name}"}) messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "did yesterday's load finish?"}] for _ in range(10): # always bound the loop resp = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=16000, tools=tools, messages=messages) messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": resp.content}) if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use": break results = [{"type": "tool_result", "tool_use_id": b.id, "content": run_tool(b.name, b.input)} for b in resp.content if b.type == "tool_use"] messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results}) # all results in one message print("".join(b.text for b in resp.content if b.type == "text")) append the full resp.content , not just its text. return failed tools as results with "is_error": true rather than dropping them. level 3 (the sdk's tool runner) does this loop for you.

running llm features in production timeouts, retries and fallbacks per call; handle refusals and rate limits explicitly. stream long outputs; use the batch api for offline bulk work. prompt caching: keep stable instructions and tool definitions first so repeated calls reuse them. log model, version, tokens, latency and outcome for every call; trace tool calls. pin model ids and re-run your evals before switching models. budget: cap tokens per request and spend per day; alert on spikes. data controls: know the provider's retention terms and the region where inference runs.

glossary context window: maximum tokens of input plus output in one call. embedding: a vector representing meaning, used for search. kv cache: stored attention state that makes generating each next token fast. quantisation: storing weights with fewer bits to save memory. lora: fine-tuning small adapter weights instead of the whole model. temperature / sampling: how random token choice is (some newer apis fix this and expose an effort setting instead). hallucination: confident output not supported by facts. grounding: tying answers to retrieved sources.

one we build: penstock to run agents on your own servers, on a hosted model or a local ollama model, see penstock , our open-source (apache 2.0) agent harness. it is ours, so we are not neutral: compare it with the runtimes on this page.

c.h: Use AI like a bulldozer, not a shovel
c.x: use ai like a bulldozer, not a shovel a shovel moves one scoop at a time while you hold the handle: ask for a line, paste it, ask again. a bulldozer moves the whole job while you choose where it goes, set the boundaries and check the result. the second gets far more done, but only if you prepare the site. and only if you know enough to manage the site: see fundamentals first on start here. shovel habit bulldozer habit "write a function that…" with no context hand over a whole task: the issue, the files, the conventions and what done means copy and paste answers from a chat window let an agent work in the repo: edit files, run the build and tests, read the errors, fix them re-explain the project in every session write the context down once (a claude.md or agents.md , skills, runbooks) so every session starts informed check its work by reading every line as it types define checks up front (tests, lint, type checks, ci) and review the finished change against them one task at a time, waiting on each run independent tasks in parallel: separate branches or worktrees, subagents for research and review fix the same mistake by hand again next week turn each correction into a rule, test or hook in the repo so it cannot recur trust it because it sounds sure trust it because the tests passed and the docs agree

preparing the site context file in the repo: what the system is, how to build and test it, the rules that are not negotiable, the traps that cost time before. fast, exact gates: the commands that prove a change is done, written down so the agent runs them itself. guardrails: permission settings and hooks that stop destructive commands (force pushes, prod deploys, deletes) unless a human approves. small, clear tasks: one concern per task, with acceptance criteria. a vague brief gets a confident guess. pinned docs: links to the official docs for the versions you use, so it checks instead of recalling. a reviewer that is not the author: a second agent or a person reviews the diff against the spec and the docs.

a brief that moves earth (an illustrative brief: the problem and the paths are examples.) goal: reject dates that do not parse, instead of storing null. why: one source sends dd-mm-yyyy; the parser turns those into null without saying so, and the rows look like "no date". where: models/intermediate/int_orders_normalised.sql and its unit tests. rules: follow claude.md. do not change the other sources. no new dependencies. done when: - a unit test with "05-05-1959" and "bad" fails before the fix, passes after - dbt build -s int_orders_normalised+ is green - the reject table counts unparseable rows out of scope: backfilling old rows (separate issue). report: what changed, the test output, anything you could not verify. goal, reason, location, rules, a checkable definition of done, scope, and what to report. the same brief works for a colleague.

c.h: Where you still drive by hand
c.x: where you still drive by hand irreversible actions: production deploys, data deletion, schema changes on live data, anything sent outside the company. unclear requirements: decide what to build first; an agent will fill gaps with plausible guesses. security and money: auth, permissions, payments, secrets. review line by line. claims about state: "prod has x" needs someone to look at prod, not a model's inference from config. judgement calls that belong to a person: priorities, trade-offs, wording that speaks for the company. the bulldozer is only as safe as its operator. speed comes from preparation and checks, not from skipping them.

c.h: Why everyone's experience of AI is different
c.x: why everyone's experience of ai is different ask ten people what ai is like at writing code and you will hear ten different answers, often strongly held, including from people who have never written code. most of them are honest. they are describing different experiences, not the same one. what you bring decides what you get. if you cannot read the code, you cannot tell good output from output that only looks good. an experienced engineer spots the bug, writes a precise brief, and knows when to stop and do it by hand. same tool, very different results. the task is different. a small demo built from nothing is not a ten-year-old system with real users, real data and real security needs. ai can shine at the first and still struggle with the second. when and how much you used it. an afternoon is not years of daily use, and the tools change month to month. a view formed once, early or late, ages quickly. where you stand. a manager sees speed. a reviewer sees more code to check. the engineer on call sees the incident. a newcomer sees a patient teacher. each is real. talking about ai and code without ever having coded is a little like describing a marathon without ever having walked: you can see the photos at the finish line, but not the miles. people who do not code still see things engineers miss, as users, designers and leaders, and their views on those things count. judging how well ai writes and maintains code takes the experience of writing and maintaining code. trust works the same way, in both directions. adaptive cruise control is a real help to someone who has driven for years, in manual and automatic cars: they know when to lean on it, and when to take the wheel back. for someone who has never driven at all, trusting it blindly and refusing it outright are both guesses. trust in ai-written code grows from the same place: solid foundations, so you know what good looks like and when to take over. and even good drivers need guard rails. roads have speed limits, crash barriers and lane markings because skilled people still make mistakes. ai-written code needs its own: tests and type checks that run on every change ( testing ), ci gates that block a red build, code review by someone who did not write it, hooks that check each edit as it happens and least-privilege permissions so an agent cannot touch production on its own ( claude code & cowork , agent harness ), secrets kept out of prompts ( security ), and a person who approves the merge. so everyone is right about what they experienced, and none of it is the whole truth for everyone else. when you hear a strong view, ask: what did you try it on, for how long, and how did you check the result? share specifics, not verdicts. and before forming your own view, try it yourself on real work, then check the result properly (see behaviours : learn by doing, not by opinion). we still need solid foundations and guard rails: learn to drive first (see start here : fundamentals first), then drive on a road with barriers.

c.h: Blueprints and frameworks, not generated boilerplate
c.x: blueprints and frameworks, not generated boilerplate ai makes boilerplate cost almost nothing to write . it does not make it cheap to own . every generated copy has to be reviewed, secured, tested, upgraded and debugged, and fifty copies that are each slightly different are fifty places to fix the same bug. a blueprint (a framework, shared library, template, terraform module or dbt package) makes each decision once, tests it once, and fixes it once for everyone. generated boilerplate blueprint or framework consistency each copy drifts: retries, logging, auth and error handling differ per service one behaviour everywhere, so people and tools know what to expect fixing a bug or cve find and patch every copy, and miss some patch once, bump the version, done review hundreds of generated lines to read in every pr review only the part that is new; the rest is already proven security each copy can reintroduce a hole the model learned from public code secure defaults built in and tested upgrades every service upgrades on its own, or never upgrade the blueprint; services follow knowledge decisions live in whichever prompt produced the code decisions are written down, versioned and reviewable ai quality the model guesses your conventions from its training data the model follows your blueprint, so its output is smaller and fits rule of thumb: if you would ask ai to generate the same thing twice, it belongs in a blueprint. use ai to build and improve the blueprint, then to fill in only the part that is specific: the business logic, the one new query, the tests for it. point the ai at the blueprint in your context file ("new jobs use modules/pipeline-job ; new services start from the service template"), so it extends instead of reinventing. generation is fine for one-off scripts, prototypes you will throw away, and filling in a blueprint's slots. examples in this guide: spring boot starters and quarkus extensions; a terraform module for every cloud run job; dbt macros, generic tests and packages; a shared library such as culvert for storage and warehouse access; a service template in backstage or cookiecutter; and a written build-loop blueprint that is ported between repos instead of re-prompted in each. more on the frameworks vs ai boilerplate tab.

how models behave tokens: models read and write tokens (pieces of words). cost, limits and latency are all counted in tokens. context window: everything the model can see in one call: instructions, history, retrieved documents, tool results. it remembers nothing between calls unless you send it again. non-deterministic: the same input can give different outputs. test with sets of examples and scores, not one run. confidently wrong: a model can produce fluent, specific, false text (hallucination). ground answers in retrieved sources and ask for citations you can check. knowledge cutoff: the model knows nothing after its training data. current facts must come from your data or tools. instructions in data: the model cannot reliably tell your instructions from instructions hidden in a document it reads.

calling a model (anthropic python sdk) # pip install anthropic — credentials from anthropic_api_key import anthropic client = anthropic.anthropic() resp = client.messages.create( model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=16000, system="you summarise customer reviews for the shop's buyers. quote the review ids you rely on.", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": reviews_text}], ) if resp.stop_reason == "refusal": handle_refusal(resp) # check before reading content for block in resp.content: if block.type == "text": print(block.text) print(resp.usage.input_tokens, resp.usage.output_tokens) # log every call's cost other current ids: claude-sonnet-5-5 (faster, cheaper) and claude-haiku-5-5 (cheapest, for bulk work). long outputs should stream. on vertex ai use anthropicvertex(project_id=…, region=…) with the same calls.

structured output, not string parsing from pydantic import basemodel class productmention(basemodel): name: str sku: str | none store: str | none quantity: int | none class extraction(basemodel): products: list[productmention] resp = client.messages.parse( model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=16000, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": f"extract every product mentioned:\n\n{text}"}], output_format=extraction, ) result: extraction = resp.parsed_output # validated against the schema the schema guarantees shape, not truth. still check values against your data: does that order exist in your data?

c.h: Tools: let the model call your code
c.x: tools: let the model call your code from anthropic import beta_tool @beta_tool def search_orders(query: str, store: str | none = none) -> str: """search the shop's orders. returns up to 10 results as json. args: query: full-text search terms. store: optional store code, e.g. "1_05". """ return json.dumps(index.search(query, store=store, limit=10)) runner = client.beta.messages.tool_runner( model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=16000, tools=[search_orders], messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "find recent orders for umbrellas in store 1_05."}], ) for message in runner: # the sdk runs the call → tool → call loop print(message) give tools the least privilege that works: read-only by default, writes behind human approval. mcp is the open protocol for exposing tools and data to any compatible client.

rag: retrieval-augmented generation step what you build where it goes wrong 1 ingest pipeline that loads documents with ids, dates and source stale or duplicate documents; no way to tell which version was used 2 chunk split into passages (by section or ~500–1,000 tokens with overlap) chunks cut through the sentence that answers the question 3 embed vector per chunk; store with metadata query and documents embedded with different models 4 retrieve vector search plus keyword search (hybrid), filtered by metadata exact names and citations missed by vectors alone 5 rerank score the top 50 and keep the best 5–10 irrelevant passages crowd out the right one 6 generate prompt with the passages, ask for citations to their ids model answers from memory when retrieval found nothing; say "not found" instead 7 evaluate measure retrieval (did the right chunk come back?) and answers separately only judging the final answer hides which step failed

vector search: postgres & bigquery -- pgvector create extension if not exists vector; create table chunks (id bigserial primary key, doc_id text, body text, embedding vector(768)); create index on chunks using hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops); select id, doc_id, 1 - (embedding <=> $1) as similarity from chunks where doc_id like 'hp%' -- hnsw filters after the index scan: can return fewer rows (pgvector 0.8+ iterative scans help) order by embedding <=> $1 limit 10; -- <=> cosine distance -- bigquery: embed with a remote model, then search create or replace table `p.ai.chunk_emb` as select * from ml.generate_embedding( model `p.ai.embedding_model`, (select id, body as content from `p.ai.chunks`)); select base.id, distance from vector_search( table `p.ai.chunk_emb`, 'ml_generate_embedding_result', (select ml_generate_embedding_result from ml.generate_embedding( model `p.ai.embedding_model`, (select 'land acquisition compensation' as content))), top_k => 10, distance_type => 'cosine');

c.h: Evals: how you know it works
c.x: evals: how you know it works build a test set of 50–200 real inputs with expected outputs or grading notes. include the hard and adversarial cases. grade with code first: exact match, schema valid, cited id exists, number within tolerance. model-as-judge for open-ended answers, with a written rubric, checked against human grades on a sample. run it in ci on every prompt, model or retrieval change, and track the score over time. hold out a test split you never tune against, so improvements are real. measure cost and latency beside quality; a 2% gain at 3× the cost may not be worth it.

security prompt injection: a web page, pdf or email the model reads can say "ignore your instructions". treat everything retrieved as untrusted data. limit the blast radius: tools get least privilege; destructive actions need human confirmation; the model never holds credentials directly. output is untrusted input: escape it before rendering, validate it before running it as sql or shell. data leakage: do not send secrets or personal data you are not allowed to process. check the provider's retention terms. log and audit prompts, tool calls and outputs (minus sensitive fields) so you can investigate.

cost & latency estimate first: (input + output tokens) × price × calls per day. log usage on every call. prompt caching: put the stable part (instructions, tool definitions, long reference text) first so repeated calls reuse it at a fraction of the price. batch api for work that can wait (bulk extraction overnight), at a lower price. right-size the model: measure whether a smaller model or lower effort holds quality on your eval before paying for the largest. trim context: retrieve 5 good passages, not 50 mediocre ones. stream long responses so users see progress, and set timeouts and retries with backoff.

working with ai coding assistants give context: the repo's conventions, the failing test, the exact error. vague asks get vague code. tests first: a test that fails before the change is the best spec and the best check. verify against docs: an assistant can invent a flag, method or version. check the official docs for anything external. review every line as you would a colleague's pr: error paths, edge cases, security. keep secrets out of prompts and pasted logs. small steps: one concern per change, so a wrong turn is cheap to undo. you own the result. "the ai wrote it" is not a review comment.

agents: when and when not start with one call. classification, extraction and summaries rarely need more. then a workflow: fixed steps in your code, a model call at each. predictable and testable. an agent (the model chooses tools in a loop) only when the steps cannot be known in advance, the value justifies the cost, and mistakes can be caught and undone. bound it: step and token budgets, timeouts, an approval gate on writes, and a full log of each tool call.

ai on google cloud vertex ai: hosted models (gemini, claude and others through model garden), endpoints, evaluation and pipelines in your gcp project and region. bigquery ml: call remote models from sql ( ml.generate_text , ml.generate_embedding ) and search with vector_search , without moving data out. data residency: pick the region deliberately; some models run only in global or specific regions. iam as usual: service accounts with vertex ai user, no api keys in code.

levels: what to expect 1 foundation call a model api and get structured output explain tokens, context, hallucination and prompt injection use an ai assistant with tests and review 2 practitioner build a rag feature with retrieval, citations and an eval set use tools and handle refusals, errors and cost brief an ai agent with context, rules and a definition of done 3 senior design ai features with evals, guardrails, observability and fallbacks tune cost and latency (caching, batch, model choice) set up repos so ai agents work safely (context files, hooks, gates) 4 expert set ai strategy, governance and security across the organisation design agentic systems and their safety boundaries build shared ai platforms, blueprints and evaluation infrastructure each level includes the ones before it. see start here for what the levels mean.

the core argument writing code was never the main cost; owning it is. every copy of generated boilerplate must be reviewed, secured, tested, upgraded, debugged and understood by the next person. generation makes the cheap part cheaper and multiplies the expensive part. a framework makes each decision once, tests it once, fixes it once, and upgrades everyone together. generate per project framework / blueprint time to first version minutes minutes, once the framework exists consistency each copy differs subtly (retries, logging, auth, errors) same behaviour everywhere fixing a bug or cve find and patch n copies; some get missed patch once, release, bump versions review burden hundreds of generated lines per pr only the business-specific part security each copy may reintroduce a known hole secure defaults, tested once upgrades (java, spring, providers) n separate migrations one migration in the framework, then a version bump onboarding every repo is a new dialect learn the framework once knowledge decisions live in prompts nobody kept decisions in versioned, reviewed code and docs ai output quality model guesses your conventions from public code model extends your framework; smaller, consistent output total cost over 2 years grows with every copy mostly fixed, shared

c.h: A cost model in one line
c.x: a cost model in one line generated: n copies × (review + security fix + upgrade + drift) per year framework: build once + maintain once + n × (small version bump) with n = 15 services, 3 framework-level fixes a year, ~1 day each: generated: 15 × 3 = 45 fix-days, plus drift framework: 1 × 3 = 3 fix-days + 15 version bumps (automatable) the numbers are illustrative; the shape is the point. the gap grows with every new copy and every year.

c.h: When generation is the right call
c.x: when generation is the right call one-off scripts and investigations you will delete. prototypes and spikes to learn whether an idea works. filling a framework's slots: the business logic, the new query, its tests. codemods: ai-written scripts that apply the same change across many repos (an upgrade, a rename), reviewed once. tests and documentation for code that follows the framework. before the third repetition: the first two times, write or generate it directly; you do not yet know what to abstract.

c.h: When not to build a framework
c.x: when not to build a framework rule of three: abstract after three real uses, not one imagined future. inner-platform effect: a framework so configurable it becomes a worse version of the language or tool it wraps. business logic in shared libraries: forces lock-step releases between teams. share infrastructure concerns, not domain rules. no owner: a framework without a maintaining team decays faster than copies. escape hatches missing: teams need a supported way to do the unusual thing without forking.

c.h: What a blueprint looks like in this stack
c.x: what a blueprint looks like in this stack area blueprint what it decides once services service template + internal spring boot starter or quarkus extension logging format, tracing, health checks, error responses, security config, dockerfile jobs a job library + terraform module for a cloud run job run records, exit codes, counters, retries, iam, scheduling data dbt macros, generic tests, packages, project template layer conventions, key computation, date parsing that rejects, test baseline infrastructure terraform modules (bucket, dataset, job, service) encryption, labels, iam, deletion protection, naming delivery harness or github actions templates; reusable workflows build once, scan, deploy by artefact, approvals, rollback apis apigee shared flows; openapi style guide and linting auth, rate limits, error format, versioning observability dashboard and alert templates; opentelemetry config golden signals, slo alerts, runbook links ai repo context files (claude.md), skills, hooks, an mcp server template, eval harness how agents work in the repo, which checks run, what "done" means

c.h: Using AI to build the framework
c.x: using ai to build the framework collect the 3+ existing implementations; ask ai to list what they share and where they differ. decide the framework's api and its escape hatches yourself; that is the design work. let ai draft the framework code, tests and documentation against that design. review it like any critical library; add contract tests. let ai write codemods that migrate each existing project onto it, one pr per repo. point every repo's ai context file at the framework, so future work extends it instead of reinventing it.

keeping a framework healthy an owning team with a roadmap, changelog and support channel. semantic versioning ; breaking changes rare, announced, with migration guides and codemods. automated upgrades (renovate or dependabot) open version bumps in every consumer. golden path, not a cage: the easy way is the right way, and the unusual way is possible. scorecards (e.g. in a backstage catalogue) show which services are on current versions. measure adoption and time to first deploy for new services.

decision guide will this exist in more than one place for more than a few months? → blueprint . does it carry security, compliance or reliability rules? → blueprint , even for two uses. is it unique business logic? → write it (with ai help) inside the blueprint's slots. is it throwaway or exploratory? → generate , and delete it afterwards. is it the same change across many repos? → ai-written codemod , reviewed once. ai is the bulldozer; the framework is the road. build the road once and drive on it, rather than bulldozing a new track for every trip.

where claude code runs surface use it for terminal cli ( claude ) interactive work in a local repository ide extensions (vs code, jetbrains) the same agent beside your editor, with diffs inline desktop app local and cloud sessions with a graphical interface claude code on the web cloud sessions in a managed container: work continues without your laptop headless ( claude -p ) scripts and ci: one prompt in, result out (text or json) github actions ( claude-code-action ) respond to issues and prs, e.g. a label that asks claude to build a task agent sdk claude code's harness as a library inside your own application

everyday commands claude # start in the current repo claude "fix the failing date parser test" claude -c # continue the last conversation claude -r # pick an earlier session to resume claude -p "summarise this diff" --output-format json < diff.txt # headless # inside a session /init create a claude.md for this repo /memory edit memory files /agents manage subagents /mcp mcp servers and their status /permissions view rules /compact summarise the conversation to free context /clear start fresh shift+tab cycle permission modes (incl. plan mode) esc interrupt

the files that shape it file holds claude.md (repo root, subfolders) project memory: what the system is, rules, commands, traps. loaded every session. ~/.claude/claude.md your personal preferences across projects .claude/settings.json shared permissions, hooks, environment, model settings (committed) .claude/settings.local.json your local overrides (not committed) .claude/agents/*.md subagents: specialised helpers with their own prompt, tools and model .claude/skills/<name>/skill.md skills: packaged procedures invoked by name or when relevant .claude/commands/*.md custom slash commands .mcp.json mcp servers shared with the team these files are the blueprint for how agents work in your repo. keep them short, specific and current; a stale rule misleads every session.

permissions and hooks // .claude/settings.json { "permissions": { "allow": ["bash(./gradlew test:*)", "bash(git status)", "bash(git diff:*)"], "deny": ["read(./.env)", "bash(rm -rf:*)"] }, "hooks": { "pretooluse": [ { "matcher": "bash", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": ".claude/hooks/guard-destructive.sh" }] } ], "posttooluse": [ { "matcher": "edit|write", "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": ".claude/hooks/check-edited-file.sh" }] } ], "stop": [ { "hooks": [{ "type": "command", "command": ".claude/hooks/stop-gate.sh" }] } ] } } permission modes: default (ask), accept edits, plan (read and propose only), and fully autonomous modes for sandboxed environments. hooks run your scripts at events (before/after a tool, on prompt submit, at stop, at session start). a hook that exits with code 2 blocks the action where the event allows it (pretooluse blocks the tool call, stop prevents stopping) and its stderr is fed back to claude. a posttooluse hook runs after the tool, so exit code 2 only feeds stderr back. use hooks for rules that must always hold (lint after every edit, block pushes to main ); use claude.md for guidance.

subagents and skills <!-- simplified example of .claude/agents/reviewer.md --> --- name: reviewer description: independent reviewer of a finished diff before a pr is opened. use at the end of every task. tools: read, grep, glob, bash model: sonnet --- review the diff against the task, claude.md and the official docs of every library it touches. report bugs, missing tests and unverified api use. do not edit files. <!-- simplified example of .claude/skills/<name>/skill.md --> --- name: release-sync description: bring a project page up to date with that project's latest release. use after a release or when a sync issue is open. --- 1. read the release tag and changelog. 2. update the version markers and the "what's new" block. 3. run the release checker until it reports 0 findings. subagents keep their own context, so a reviewer is not anchored on the builder's reasoning. skills turn a procedure that cost a debugging cycle into something every session follows.

c.h: A worked example: an autonomous build loop
c.x: a worked example: an autonomous build loop /new-issue turns an idea into a ready issue. /build-task builds it: verify docs, write a failing test, implement. hooks check every edit; a stop hook runs the full check before the turn can end. a reviewer subagent checks the finished diff independently. fix what it finds, at most three attempts , then write a blocker summary instead of looping. /compound turns what went wrong into a permanent guard (a test, hook or rule). open a pr; a human (or a gated merge skill) merges. each step is a skill, agent or hook committed to the repository, so every session follows the same loop.

claude cowork cowork applies claude's agentic loop to everyday knowledge work rather than code: it works through multi-step tasks on your files, documents and connected apps from the claude desktop app, and checks in with you as it goes. claude code claude cowork main users engineers anyone doing knowledge work: analysts, operations, legal, sales, founders works on repositories: code, tests, builds, git folders, documents, spreadsheets, presentations, connected apps extended by claude.md, skills, subagents, hooks, mcp, plugins skills, plugins and connectors (mcp), often packaged per role typical tasks implement a feature, fix a bug, review a pr, run a migration prepare a report from files, reconcile spreadsheets, draft documents, run a recurring brief plugins bundle skills, commands, agents and connectors for a role or team, so the organisation's way of working is installed rather than re-explained. same rules as any agent: give it a clear brief and a definition of done, limit what it can access, and review what it produces before it is sent anywhere. features and availability change frequently; check anthropic's current product documentation.

working well with claude code plan first for anything non-trivial: plan mode, read the plan, then let it build. give it a way to check itself: exact test and lint commands in claude.md. one task per session; /clear between unrelated tasks to keep context clean. worktrees for parallel sessions, so they never edit the same checkout. verify claims: ask what it ran and what the output was; "done" means a green check you can see. turn every correction into a rule in claude.md, a skill or a hook.

one we build: persona persona is memory for ai coding agents: penstock keeps what was asked, decided, refused and learned as plain files you own and, when memory is on, hands them to the model before it writes. it works with claude code over mcp. the persona that speaks from it is planned. it is ours, so we are not neutral.

parts of a harness part does gets it wrong when loop send messages, run requested tools, return results, repeat until done no step or token budget: runaway cost tools functions the model can call (files, shell, search, apis, mcp) too many, vague descriptions, huge outputs, no error detail context management decide what the model sees: instructions, history, retrieved files; compact or clear old content context fills with noise and the model loses the thread memory persist knowledge across sessions (project files, notes, memory tools) stale memory states things that are no longer true permissions and sandbox limit what tools may touch; ask a human for risky actions broad credentials; destructive commands unguarded gates and hooks deterministic checks that run regardless of the model (lint, tests, policy) the agent decides on its own when it is "done" sub-agents delegate research or review to fresh contexts hand-offs lose detail; reviewers anchored on the builder's view state and resume save progress so work survives restarts a crash loses hours of work observability log every model call, tool call, cost and decision nobody can say why the agent did something evaluation measure task success, cost and interventions on a test set changes judged by impression

build or use? option you own manual loop on the model api everything (code on the llms tab) sdk tool runner tools and hosting; the sdk runs the loop claude agent sdk prompt, options, hosting; claude code's harness and built-in tools come with it managed agents (hosted) agent configuration and your own tools; the provider runs loop and sandbox agent frameworks (e.g. langgraph) graph of steps and state; framework handles orchestration ready-made agents (claude code, cowork, copilot) configuration: context files, skills, hooks, connectors configure a ready-made harness before building one. build your own only when the task, tools or deployment need something they cannot give.

principles for a reliable harness done is decided by checks, not by the model: tests, linters, schema validation, a reviewer. bound everything: steps, tokens, time, money, attempts at the same failure (three, then stop and report). least privilege tools; human approval for anything irreversible or external. append-only history: do not rewrite past turns; summarise forward when context is full. fresh eyes for review: a separate agent or person who sees the code, not the builder's conclusions. make lessons permanent: each failure becomes a rule, test or hook in the repo. never let the agent weaken a gate (skip a test, disable a check) to get to green.

context engineering put stable things first (system prompt, tools) so they are cached and consistent. load just in time: give the agent tools to find files instead of pasting everything up front. keep tool outputs compact; return summaries with a way to fetch details. compact or clear old tool results in long sessions. use sub-agents to read widely and return only conclusions. write state to files (plans, progress notes) so a new context can pick up the work.

designing tools for agents few tools, each matching a task a person would do ("search orders", "run tests"), not every api endpoint. names and descriptions written for the model: what it does, when to use it, what it returns. typed inputs with enums and examples; strict schemas. errors that say what went wrong and how to fix it. distinguish "no results" from "could not search". read-only by default; writes need confirmation.

failure modes to design against runaway loops repeating the same failing action. context rot: long sessions where early instructions are drowned out. false completion: claiming success without running the check. gaming the check: editing tests or disabling guards to pass. prompt injection from files, web pages or tool outputs. scope creep: changing more than the task asked. credential misuse: acting with more access than the task needs.

measuring a harness task success rate on a fixed set of real tasks, judged by checks. cost and time per completed task , not per request. intervention rate: how often a human had to step in. regression rate: changes that later had to be reverted. gate failures caught before merge vs after.

one we build: penstock penstock is a headless, self-hosted agent harness: it runs agents from ci, slack or webhooks on copilot, anthropic, openai or a local ollama model, and with database storage it logs every model call and tool call. it is open source (apache 2.0). run together with cistern, the two are headworks . it is ours, so we are not neutral: compare it with the other harnesses on this page.

the shape of it need on github in your google cloud project a place to work codespaces cloud workstations: managed development environments from a container image you define, in the browser or your own ide run an agent task an actions job a cloud run job: a container that runs to completion, with its own service account, timeout and retries start it issue, comment, schedule cloud scheduler, pub/sub messages, eventarc events, or a workflow several steps and a human approval workflow jobs and environments workflows, which can run steps in order, wait, and call your services secrets repository secrets secret manager, with iam on each secret and audit logs of every access build and test actions cloud build a live preview a preview deployment a cloud run revision with no traffic and its own tagged url the model copilot, or a key in a secret vertex ai (google's models and partner models in model garden), or any provider with its key in secret manager git stays: the history of the code still lives in a git repository, wherever you host it. what moves is where the agent runs, what it can reach, and who can see what it did.

why run it yourself your data stays in your project and region. useful when code or data may not leave a country or a company. one identity model. the agent is a service account with exactly the iam roles it needs, like any other workload. one audit trail. cloud audit logs record what the agent touched, next to everything else in the project. your choice of model, including models you are allowed to use under your own agreements. the trade-off: you build and run the plumbing that a hosted service gives you for free. start small.

a shared workspace, replit style # a workspace image you control, in your project gcloud workstations configs create agent-ws \ --cluster=dev --region=europe-west2 \ --machine-type=e2-standard-4 \ --container-custom-image=europe-west2-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/tools/agent-ws:1 \ --service-account=agent-ws@my-proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com \ --idle-timeout=3600 \ --disable-public-ip-addresses gcloud workstations create alice \ --config=agent-ws --cluster=dev --region=europe-west2 gcloud workstations start alice \ --config=agent-ws --cluster=dev --region=europe-west2 bake the agent's tools (cli, language runtimes, test tools) into the image, so every workspace and every agent run starts the same. --idle-timeout is in seconds and stops idle workspaces, which saves money.

c.h: An agent task as a Cloud Run job
c.x: an agent task as a cloud run job gcloud run jobs create agent-task \ --image=europe-west2-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/agents/runner:1 \ --region=europe-west2 \ --service-account=agent-runner@my-proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com \ --set-secrets=model_api_key=model-api-key:latest \ --task-timeout=30m --max-retries=0 # run one task and wait for the result gcloud run jobs execute agent-task --region=europe-west2 \ --update-env-vars=task="add tests for the date parser" --wait # or on a schedule, calling the cloud run api gcloud scheduler jobs create http nightly-triage \ --location=europe-west2 --schedule="0 6 * * 1-5" \ --uri="https://run.googleapis.com/v2/projects/my-proj/locations/europe-west2/jobs/agent-task:run" \ --http-method=post \ --oauth-service-account-email=scheduler@my-proj.iam.gserviceaccount.com one container, one task, a hard timeout, and no automatic retries for work that changes things: an agent that failed halfway should be looked at, not rerun blindly.

preview what the agent built # deploy the agent's branch with no traffic, at its own url gcloud run deploy web --image=…/web:agent-1234 \ --region=europe-west2 --no-traffic --tag=agent-1234 # open https://agent-1234---web-xxxxx.a.run.app, then # move traffic only after a person has looked this is the "see it running" moment that makes replit-style tools feel good, with the same blue-green and canary steps as any release (see devops ).

c.h: Guard rails, before the first run
c.x: guard rails, before the first run a service account per agent, with only the roles its task needs. no owner or editor roles, ever. no direct path to production. the agent proposes (a branch, a preview, a plan); a person approves the merge or the deploy. secrets from secret manager at run time, never in the image, the prompt or the repository. limit the network: private workspaces ( --disable-public-ip-addresses ), egress only to what the agent needs, and vpc service controls around sensitive data. budgets and alerts on the project, and timeouts on every job, so a runaway loop costs minutes, not a month. log every step the agent takes with a run id, so a person can follow the journey and undo it if needed (see observability ). evaluate the agent on real tasks before trusting it with more (see agent harness ). one open-source option for the agent runtime itself is penstock , our headless, self-hosted harness, which runs agents from ci, slack or webhooks and can run as a container like the job above. it is ours, so we are not neutral.

architecture phase steps runs ingestion (offline) load documents → parse (pdf, html, ocr) → clean → chunk → add metadata → embed → index (vector + keyword) as a pipeline: batch or on change retrieval (online) query → rewrite (optional) → hybrid search with permission and metadata filters → rerank → top passages per question, in milliseconds generation (online) prompt with passages and ids → model answers with citations → validate citations → respond, or say "not found" per question, in seconds evaluation (continuous) golden questions → retrieval metrics + answer metrics → dashboard and ci gate on every change, and sampled in production

ingestion and parsing keep a stable document id, source, version and date on everything, so each answer can name exactly what it used. parse structure, not just text: headings, paragraphs and numbered sections are the best chunk boundaries. tables need special handling. scanned pdfs need ocr (document ai, tesseract); measure its error rate on your documents. clean: strip headers, footers, page numbers and boilerplate that pollute retrieval. run ingestion as an idempotent, incremental pipeline with run records: documents in = chunks indexed + rejected. handle updates and deletions: re-embed changed documents, remove withdrawn ones, and never serve a stale version silently.

chunking strategy how notes fixed size n tokens with overlap simple baseline; cuts through sentences recursive split by section, then paragraph, then sentence until small enough good default for prose structural one chunk per section or numbered paragraph best for legal and technical documents with structure parent-child retrieve small chunks, give the model their larger parent section precise search, enough context to answer contextual prepend a short summary of where the chunk sits in its document before embedding reduces retrieval failures for chunks that make no sense alone typical sizes are 200–1,000 tokens. measure: the right size is the one that maximises retrieval recall on your golden questions.

embeddings and indexes embedding model: choose by quality on your domain and language, dimension (storage and speed), and cost. options include vertex ai text embeddings and other providers' embedding apis, or open models. same model for documents and queries, and re-embed everything when you change it. store the model name and version with each vector. distance: cosine is the usual choice; normalise vectors if the model expects it. approximate indexes (hnsw, ivf) trade a little recall for speed. tune and measure recall against exact search on a sample. where to store: pgvector (postgres, alloydb), bigquery vector_search , vertex ai vector search, elasticsearch/opensearch. keep vectors next to the metadata you filter on.

hybrid search with rank fusion (postgres) -- chunks(id, doc_id, body, tsv tsvector, embedding vector(768), store text) with vec as ( select id, row_number() over (order by embedding <=> $1) as r from chunks where store = any($3) -- filter first: permissions, metadata order by embedding <=> $1 limit 50 ), kw as ( select id, row_number() over (order by ts_rank_cd(tsv, q) desc) as r from chunks, websearch_to_tsquery('english', $2) as q where tsv @@ q and store = any($3) order by ts_rank_cd(tsv, q) desc limit 50 ) select id, sum(1.0 / (60 + r)) as score -- reciprocal rank fusion, k = 60 from (select * from vec union all select * from kw) as both_lists group by id order by score desc limit 20; -- then rerank these 20 vectors find meaning ("money back for a parcel that never came"); keywords find exact names, citations and section numbers that vectors miss. fusion combines both without tuning score scales.

reranking and query handling rerank the top 20–50 with a cross-encoder or reranking api (for example vertex ai ranking, or a provider's rerank model); keep the best 5–10. query rewriting: turn a conversational follow-up into a standalone query ("and last year?" → full question). multi-query: generate a few phrasings and fuse their results. metadata extraction: pull filters out of the question (store, year) and apply them in sql. agentic retrieval: let the model call a search tool several times when one search is not enough, with a step budget.

generation with citations import anthropic client = anthropic.anthropic() passages = retrieve(question, stores=user.allowed_stores) # hybrid + rerank, top 8 content = [ {"type": "document", "source": {"type": "text", "media_type": "text/plain", "data": p.body}, "title": f"{p.title} ¶{p.paragraph} ({p.doc_id})", "citations": {"enabled": true}} for p in passages ] content.append({"type": "text", "text": "answer only from the documents above. if they do not contain the answer, " "say you could not find it. question: " + question}) resp = client.messages.create(model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=16000, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": content}]) # text blocks carry a citations list pointing at the exact cited text in each document put instructions in the system prompt; treat retrieved text as data, never as instructions. check that every cited document was actually retrieved; drop or flag answers with no citations. when retrieval returns nothing relevant, answer "not found". when the index is unavailable, say so: that is "cannot see", not "nothing exists".

rag on bigquery -- 1. embed chunks with a remote embedding model create or replace table `p.rag.chunk_emb` as select * from ml.generate_embedding( model `p.rag.embedding_model`, (select chunk_id, doc_id, store, body as content from `p.rag.chunks`)); -- 2. optional vector index for large tables create vector index chunk_idx on `p.rag.chunk_emb`(ml_generate_embedding_result) options (index_type = 'ivf', distance_type = 'cosine'); -- 3. search select base.chunk_id, base.doc_id, base.content, distance from vector_search( (select * from `p.rag.chunk_emb` where store in ('1_05', '4_12')), 'ml_generate_embedding_result', (select ml_generate_embedding_result from ml.generate_embedding( model `p.rag.embedding_model`, (select 'compensation for land acquisition' as content))), top_k => 20, distance_type => 'cosine'); good for batch rag and analytics over large corpora. for interactive latency, serve from postgres/alloydb or vertex ai vector search.

evaluating rag measure question it answers recall@k is the right passage in the top k results? mrr how high is the first right passage? faithfulness is every claim supported by the retrieved passages? answer correctness does it match the expected answer? citation accuracy do citations point to passages that support the sentence? abstention does it say "not found" when the corpus has no answer? build 100–300 real questions with the passages that answer them, including unanswerable ones. evaluate retrieval and generation separately, so you know which step to fix. run in ci on every change to chunking, embeddings, prompts or models.

security and access control filter by permission at retrieval time. never retrieve documents the user may not see and hope the model ignores them. prompt injection: documents can contain instructions. keep tools read-only, constrain outputs, and do not let retrieved text trigger actions. legal holds and erasure requests apply to the index too: remove or filter those documents immediately. personal data: decide what may be embedded and sent to a model; embeddings can leak content. audit: log the question, retrieved ids and answer (with sensitive fields protected).

failure modes and fixes symptom likely cause right document exists, never retrieved chunking splits the answer; missing keyword search; embedding model weak for the domain retrieved, but answer wrong too many passages, noisy context, prompt does not demand grounding exact citation or section number missed vector-only search; add keyword or exact-match lookup old version quoted re-ingestion not incremental; no version filter slow no ann index, reranking too many, large context confident answer with no source no abstention instruction or citation validation

what mcp is without mcp, every ai application needs custom integration code for every tool. with mcp, a tool or data source is wrapped once as an mcp server , and any mcp-capable client (claude code, claude apps, ides, your own agent) can use it. think of it as a standard port between models and systems. concept meaning host / client the ai application and its connection to a server server a program exposing capabilities over mcp tools functions the model can call (query a table, check a pipeline run) resources read-only data the application can load into context (a file, a run record) prompts reusable prompt templates the server offers transport: stdio server runs as a local process; messages over stdin/stdout transport: streamable http server runs remotely over http; authorisation with oauth

a server in python (mcpserver) # pip install "mcp[cli]" google-cloud-bigquery (mcp 2.x) from mcp.server import mcpserver from google.cloud import bigquery mcp = mcpserver("pipeline-status") bq = bigquery.client() @mcp.tool() def latest_runs(run_date: str) -> list[dict]: """latest state of every pipeline stage for a run date (yyyy-mm-dd).""" sql = """select stage, state, objects_examined, objects_failed, event_ts from `my-proj.ops.v_job_run_latest` where run_date = @d order by stage""" cfg = bigquery.queryjobconfig(query_parameters=[ bigquery.scalarqueryparameter("d", "date", run_date)]) return [dict(r) for r in bq.query(sql, job_config=cfg).result()] @mcp.resource("ledger://{run_date}") def ledger(run_date: str) -> str: """the full event history for a run date, as text.""" return format_events(read_events(run_date)) if __name__ == "__main__": mcp.run() # stdio by default # mcp.run(transport="streamable-http") # to serve over http the function name, type hints and docstring become the tool's name, schema and description. write the docstring for the model: what it does, inputs, and what it returns. a typescript sdk exists with the same concepts. in mcp 1.x the same class was fastmcp , imported from mcp.server.fastmcp ; that import fails on 2.x.

c.h: Add it to Claude Code and test it
c.x: add it to claude code and test it # local stdio server, shared with the team via .mcp.json in the repo claude mcp add --scope project pipeline-status -- python mcp/pipeline_status.py # remote server over http claude mcp add --transport http pipeline-status https://mcp.example.com/mcp claude mcp list # inside claude code: /mcp shows servers, status and tools # interactive testing without a model npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector python mcp/pipeline_status.py project scope writes .mcp.json , so everyone on the repo gets the same server. keep credentials out of .mcp.json ; servers read application default credentials or environment variables. approve which tools may run without asking in claude code's permission settings.

c.h: Call MCP servers from the API
c.x: call mcp servers from the api resp = client.beta.messages.create( model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=16000, betas=["mcp-client-2025-11-20"], mcp_servers=[{"type": "url", "name": "pipeline", "url": "https://mcp.example.com/mcp"}], tools=[{"type": "mcp_toolset", "mcp_server_name": "pipeline"}], messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "summarise yesterday's pipeline run."}], ) the mcp connector needs both halves: the server in mcp_servers and a matching mcp_toolset in tools . it reaches remote (http) servers only; check the docs for authentication options and current beta name.

c.h: MCP and a data pipeline: four patterns
c.x: mcp and a data pipeline: four patterns pattern what the mcp server exposes who uses it rule 1. pipeline observability run records, stage states, freshness per source, failures with reasons engineers in claude code: "why did raw_load fail on 19-09?" read-only. reports unknown when it cannot read the ledger. 2. governed warehouse access table catalog, schemas, a guarded query tool analysts and engineers asking questions in natural language dry-run first, byte cap, allow-listed datasets, read-only service account 3. data catalog and lineage table descriptions, owners, upstream and downstream models (dbt manifest, dataplex) anyone changing a model: "what breaks if i rename this column?" generated from the source of truth, never hand-maintained 4. llm step inside the pipeline reference data or lookups the model needs while extracting or classifying a pipeline job calling a model (e.g. extracting product names from support tickets) prefer plain tool calls or batch jobs; validate outputs; never let the model write to production tables directly mcp sits beside the pipeline, not inside its critical path. the pipeline must run, record and alert without any ai involved; mcp makes it easier to ask questions about it.

a guarded bigquery query tool allowed = {"analytics", "mart", "ops"} max_bytes = 5 * 1024**3 # 5 gib per query @mcp.tool() def run_query(sql: str) -> dict: """run a read-only googlesql select over the analytics, mart and ops datasets. returns at most 200 rows. fails if the query would scan more than 5 gib.""" if not sql.lstrip().lower().startswith(("select", "with")): return {"error": "only select queries are allowed"} dry = bq.query(sql, job_config=bigquery.queryjobconfig( dry_run=true, use_query_cache=false)) datasets = {t.dataset_id for t in dry.referenced_tables} if not datasets <= allowed: return {"error": f"datasets not allowed: {sorted(datasets - allowed)}"} if dry.total_bytes_processed > max_bytes: return {"error": f"would scan {dry.total_bytes_processed/1e9:.1f} gb; add filters"} job = bq.query(sql, job_config=bigquery.queryjobconfig(maximum_bytes_billed=max_bytes)) rows = [dict(r) for r in job.result(max_results=200)] return {"rows": rows, "bytes_processed": job.total_bytes_processed} the real protection is the service account: give it only dataviewer on those datasets and jobuser . the string checks are a convenience, not a security boundary.

deploying a remote mcp server serve with streamable http and run it on cloud run with its own service account. require authentication: oauth for user-facing clients (the mcp authorisation spec builds on oauth 2.1), or cloud run iam for internal callers. rate-limit and log every tool call with the caller's identity. version tools like an api: add new ones rather than changing behaviour under the same name. ready-made servers exist for many systems, for example google's mcp toolbox for databases (bigquery, postgres and others). review what they expose before connecting them.

designing good mcp tools few, task-shaped tools ("pipeline status for a date") beat many thin wrappers over every api call. clear names and descriptions : the model chooses tools from them. typed, validated inputs with enums and formats where possible. compact outputs: summarise and paginate; huge results waste context. honest errors: return what failed and how to fix it; distinguish "no data" from "could not read". read-only by default; any write needs explicit human approval in the client.

security an mcp server runs with its own credentials: give it least privilege, as you would a service. only install servers you trust and have reviewed; a malicious server can return instructions that steer the model (tool poisoning). treat tool outputs as untrusted data in the model's context. never put secrets in tool descriptions, outputs or .mcp.json . audit tool calls; alert on unusual volume or failed authorisation.
ones we build cistern puts an mcp server in front of a data pod you own, and penstock works with claude code over mcp. both are open source (apache 2.0). they are ours, so we are not neutral.
