web3 building blocks blockchain: a replicated, append-only ledger agreed by consensus (proof of stake on ethereum), without a central operator. wallet and keys: a private key controls an account; whoever holds the key controls the assets. lost key, lost assets. smart contract: a program deployed on the chain (solidity on ethereum), public, and immutable unless designed to be upgradeable. tokens: fungible (erc-20) and non-fungible (erc-721 nfts) assets defined by contracts. gas: fees paid for computation and storage on chain. layer 2 rollups: process transactions off the main chain and post proofs to it, for lower fees. oracles: bring outside data on chain, a trust point in themselves. decentralised storage: ipfs and similar address content by its hash. defi and daos: financial services and organisations governed by contracts and token votes.

a minimal smart contract // spdx-license-identifier: mit pragma solidity ^ 0.8.24 ; /// records a document hash and who registered it, once. contract documentregistry { mapping(bytes32 => address) public registeredby; event registered(bytes32 indexed dochash, address indexed by); function register(bytes32 dochash) external { require(registeredby[dochash] == address(0), "already registered"); registeredby[dochash] = msg.sender; emit registered(dochash, msg.sender); } } tooling: foundry or hardhat to build and test, ethers.js or viem to call contracts, a testnet before mainnet, and an external audit before holding real value. deployed bugs are public and often permanent.

do you need a blockchain? do several parties need to write to shared data? do they not trust each other, or any single operator? is there no acceptable trusted intermediary (a database run by a neutral party, a regulator)? is public, permanent, tamper-evident history worth the cost, latency and loss of privacy? if any answer is no, a conventional database, an append-only ledger table, signed records or a timestamping service is simpler, cheaper and easier to correct. also weigh regulation: rules for crypto assets differ by country and change often (india, for example, taxes crypto transfers and has evolving rules). personal data on an immutable public chain conflicts with deletion rights.

c.h: The Semantic Web and linked data
c.x: the semantic web and linked data rdf: data as triples (subject, predicate, object), each named by a uri, so data from different sources joins up. vocabularies and ontologies: shared meanings (schema.org, dublin core, foaf; owl for formal ontologies). formats: turtle, json-ld (linked data in ordinary json), rdf/xml. sparql: the query language for rdf data and knowledge graphs. knowledge graphs: entities and relationships, used in search, ai grounding and data integration. for product data: schema.org's product type, with identifiers such as sku and gtin codes ( gtin13 ), gives items stable, linkable identities across shops. <!-- json-ld with schema.org, embedded in a web page --> <script type="application/ld+json"> { "@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": "product", "name": "folding umbrella", "sku": "umb-001", "offers": { "@type": "offer", "price": "12.99", "pricecurrency": "gbp" } } </script> # sparql: products in a given category, newest first prefix ex: <https://example.org/shop#> select ?p ?date where { ?p ex:incategory <https://example.org/category/umbrellas> ; ex:listedon ?date . } order by desc(?date)

how solid works piece is pod a personal data store on a solid server, self-hosted or from a provider; organisations can run pods for their users webid a uri that identifies a person or agent, pointing to a profile document solid-oidc authentication built on openid connect: the user logs in with their identity provider; apps act on their behalf access control web access control (wac) or access control policies (acp): who may read, write, append or control each resource resources files and containers in the pod, read and written over http (get, put, post, patch, delete) linked data structured data stored as rdf (often turtle) with shared vocabularies, so different apps understand the same data notifications apps can subscribe to changes in resources the key shift: apps and data are separated. a user can switch apps without losing data, and grant or revoke access per app or person.

data in a pod # a public profile document (turtle) @prefix foaf: <http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/> . @prefix solid: <http://www.w3.org/ns/solid/terms#> . <#me> a foaf:person ; foaf:name "asha rao" ; solid:oidcissuer <https://login.example-provider.com> . # read it over plain http curl -h "accept: text/turtle" https://asha.pod.example/profile/card # web access control: owner has full control of a folder @prefix acl: <http://www.w3.org/ns/auth/acl#> . <#owner> a acl:authorization ; acl:agent <https://asha.pod.example/profile/card#me> ; acl:accessto <./> ; acl:default <./> ; acl:mode acl:read, acl:write, acl:control .

c.h: An app reading from a Pod (JavaScript)
c.x: an app reading from a pod (javascript) import { login, handleincomingredirect, getdefaultsession, fetch } from "@inrupt/solid-client-authn-browser"; import { getsoliddataset, getthing, getstringnolocale } from "@inrupt/solid-client"; await handleincomingredirect(); if (!getdefaultsession().info.isloggedin) { await login({ oidcissuer: "https://login.example-provider.com", redirecturl: window.location.href, clientname: "order notes" }); } const profileurl = "https://asha.pod.example/profile/card"; const dataset = await getsoliddataset(profileurl, { fetch }); // authenticated fetch const me = getthing(dataset, profileurl + "#me"); const name = getstringnolocale(me, "http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/name"); libraries: inrupt's javascript client libraries, and others for java and python. servers: the open-source community solid server for development and research; commercial servers for production.

where it fits personal data that many services need: health records, education credentials, identity documents, preferences. public-sector data sharing with citizen consent; some governments are piloting or running solid-based services. portability: users switch apps without exporting and importing. consent you can audit: access is granted per resource and can be revoked. challenges: app ecosystem still small, linked-data skills are less common, querying across many pods is slower than a central database, and pod providers must be trusted to run storage well.

one we build: cistern cistern is a self-hostable data pod with an mcp server: every request from an ai agent is checked against your rules when it is made, never from a cache, and gets a receipt naming the rule that decided it. its readme describes it as an open solid pod server. it is open source (apache 2.0). it is ours, so we are not neutral: compare it with the other solid servers on this page.
